News.title: Two huge superyachts worth £410MILLION both belonging to US billionaire appear at UK harbour
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

SHIP AHOY Two huge superyachts worth £410MILLION both belonging to US billionaire appear at UK harbour

TWO major superyachts worth a combined £410m have moored up in a popular south coast harbour.

The fleet, which belongs to billionaire American video game developer Gabe Newell, is turning heads in Poole Harbour.



Leviathan and Draak are the latest superyachts to visit the Dorset harbour, renowned for hosting some of the world’s most expensive private boats.

Leviathan, which is 364ft long, was commissioned by Mr Newell and worked on by Dutch boat builders.



Work on the lavish boat began in 2020 and was completed last year.

On board there are 11 suites for up to 26 guests as well as accommodation for its 37 crew.



There is also a communal dining area for up to 54 people on the main deck.

Leisure facilities include a gaming lounge with 15 stations, two racing simulators, a gym, spa, sauna and jacuzzi and a basketball court.



There are also conference facilities on board.

The 5,000 tonne yacht, estimated to be worth a staggering £300million, is powered by a hybrid diesel-electric engine and has a maximum speed of 17 knots.

It is accompanied by Draak, also built by Oceanco, which is 300ft long and has an Oriental themed interior with bamboo, wenge and gold leaf.



The yacht’s facilities include a beach club, spa, gym, sauna, Turkish bath and a 20 square metre swimming pool with jets.

Mr Newell acquired it in 2023 and it is said to be worth £110million.

Poole has deep-water berths, top security and is relatively close to London.

It has also been awarded five gold anchors, the prestigious global marina accreditation scheme managed by The Yacht Harbour Association (TYHA).

Marinas are rated across categories such as ambience, customer service, on-water and onshore facilities and infrastructure.



The Poole Harbour Commissioners hope it will become the UK’s number one marine leisure location.

Earlier this month, the £220million new superyacht Milky Way, which has a 50 sqm swimming pool on board, moored in the harbour.

Poole Harbour is next to the millionaires‘ playground of Sandbanks.

News.title: Moment rookie Russian soldier accidentally fires RPG at his own FEET as trainer yells ‘are you a f***ing idiot?’
News.content:
THIS is the wild moment a rookie Russian fiend fires an RPG at his own feet as his commander screams “are you a f***ing idiot?”

Shocking footage shows the hapless soldier struggling to balance the gun on his shoulder – before it humiliatingly slides out of his grasp.



The wannabe warrior had difficulty even hoisting the deadly weapon off the ground.

For several seconds he fumbles with the anti-tank shooter, bending his neck awkwardly to fit it into his grasp.



While apparently trying to adjust his position, the RPG suddenly fires into the ground – setting off a small explosion and sending the foolish owner running.

In the background his trainer, who was filming the incident, screamed: “You f***ing idiot, move back! What, are you stupid?”

The f-bombs continued, with the man adding: “Have you gone crazy? Are you a f***ing idiot?”

It comes amid mounting pressure on Vladimir Putin’s war machine.

Ukrainian forces have repeatedly pummelled the nation’s equivalent of Amazon and are systemically blasting apart their fuel hubs.

For a third night in a row, Ukrainian drones have blitzed Ozon, Russia’s second-biggest online retailer, in an attempt to bleed Vladimir Putin‘s war chest dry.



Dramatic footage showed the warehouses engulfed in flames, with huge clouds of black smoke pouring from the sites.

Bombs have rained down on an area roughly the size of 42 football pitches and Volodymyr Zelensky tightens the screw.

Several were injured in the strikes – which coincided with Ukraine‘s independence day.

The national holiday was also marked by a visit from British prime minister Andy Burnham – the first trip abroad since taking office.

In a speech in Kyiv, Burnham vowed to stand with Ukraine “as long as it takes”.



He has promised to give the war-torn nation a blueprint to produce long-range missiles – as well as components to help build drones.

The PM said: “The friendship between our two countries will long outlast Russia’s illegal war.

“In both the fight and in the rebuilding to come, we will stand with Ukraine.

“And deliver opportunities for people across both our countries.

“Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve.



“We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace.”

News.title: Masked youths set off flares as balloons released in memory of joyrider dead after A66 wrong-way crash that killed cops
News.content:
MASKED youths set off flares and released balloons in memory of a joyrider killed in the horror A66 crash that also killed two cops.

The gathering took place on South Bank field near Middlesbrough and only a few hundred yards away from the crash site which claimed seven lives.



The shocking smash saw a Volkswagen Passat crash into a cop car while driving in the wrong direction, killing PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38.

The five young men in the Passat, who also died, were named as Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Cole Robert Worthy, 17, Jacob Matusiak, 23, and Makai Saddington, 18.



And tonight, the life of one of the joyriders was celebrated with flares, fireworks and a cavalcade of masked bikers.

What set out as a balloon release to commemorate Jakub Matusiak became a rowdy mob of around 200 people who lit up the sky with rockets and orange smoke.



It comes after:

A gang of around 20 masked youths on scooters, off-road bikes and quad bikes roared around a field in South Bank, near Middlesbrough, in honour of Matusiak, who himself had convictions for motoring offences.

At just after 5pm hundreds of orange balloons – chosen because it was his favourite colour – were released into the sky amid cheers from the crowd.

One female attendee in her 20s was indignant at the tone of the coverage of the deaths of the five youths and young men responsible for the deaths of PC Tom Clough and PC Matthew Blades.

She said: “Jakub was a lovely, caring lad and he’s somebody’s son and somebody’s brother, he’s not some scumbag who should just be written off and forgotten.



“It was an accident that those police officers died, they weren’t trying to kill anyone and they lost their own lives but they’ve just been written off as if they don’t matter.

“The number of people who have come out for Jakub today should show you that they do matter, they were loved and they will be missed.”

Cleveland Police attended but kept a low key presence, a patrol car from the Matrix team – which the two constables worked in – was parked 500 yards away alongside a police van.

Not all the residents of the surrounding streets chose to attend.

Looking at the police officers standing beside their vehicles, a 58-year-old grandmother said: “What must they be thinking right now? This is nothing but a mockery of the lives of those two policemen.



“I’ve watched them walking down there drinking and smoking weed and razzing about on their motorbikes. There’s nothing here to celebrate.”



The nearby St John the Evangelist Church opened its doors for people from the community to pay their respects, but was largely untroubled by visitors on their way to the field.

However Redcar’s Labour MP Anna Turley attended to pay her respects.

She said: “I thought it was really important to come together. I was really pleased that the church has opened themselves up for the community to come together, because it’s such a devastating incident.

“The whole community here is reeling, and we’ve lost lives, particularly those lives of brave police officers who are out in action to keep us safe. It’s a tragic incident.

Previous convictions of four occupants Cole Worthy Use threatening abusive language to cause harassment, alarm and distress on 27 October 2024 and pleaded guilty Failing to surrender to custody on 14 May 2025 and pleaded guilty Common assault of a police officer on 27 April 2025 and pleaded guilty Driving without a licence on 7 June 2026 and pleaded guilty Using a vehicle without insurance on 7 June 2026 and pleaded guilty Driving without reasonable consideration on 7 June 2026 and pleaded guilty Driving using a mobile phone on 7 June 2026b and pleaded guilty Jakub Matusiak Using a vehicle without insurance on 22 March 2026 and pleaded guilty Driving without a licence on 22 March 2026 and pleaded guilty Makai Saddington Possession of a controlled class C drug on 31 May 2025 and pleaded guilty Possession of a knife in a public place on 31 May 2025 and pleaded guilty 11 October 2025 three offences for assaulting a police officer and pleaded guilty Assaulted a police officer on 9 June 2026 and pleaded guilty Racially aggravated intentional harassment, alarm and distress on 9 June 2026 and pleaded guilty Theo Rae 12 shoplifting offences between 21 October 2023 and 4 May 2024 and pleaded guilty to all offences Three thefts from motor vehicle offences between 31 January 2024 and 25 September 2024 and pleaded guilty to all offences One theft of vehicle on 13 April 2024 and pleaded guilty Possession of cannabis on 22 April 2024 and pleaded guilty Aggravated vehicle taking on 16 May 2024 and pleaded guilty Aggravated vehicle taking 2 January 2025 and pleaded guilty Conviction of an offence while a youth rehabilitation order is in force on 26 February 2025 and pleaded guilty Assaulted a police officer on 30 April 2026 and pleaded guilty Michael Robert Cahill No convictions

“The whole community, I think, needed a space to come to express that grief, to pay a tribute, particularly to those officers, and have somewhere to think and reflect and try to come to terms with the terrible incident we’ve seen on the A66.



“There’s a reason the police were out that night – to keep us safe and to protect us. I know more information will come out over the coming days, as the IOPC continue their report, but I think it just highlights the gravity of some of the issues we’ve been facing in this area for some time now.

“It’s horrendous that two officers have lost their lives in the line of duty. We just want to take the time to reflect on their lives, pay tribute to them, give our thanks for their service and bravery.”

Earlier in the day, Cleveland Police revealed they were trying to stop the A66 joyriding gang in connection with the ramming of properties in the Middlesbrough area by an organised crime group.

As part of a “wide-scale investigation into the criminality which took place prior to the fatal crash” the force arrested 12 people.

They had received several reports of two vehicles being driven dangerously in the early hours of Saturday.



The first vehicle, which is believed to be a Volvo XC60, was witnessed to be ramming properties in the Middlesbrough area.

The second vehicle, a Volkswagen Passat, is believed to have been associated with the activities of the Volvo XC60.

COPS MAKE 12 ARRESTS Twelve people have been arrested on offences, including being involved with organised crime, by detectives investigating the lead-up to the A66 crash which killed two police officers. Two men, aged 24 and 19, were arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and possession of an offensive weapon, and are currently in police custody.

A woman, aged 30, was arrested on suspicion of assisting an offender and is in police custody.

A 35-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group and possession of an offensive weapon, and is in police custody.

A man, aged 21, was arrested on suspicion of participating in an organised crime group, possession of an offensive weapon and criminal damage. He has been remanded on recall to prison.

A 20-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of threats to cause criminal damage and public order, and is in police custody.

A woman, aged 61, was arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate and has been released on conditional bail.

A woman, aged 47, was arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs and possession of class C drugs, and has been released on conditional bail.

A 18-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs and possession of class C drugs. He has been released on unconditional bail.

A man, aged 39, was arrested on suspicion of possessing a firearm without a certificate, possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs and possession of class C drugs, and was released on conditional bail.

A 26-year-old man from Redcar has been charged with possession with intent to supply class A and class B drugs and possession of criminal property.

A man, aged 39, who was arrested on suspicion of threats to kill has been released on conditional bail.

Both vehicles were operating with cloned number plates to avoid detection but were picked up by the force’s automated number plate recognition technology.

The Volvo XC60 involved in the initial reports has been traced and recovered in Middlesbrough as part of the criminal investigation.

Throughout the course of the weekend Cleveland Police, supported by officers and staff from Durham, Northumbria and North Yorkshire Police, have worked to establish the circumstances which led to the fatal collision.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Nine men and three women, aged between 19 and 61 have been arrested on suspicion of offences ranging from possession of a firearm to participating in the activities of an organised crime group.

Cleveland police also say there is no evidence to indicate that filming of the activities that took place on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for the purposes of TikTok.

News.title: Can you resit GCSE exams in 2026? All you need to know as pass rate slumps to 7-year low
News.content:
THOUSANDS of pupils returned to school last Thursday to open their long-awaited GCSE results.

The proportion of entries getting at least a 4 or a C grade – considered a “standard pass” – has fallen to the same levels as 2019.

It slumped from 67.4% in 2025 to 67.3% this year – a drop of 0.1 percentage points.



In England, students who do not pass both English Language and Maths with at least a grade 4 are typically expected to retake the subject.



Students are able to resit GCSE English and Maths in the upcoming autumn term, with all boards scheduling the exams between November 3 and 9.

For English Language, Paper 1 will take place on the morning of November 3, 2026, and Paper 2 on the morning of November 5, 2026.

Maths resits are also scheduled at the beginning of November, with all three papers for Foundation and Higher taking place between November 4 and November 9 for AQA, Edexcel and OCR.



Although it is not compulsory, pupils wanting to resit any other GCSEs, including Science, English Literature and History, will have to wait until the summer exam period in May or June 2027.

The government says: “You’ll need to continue studying GCSE English, GCSE mathematics, or both if you’re on a 16 to 19 study programme and do not have a grade 4 or above in one or both of these subjects.

“You’re not required to resit the exam, but you can if you and your institution think you’re ready.”

If a pupil believes they may have received an unjustifiably low mark, or there has been a marking error, a school can apply for an Ofqual remark on behalf of the student.



However, appeals can become pricey, costing between £44 and £68 per paper depending on the exam board.

Reports in The Observer have suggested that thousands of kids may have to take their English Language GCSE again because of the examiner with around 39,000 pupils predicted to have achieved higher.

News.title: Mum-of-two killed after plane smashes into busy motorway and wipes out four cars during emergency landing
News.content:
‘FOREVER MISSED’ Mum-of-two killed after plane smashes into busy motorway and wipes out four cars during emergency landing

A DEVOTED mum has tragically died in a horror plane crash after being forced into an emergency landing on a busy motorway.

Alex Garneau was killed after the aircraft lost power to one of its engines and crashed into four vehicles when it landed in traffic.



Alex, a mum-of-two, was the only victim of the fatal accident despite there reportedly being two crew members and six other passengers on board.

The tragedy occurred on August 20 in Foothills Boulevard, Prince George, Canada.



The plane, a Beechcraft King Air 200, was scheduled to fly from Sturdee River airstrip to Prince George International Airport.

Jaime Pawliuk, a survivor of the crash on the ground, says he was driving to work when he saw the aircraft hurtling towards him.

He said: “All of a sudden it was on top of me.

“I was only able to make it just a little ways before the wing just sheared the entire top of my vehicle off and showered me with glass.”

Paramedics assessed 10 people following the crash, with two taken to hospital in a stable condition.

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada has taken over the investigation, police said.



A GoFundMe set up for Alex described her as a devoted “hockey mom” who was actively involved in her children’s lives.

The tribute added: “She was fiercely devoted to her family, she will be forever missed and remembered.”

The two fundraisers established for her family have together raised more than $70,000 in just a few days.



Organisers Laura Creighton and Katie Trottier said Alex was a loyal friend who always showed up when people needed her, making those around her feel like they belonged.

The money will be used to support Alex’s family with their immediate and long term needs.

A second appeal launched through the Junior Ducks Hockey Club described Alex as “so much more than a hockey mom” and a major part of their wider hockey family.

She regularly helped organise activities, supported young players and travelled with the team.

The club said Alex brought warmth to a room simply by being there and had given so much of herself to her family and the people around her.



It added: “We love you, Alex. You will never be forgotten.”

News.title: It’s time joyriding TikTok idiots are treated same as groomers & paedos – if social media giants won’t act, cops MUST
News.content:
ROSS CLARK It’s time joyriding TikTok idiots are treated same as groomers & paedos – if social media giants won’t act, cops MUST

WE have heard endlessly about the dangers of sexual exploitation faced by children on the internet.

The previous government even passed a law, the Online Safety Act, placing responsibility on the heads of tech companies, with punitive fines for those who fail to tackle the threat posed by predatory paedophiles grooming their victims, often by pretending to be children themselves.



The laws extend to videos and apps which encourage children to harm themselves.

Woe betide any tech firm which fails to take down dangerous content quickly.



But something seems to have slipped through the net: social media videos showing joyriders and motorcyclists showing off by wilfully breaking the speed limit on public roads.

The failure to tackle this material is causing the sort of carnage seen near Middlesbrough on Saturday morning when a car driving the wrong way down the A66 dual carriageway collided with a police car travelling in the opposite direction.

Five youths in the car, as well as two officers in the police car, Matthew Blades and Tom Clough, were killed.



It came just a few days after a similar incident in the Republic of Ireland, which also killed five youths in a car driven far above the speed limit.



It doesn’t take too much imagination to see how irresponsible behaviour can spread among easily-led young people who are out to impress others.

For some people, modern life seems to revolve around the search for followers and ‘likes’. In this case it is a pursuit which far too often leads to their death.



But why is this sort of material still so easy to post on social media and so easy for others to view?

Paedophiles in search of sexualised images of children are forced to delve into the dark corners of the internet, but I typed ‘speed’ and ‘driving’ into the search bar on TikTok and was immediately presented with dozens of videos showing illegal behaviour on the roads.

﻿

‘Nolimitspecs’ wants us to see how he weaves between lorries on a stretch of motorway, which appears to be in Britain.



Some might find it exhilarating, but he is just inches from death as he straddles the lanes.

‘Mercy’ shows himself driving fast at night, with the words “Being young driving fast cars is a feeling I never wanna get rid of.” ‘FastChase’ is riding a motorbike, weaving through impossibly narrow spaces through a series of tunnels.



It isn’t just men. ‘Zoe first time Mum’ has filmed herself rattling down a narrow country lane, bound between high hedges, at irresponsible speed, and captioned it “it this what it feels like when your [sic] about to die”.



It isn’t hard to work out what would happen if she finds herself faced with another vehicle – or another mother pushing a pram.



I went onto YouTube and found much the same: videos showing irresponsible driving.

Many have been filmed, or claim to have been filmed, on German autobahn, stretches of which have no speed limit.

They are, therefore, not necessarily breaking the law simply by speeding, except that they then show cars weaving between lanes in a way which must surely be illegal, even in Germany.



Some, though, quite clearly are in Britain. In one video, a driver films his speedometer as he reaches 201 mph in an Audi on the motorway.



It is hardly as if YouTube has had chance to take it down: it says it was posted 6 years ago and has clocked up 896,000 views.



If social media companies won’t act, surely the police should be doing so. The identity of the driver must be easy enough to trace, as can the location of the crime.

If you get caught driving 200 mph on a public road you will most likely go to jail, so why has the relevant police force not acted on this self-incriminating video?



The Online Safety Act was preoccupied with the image of teenagers sitting alone in their bedrooms and being manipulated by evil influences.

This is, of course, a genuine problem. We have had children hanging themselves, deliberately or accidentally, or drawn to take illegal substances.





But the harm wrought by furious driving videos is even more dreadful.

Teenagers alone in their bedrooms tend to hurt only themselves. Drive a car dangerously on the roads and you can kill several innocent people.



It is time the government acted and put an end to this sort of material for good, by adding it to the list of prohibited material in the Online Safety Act.

Social media companies which allow it to be posted should face the consequences.



They can hardly moan that it is impossible to detect videos of dangerous driving – and to pick it up before it is even posted.



Before you publish a video on YouTube it gets scanned for copyrighted content.

Social media giants seem to be able to identify and remove images of child abuse, which thankfully disappeared from visible parts of the internet.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

We have lost far too many young people, and innocent victims who happen to be in the wrong place.

The deaths of Matthew Blades and Tom Clough should mark a watershed when finally the law catches up with people glorifying and encouraging recklessness on the roads.

News.title: Sudanese migrant allowed to remain in UK as she is married to her cousin & being deported would breach her human rights
News.content:
MIGRANT ROW Sudanese migrant allowed to remain in UK as she is married to her cousin & being deported would breach her human rights

A MIGRANT has been granted permission to stay in the UK after she married her cousin.

The Home Office formerly denied Isra Abdallah Ibrahim asylum in the UK, claiming she had only married her cousin so she could join him in Europe, once his refugee status was granted.

But Ibrahim maintained that the marriage was an Islamic custom, overseen in their home country of Sudan years before, in 2011.

She claimed it would be a breach of her rights to a family life under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) if she was forced to leave the UK and her husband.





British authorities became suspicious when they struggled to track down any official documentation of the marriage, with Ibrahim claiming it was “local tradition” not to record it.

The Home Office initially suspected the marriage was a means of negotiating entry into Europe and that the husband had “never intended to set down roots”.

However, Ibrahim’s husband convinced the tribunal he had always planned to stay in Libya and had no intentions of coming to Britain.

Ibrahim won her case at the Upper Tribunal in Manchester on August 24, after appealing the decision on the grounds that it violated her rights.

At the Tribunal, she said: “In accordance with local tradition, it was asserted that the customary marriage was not recorded in any official documentation.”

A couple of years after their marriage, her husband left for Libya without her and worked for two years before marrying her by proxy.

This was allegedly because Libyan authorities would not have recognised the Sudanese “customary marriage”.

After conditions “seriously deteriorated” in Libya, he made the decision to flee for Europe.



He received refugee status in the UK in 2015 and Ibrahim later came to join him.

The fact that the couple were cousins was initially contentious, with concerns it would violate the “prohibited degree of relationship set out in the applicable rules”.

However, they were not found to have breached any laws, as it is technically legal to marry your cousin in Britain.

Upper Tribunal Judge Paul Lodato said: “When I stand back and assess the overall evidential picture, [Ibrahim] has established on the balance of probabilities, through the fully tested evidence of her sponsor, that she married her husband in 2014 when he was habitually resident in Libya.

He added that when the pair married by proxy in 2014, the husband had been working in Libya for over a year and had made no attempts to leave the country.



“I am satisfied that this all weighs in favour of the sponsor having settled in Libya with a degree of continuity over an appreciable and meaningful period of time,” he said.

“Having found that the couple were married when the sponsor was in his country of habitual residence, and in accordance with the parties agreement that this was a decisive and dispositive question of fact, the appeal is allowed because [Ibrahim] met the applicable rules which renders the refusal decision demonstrably disproportionate.”

News.title: Teen cousins, 18, missing for 4 months found dead after final CCTV showed them going into nightclub ‘with their killer’
News.content:
TWO teenage cousins who have been missing for four months have been found dead, sparking a renewed probe into their suspected murder.

Letycia Garcia Mendes and Sttela Dalva Melegari Almeida, both 18, were last seen on CCTV going to a nightclub in Brazil with a man who cops believe may be their killer.



Footage from the night of April 21 shows the women with Clayton Antonio da Silva Cruz, 39, who was also wanted by police for aggravated robbery.

Known on the streets as “Sagaz” and “Dog Dog”, the man used a false identity and called himself “Davi” when talking to the two young women.



The trio reportedly had an argument in the early hours of the morning before leaving the nightclub in Paranavai, Parana, at around 1.10am.

New clues in the case suggest that the teen cousins were murdered between 4.00 and 4.40am on the night of their disappearance on April 21.

Remains discovered in a rural area near Paraiso do Norte on Friday 21 August are believed to be those of Letycia and Sttela.

Although forensics has not officially identified the bodies.



The breakthrough discovery was made after cops arrested an alleged accomplice – nicknamed Magrao – who told police where he had helped bury the bodies.

Police have also released CCTV footage believed to be from the night of their alleged murder.

Detective Luis Fernando Alves Silva said: “The images from the surveillance cameras show that there was a previous argument and that he was very agitated with them.



“The argument continued inside Clayton’s car and became more intense. There were verbal threats that one would kill the other, with disagreements over one wanting to stay with the other, as well as commercial and financial issues.”

Police then claim that Antonio da Silva Cruz pulled out a gun and ordered the girls out of the truck.

One of the teenagers tried to fight him – but the suspected thug and drug-dealer allegedly shot her in the head.

When the other girl tried to flee, she was shot and killed also.

Investigators believe that the suspected gunman then bundled the bodies into his pickup truck and dumped them in a sugar-cane field.



His long-time partner in crime, Magrao, then allegedly helped the Antonio da Silva Cruz dig a grave for the dead bodies.

Cops only discovered the whereabouts of the bodies after arresting Magrao – who confessed to his role in the horror crime.

Prime suspect Antonio da Silva Cruz had been on the run since April – but officers finally caught up with him on August 21.

They had followed his trail from a separate crime – a vehicle-robbery investigation.

When the cops cornered him, the suspect broke into a house and allegedly held a family hostage in a bid to avoid arrest.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Police killed him while trying to take him into custody.

The investigation into the alleged double murder – and the motive of the suspected killer – is still underway.

News.title: How the deadly A66 crash unfolded leaving seven dead
News.content:
Two police officers and five people within a Volkswagen Passat travelling the wrong way down the A66 motorway were killed after the car collided with a marked police car around 03:30 BST on Saturday.

Using doorbell footage, pictures of the scene and police reports, we can now piece together exactly how this fatal incident unfolded.

We also know that four of the five people in the car had previous convictions. One of them, Makai Saddington, 18, previously pleaded guilty to assaulting a police officer.

PC Matthew Blades and PC Tom Clough were the two police officers who died in the crash.

The BBC's UK correspondent Daniel Sandford explains what we know so far.

More on this story.

News.title: Snooker champion Graeme Dott guilty of child sex abuse
News.content:
Former world snooker champion Graeme Dott has been found guilty of child sexual abuse.

The 49-year-old denied two charges of lewd and libidinous behaviour towards a girl and a boy between 1993 and 2010.

During a trial, the High Court in Glasgow heard that Dott had exposed himself and inappropriately touched a primary school girl in the 1990s and attacked a young boy between 2006 and 2010.

Lord Harrower told Dott, who won the World Snooker Championship in 2006, he would be sentenced at a separate hearing in Edinburgh on 29 September.

Dott covered his face with his hands and shook his head while the verdict was delivered by jurors following a five-day trial.

He previously called the allegations made against him "disgusting".

News.title: Prince Harry steps down from African wildlife charity board
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex has stepped down from the board of an African wildlife charity whose rangers had been found to have committed human rights abuses against indigenous people.

A spokesman for Prince Harry confirmed he was stepping down after being president for the charity, African Parks, for six years before becoming a member of its board of directors in 2023, but said he remains a "supporter of its mission".

Last year the organisation admitted human rights abuses were committed by its rangers in Congo-Brazzaville.

Prince Harry's resignation comes shortly after it was announced he was relocating with the Duchess of Sussex, Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet from California to the UK.

Prince Harry's spokesman said "the Duke is proud of his 10 years with African Parks and fully supports the ongoing strengthening of its board.

"His commitment to conservation in Africa continues, and he remains a supporter of African Parks' mission."

African Parks manages around 20 national parks and protected areas across 12 countries.

It was subject to an independent human rights investigation into allegations guards managed and paid by the charity had beaten, raped and tortured indigenous people in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park.

The charity said in 2025 it had improved its safeguarding processes both in the Odzala-Kokoua National Park and institutionally.

Announcing a "governance refresh of its board of directors", the charity thanked Prince Harry for his association, saying he had "brought global attention to the urgent need for biodiversity protection for the benefit of people and wildlife, and has contributed greatly to promoting philanthropy for the cause of conservation in Africa".

It added: "The duke remains deeply committed to this cause, and remains a strong supporter of African Parks' work."

The charity's website says Prince Harry served as part of the expert team that helped implement the first phase of the 500 Elephants project, which was "one of the largest and most significant elephant translocations in conservation history".

It saw wildlife experts attempt to move elephants from a park in Malawi to help increase population in areas where they have been heavily poached.

Prince Harry has said helping move elephants to safer homes was an "amazing" experience.

The Sussexes are back in the spotlight after their announcement last week they were returning to the UK imminently their children enrolled in school to start at the beginning of September.

No change is expected to the official status of Prince Harry and Meghan and they will remain as private individuals.

Their pending return to the UK has raised questions on their security arrangements.

Last year, Prince Harry lost a legal challenge over the levels of security he and his family are entitled to while in the UK.

It is unclear what provisions will be made for their security once they return to the UK.

The couple's plans while they are in the UK are also unclear.

The BBC learned the Duchess of Sussex was in talks to return to acting with a role in Netflix series The Gentlemen, which would be her first significant acting role since her marriage to Prince Harry.

In early 2020, the Sussexes left the UK and stepped back from their royal duties before settling in California in March that year.

News.title: World's oceans hit highest temperature on record as El Niño grows
News.content:
The world's oceans are hotter than ever recorded, new data suggests, as they suffer from human-caused climate change and the growing El NiÃ±o weather phenomenon.

The average surface temperature of the planet's seas outside the polar regions hit 21.1C (70F) on Saturday, according to figures from the European Copernicus climate change service.

That edges past the 21.09C recorded on three separate days in March 2024, and is far above average for the time of year.

Warmer oceans can have wide-reaching consequences, including supercharging extreme weather, raising sea levels and harming marine life.

"This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress," said Dr Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus.

"El NiÃ±o is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming," she added.

News.title: Race Across the World star Jo Gardiner dies aged 61 one year after son's death
News.content:
A former Race Across the World contestant has died, a year after her son and co-star's death in a car crash.

Jo Gardiner, 61, died "following a long and courageous battle with cancer", her family said.

Gardiner, a physiotherapist from Manchester, travelled across South America with her son Sam in the second series of the BBC show, which aired in 2020.

Her family said she was "one of a kind" who "lived fully, fiercely and never did anything by halves".

News.title: Briton fighting for Russia killed in Ukraine
News.content:
A British national has been killed in Ukraine while fighting for Russia.

Bradley Townsend is said to have died following an attack by a remote-controlled FPV drone in Ukraine's eastern Donetsk region. His death, on 10 June, is believed to be the first of a British citizen fighting for Russia in the conflict.

The 33-year-old left his home in Barnsley, South Yorkshire, earlier this year after telling his family he was going to Romania, according to the Yorkshire Post, external.

The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) confirmed it was aware of reports a British national had died in Ukraine, adding it was in contact with his family.

The news emerged as Andy Burnham arrived in Kyiv for his first foreign trip as UK prime minister.

The visit coincides with the 35th anniversary of the country's independence from the Soviet Union.

The government has agreed to hand over blueprints for British-made components for the Scalp missile, a French version of the UK's Storm Shadow cruise missile - allowing Ukraine to produce the weapon domestically.

News.title: Carse dropped from England squad for second Test after nightclub incident
News.content:
Pace bowler Brydon Carse has been removed from England's squad for the second Test against Pakistan amid an ongoing investigation into an incident that led to him being briefly arrested.

Images that appeared on social media on Sunday showed Carse, 31, in handcuffs outside a bar in Derby on Saturday night.

Derbyshire Police have confirmed a man was arrested and subsequently de-arrested.

"A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in Derby city centre on Saturday night, 22 August," said a police statement.

"However the man was de-arrested shortly afterwards having agreed to leave the area."

The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) has referred the incident to the Cricket Regulator.

The Regulator will investigate and, as a result, Carse has been removed from the squad and replaced by Sonny Baker.

It is the latest in a string of off-field incidents involving the England team - Carse has become the third player this summer to miss a Test because of a disciplinary issue.

"Following a referral from the ECB, the Cricket Regulator have confirmed that they will investigate events on Saturday night in Derby," said an ECB statement.

"Brydon Carse will no longer be available for selection for the second men's Test while this investigation is ongoing and the full facts are obtained."

Carse was part of the England squad for the first Test against Pakistan, which the hosts won by an innings inside three days at Headingley.

When he was not named in the starting XI, Carse was released to play for Durham away at Derbyshire, a game the Division Two leaders won on Saturday evening.

Following that win, Carse was filmed in handcuffs outside a bar in Derby. The incident occurred less than 48 hours before Carse was scheduled to arrive in London to join up with the rest of the England squad for the second Test at Lord's.

Also in the footage was Carse's Durham team-mate Matthew Potts, while former England captain Ben Stokes could be seen in the background. Though Stokes has retired from international cricket, he is still under a central contract with the ECB, as are Potts and Carse.

In June, Stokes and Gus Atkinson were present in a London nightclub when a member of England's security staff was struck by a Saracens rugby player.

Both men missed the second Test against New Zealand while the incident was investigated, and the pair were eventually given a written warning as to their conduct.

Stokes and Atkinson breached an England team curfew that was introduced following late-night incidents during the winter.

Harry Brook was punched by a bouncer outside a nightclub in Wellington and Ben Duckett was filmed, apparently drunk, on England's Ashes holiday in Noosa.

On replacing Stokes as England captain, Joe Root began his second spell in charge by removing the curfew. Guidelines issued to players on the consumption of alcohol around matches and in public were also relaxed.

On the day before the first Test against Pakistan, Root called on his players to be "really good role models and good human beings".

"You always want to represent your country in the best possible light," Root told BBC Sport.

"We might have fallen short of that on a few occasions in the recent past. The only thing we can do to rectify that is be really good role models, good human beings and put in really strong performances on the field."

In the summer of 2024, Carse was given a three-month ban for historical betting offences.

He has subsequently rebuilt his career to become an England regular across formats. Since Carse made his Test debut in October 2024, no England bowler has taken more than his 58 wickets.

It is unlikely Carse would have played at Lord's - instead he would probably have been a back-up to England's four frontline seamers from Headingley.

His omission means another opportunity for 23-year-old Baker, who won his only Test cap in the second match of the series against New Zealand in June.

News.title: Victims describe 'house of terror' abuse by mother, grandmother and stepfather
News.content:
A mother, grandmother and stepfather who subjected three children to years of abuse in a "house of terror" have avoided jail.

Shirley Freeman, Julia Stephen and David McColl's victims were beaten, starved and psychologically tormented between 2003 and 2012.

Freeman, 51, and Stephen, 69, were earlier found guilty of cruel and unnatural treatment. McColl, 50, admitted the crimes.

At Aberdeen Sheriff Court, Sheriff Craig Findlater said no sentence could "repair the awful childhoods" of the trio's victims.

Warning: This article contains descriptions of child abuse

Freeman was sentenced to 18 months probation, 240 hours of unpaid work, and a 12-month restriction of liberty order, as a direct alternative to custody.

Stephen was ordered to carry out 150 hours of unpaid work and given 18 months probation.

And McColl was sentenced to 220 hours of unpaid work, 18 months probation, and an 11-month restriction of liberty order.

News.title: Rail companies sued for £5m over oil spill caused by derailment
News.content:
Network Rail is suing two rail companies for more than Â£5m after a fuel spill caused by a train derailment threatened an "environmental disaster" at a designated site for protection.

The body filed a legal claim earlier this month against DB Cargo UK and Touax Rail over the derailment near Llangennech, Carmarthenshire, in August 2020.

The incident saw 10 wagons of the 25-wagon train derail, causing 446,000 litres of fuel to spill, and about 300 people had to leave the area due to the blaze.

In High Court documents, Network Rail claimed that the derailment occurred because the wagon had "not been maintained with reasonable care" and is seeking damages for negligence.

No one was injured, but 116,000 litres of fuel ignited while 330,000 litres drained into surrounding wetlands, which form part of a Site of Special Scientific Interest (SSSI) and a Special Area of Conservation.

The Rail Accident Investigation Branch (RAIB) concluded in January 2022 that the derailment was caused by a set of wheels on one of the wagons locking, likely the result of a brake defect after "inadequate maintenance practices" were found in the investigation.

Network Rail, which owns, operates, maintains and develops Britain's railways, claimed that the derailment occurred because the wagon had "not been maintained with reasonable care" by Touax.

News.title: Teen pleads guilty over Channel boat with 165 migrants
News.content:
A teenager who piloted a dinghy carrying a then-record 165 migrants across the English Channel to the UK has pleaded guilty to endangering others during a sea crossing.

Chan Mathok Atak, 19, originally from South Sudan, admitted the offence at Canterbury Crown Court in relation to a crossing on 23 July.

Rescuers said they were astonished and alarmed to see the number of people packed onto the dinghy.

It was said to have been about the same length as a bus before it began deflating in the world's busiest shipping lane.

Prosecutors said Atak created a risk of death or serious personal injury to others on board the boat.

Endangerment at sea is a new offence created to target those alleged to have steered small boats over the Channel.

At the time of the crossing, the dinghy set a record for the largest number of people brought over in a single boat since dinghy arrivals began on the south coast in recent years.

The figure has since been surpassed, and earlier this month, a record 230 people reached the UK in a so-called "mega dinghy".

Atak is due to be sentenced on 11 September.

News.title: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests
News.content:
The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.

Jobs website Adzuna said it had just 8,383 graduate vacancies listed in July, down from 15,397 at the same point last year.

Adzuna also found competition among job seekers across all levels is rising, with an average of 2.14 job seekers per vacancy in July, up from 1.93 a year earlier.

However, some have said the data might not be reflective of the whole graduate job market and may instead suggest a shift in the way the roles are advertised.

Businesses have said employer national insurance and minimum wage hikes have made hiring more expensive, particularly for junior staff.

The number of graduate vacancies listed hit its lowest level since Adzuna started recording such data in 2016. The firm pointed to a peak for graduate roles in 2017, when it had more than 55,800 listed on its website. That is more than six times the number of roles listed on the site in July.

Andrew Hunter, the co-founder of Adzuna, said the figures show "employers still haven't found a reason to open up hiring" for recent graduates.

But graduate jobs expert Charlie Ball said the numbers might not be as bad for graduates as they first appear.

He said they could instead suggest that firms are advertising fewer roles specifically for graduates, even if the roles themselves still exist and end up being filled by graduates.

From his experience in the sector, Ball said the graduate market has "not collapsed" but added: "We know the graduate jobs market is weak. We know it's not in great shape."

Official figures show the UK's youth unemployment rate - which covers 16-to-24-year-olds - was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026. The number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is now over one million.

Young people have told BBC News previously they have applied for hundreds of jobs before even receiving a response.

They also expressed frustration at the growing number of employers using AI to screen applications.

Former government minister Alan Milburn is leading a major review of the youth unemployment crisis. He has previously said the number of entry-level jobs is shrinking, as is the number of part-time jobs traditionally filled by teenagers and students.

The Adzuna data also showed vacancies for jobs in travel, teaching and construction rose in recent weeks.

But sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently changed the rules for public contracts so that companies bidding for them have to show how they will create jobs and training opportunities.

A government spokesperson said on Monday: "The latest figures show there are 253,000 more people in work than this time last year with unemployment continuing to fall.

"We are determined to go further to restore opportunity for young people through our Â£2.5bn youth employment package which will deliver almost one million opportunities to earn or learn."

News.title: Sharing dangerous driving videos is 'truly reprehensible', PM says
News.content:
The government has urged social media companies to remove posts celebrating dangerous driving, as Prime Minister Andy Burnham branded sharing them "truly reprehensible".

Earlier Defence Minister Luke Pollard told BBC Breakfast that "social media companies could take the content down easily and adjust their algorithms to stop it being distributed".

Two police officers died when a car going the wrong way down a dual carriageway crashed into their vehicle near Middlesbrough on Saturday. Five passengers in the other car were also killed.

A TikTok account believed to belong to one of the five passengers, 18-year-old Makai Saddington, previously shared videos appearing to show dangerous driving, which have since been removed.

But Cleveland Police said "there is no evidence to indicate that filming of the activities that took place on Friday night and Saturday morning has taken place for the purposes of TikTok".

News.title: 'It's not Alton Towers' - rows break out over queuing at Wales' highest mountain
News.content:
Visitors to Wales' highest mountain are being urged to respect others by not skipping queues to reach the top following rows among climbers.

Recent hot weather means there have been bumper summer crowds at Yr Wyddfa, also known as Snowdon, where people have reportedly waited more than one hour to reach the 1,085m (3,560ft)-high summit.

Social media videos have shown arguments among queue-jumpers and those patiently waiting their turn to touch the metal plate that marks the top.

A recent video showed Marc Screeton, from Manchester, being heckled as he bypassed the line, saying: "Imagine queuing on a mountain? No chance."

But others have said queuing is necessary for safety reasons.

Eryri National Park Authority said its policy remained one of "self-policing" at the summit.

News.title: Woman pleads guilty to breaching anonymity order in Jeffrey Donaldson case
News.content:
A 55-year-old Ballynahinch woman has pleaded guilty to breaching a lifetime anonymity order by posting information likely to reveal the alleged identity of a victim in the Jeffrey Donaldson sex abuse case.

Donna Toman of Lord Moira Park appeared at Downpatrick Magistrates' Court on Monday.

A defence lawyer said she was entering a guilty plea to a charge relating to a social media post earlier this year.

The charge states the post "was likely to lead members of the public to identify a person as the person against whom a qualifying offence is alleged to have been committed".

On 29 July police stated that the woman's arrest related to the Jeffrey Donaldson trial.

District Judge Magill said he wanted a pre-sentence report by 12 October adding that it was a "serious offence".

The court heard the offence can bring a six-month sentence.

Donaldson, who was an MP from 1997 until 2024, was convicted in June of 18 counts of sex abuse including one count of rape, which he committed against two women when they were children.

He was told by the judge that the sentence would be a lengthy one.

It has since been confirmed he is to appeal his convictions.

News.title: Pubs and hotels could see business rates reformed after review
News.content:
A review is being launched into the way business rates are calculated for pubs and hotels in England and Wales, and could lead to a reform of the system.

The Treasury says business rates expert Jerry Schurder will lead the review into rate valuations and report back in March 2027, with the government calling for the views of landlords, hoteliers and business owners to feed in to the process.

Last month, Andy Burnham announced a 20% cut in business rates for pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England, to come into effect in April.

Pub groups have argued they face disproportionately higher rates bills, but other businesses have called for a wider reform of the rates system.

According to the British Beer and Pub Association (BBPA), 161 pubs closed in the first three months of this year across England, Scotland and Wales, equating to the loss of around 2,400 jobs.

Rising business rates are cited as one issue facing the sector, although there have also been complaints that increases in National Insurance and the minimum wage have made staff costs more expensive.

James Murray, financial secretary to the Treasury, said the new review would look at "a rethink of valuations - so that we can build a fairer system for the future".

Emma McClarkin, chief executive of the BBPA, said: "For years pubs have paid a disproportionately higher business rates bill which has ground down their ability to keep the doors open, so this review is sorely needed and hugely welcome."

The BBPA says pubs are valued differently for rates than retail venues. Instead of being based just on floor area, they are judged by a measure called Fair Maintainable Trade (FMT) - which means when a pub's turnover increases, so does its rates bill.

Jonathan Lawson, the chief executive of Butcombe Group, which has 120 pubs across the south and south west of England, told the BBC's Today programme that the use of FMT meant pubs were effectively being "punished for success", while large online retailers that operate out of warehouses were not subject to revenue-based rates calculations.

Their rates, he said, "are calculated based on what is deemed to be the market rent for that area, and takes very little on board in terms of revenue driven through that site".

"You can have a very large site paying a relatively low level of business rates versus a relatively small pub... paying a very high level of business rates."

Schurder is a former business rates policy lead at advisory firm Newmark UK, and his review will feed into the next rates revaluation in 2029.

Northern Ireland and Scotland set their own valuations, while Wales presently chooses to align its methodology with England. As the same approach is used across England and Wales, the review will be looking for responses from both nations.

Schurder's appointment was welcomed by Craig Beaumont of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB) who said he would bring "crucial heavyweight business rates expertise into the Treasury".

However, Beaumont said the government needed to address the wider business rates system and exempt more smaller firms by increasing the rates relief threshold for small businesses.

Jonny Haseldine from the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC) also said the review of valuations should be wider.

"The full reform of business rates, promised by the government at the last election, is urgently needed. This continued piecemeal approach to reform is the wrong approach," he said.

While the BCC said hospitality was the sector most worried about rates, Haseldine warned firms in every sector were struggling with the "complex and outdated" system.

Shadow Chancellor Sir Mel Stride said the review was "far too late for a sector this Labour government has already done its best to kill off".

"Tax hikes on business premises and jobs, alongside job-destroying regulation in the Employment Rights Act, have left many hospitality businesses on the brink," he said.

Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson Daisy Cooper said reform of business rates was "long overdue", but also called for an emergency VAT cut and a reverse to jobs tax changes "which have hammered hospitality in particular".

A Colorado family says a police K-9 who lived next door attacked their 2-year-old daughter, leaving her and her father with significant injuries and hundreds of thousands of dollars in medical debt.

During the second birthday celebration for twins Lily and Ollie on August 11, 2024, a police K-9 escaped their neighbor’s home, scaled the fence of their Castle Rock home and attacked Lily, Fox 31 reported.

Their neighbor, former Jefferson County sheriff’s deputy Zachary Oliver, was found not guilty of criminal charges in the attack last year — leaving the family on their own to pay off $300,000 in medical debt.

The dog “beelined for Lily and latched onto her leg and proceeded to just whip her like a rag doll,” said Lindsey Speer, a family friend who witnessed the attack. “Like the most horrific thing that you could ever see.”

Lily’s dad, Nick Dean, threw himself on the dog as his sister tried to rescue Lily. Their neighbor, who worked as a sheriff’s deputy at the time, was later able to control the dog.

A Colorado family says they’ve been left with $300,000 in medical debt after a police dog attacked their two-year-old daughter during her birthday party ( GoFundMe )

After the attack, Lily and her dad were both taken to the hospital for their injuries, which they say are still affecting them even two years later. According to a GoFundMe set up by the family to help cover their medical costs, Lily suffered lacerations across her abdomen and had a punctured femur from the dog’s bite.

Meanwhile, her father suffered injuries to his chest, neck, back and hip. He “continues to live with the lasting psychological effects of that day, including PTSD,” according to the fundraiser.

“It’s just the combination of not feeling strong enough to protect my family, and the pain,” Nick Dean told the outlet. “The chronic pain is like having an operating system going on in the background that just never shuts off, and it’s tiring.”

Colorado’s 23rd District Attorney pressed charges against the sheriff’s deputy, but a jury found him not guilty of criminal charges after his lawyers argued a contract he had with the county gave him immunity.

Oliver resigned from the sheriff’s office last year and his K-9 is also no longer working with the department. He also moved out of the neighborhood, according to the report. The family said they hoped the sheriff’s department or county would help them pay off their $300,000 in medical debt after the attack, but they haven’t.

“When the criminal proceedings turned into nothing, we thought, well, of course, the Jefferson County Sheriff’s Department is going to do what’s right by our family,” Nick Dean said.

A lawyer for Jefferson County said in an email to Dean’s attorney that “it is not the policy of Jefferson County to use taxpayer monies to pay claims for which there is no legal liability.” The Independent has contacted the sheriff’s office for comment.

The GoFundMe the family launched to help offset their mounting medical debt had received over $63,000 in donations as of Monday.

Major earthquakes have caused devastation around the world this summer.

A 7.7 magnitude earthquake hit the Philippines in June, triggering a tsunami. Twin quakes with magnitudes over 7.0 struck Venezuela back to back the same month, killing thousands. In July, a 6.8-magnitude tremor rattled Japan, and a 7.3 hit off the coast of southern Mexico.

Earlier this month, a 7.4-magnitude earthquake shocked Colombia, one of the largest there in years, and a 7.7 displaced some 40,000 people in Indonesia. This week, a 4.9 quake led to evacuations of hundreds in Spain.

The number of major earthquakes in such a short span of time may seem shocking but experts tell The Independent this is par for the course on a shifting planet.

“There’s nothing I’m seeing here that is unusual, this is all within the typical variations in earthquake rates that we see,” Zachary Ross, a professor of geophysics at Caltech, said.

open image in gallery Rescuers search for survivors amid the rubble of a collapsed building after an earthquake in Pereira, Colombia, earlier this month. Multiple major earthquakes have wrought havoc around the globe this summer ( AFP via Getty Images )

open image in gallery A man removes the debris of a collapsed house after an earthquake in Pereira, Colombia, earlier this month. The earthquake there was one of the country’s largest in year ( AFP via Getty Images )

Earthquakes happen when pieces of the Earth underground known as tectonic plates rub up against each other, creating the shaking sensation we feel on the surface. The quakes help release heat from the planet’s core.

Over 7.0 - the second-highest level on the Richter scale that measures earthquake strength - is considered to be “major” and can cause serious damage over larger areas.

There have been 11 of those earthquakes this year but that’s just below the annual average of 15-18, said Maureen Long, the Bruce D. Alexander professor and Chair of Yale University’s Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences.

“It feels like a pattern because unfortunately, several of these events have occurred in populated areas and caused significant damage, so we have all seen a lot of headlines,” she told The Independent.

This year, 17 or 18 quakes are expected, Dr. Allen Husker, a research professor of geophysics at Caltech, said. That’s based on the track for a typical active year, which sees 20.

open image in gallery Rescue officials work at the site of a house damaged in an earthquake in Yatsushiro, Japan, last month. The East Asian country saw a 6.8-magnitude quake ( JIJI Press/AFP via Getty Images )

open image in gallery A man walks past a mosque collapsed during an earthquake in Lamba Leda, Indonesia, on Tuesday. Tens of thousands of people were displaced by the quake ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved. )

“If we reach that number, it would be a little high, but not unusual,” he said.

There is also no indication that the quakes this summer are connected - and are “almost certainly a coincidence,” John Emilio Vidale, a seismologist at the University of Washington, said.

“All of the large earthquakes that have recently occurred have happened in different plate boundary zones and in different plate boundary environments,” William Barnhart, the assistant coordinator of the U.S. Geological Survey’s Earthquake Hazards program, added.

“While they seem close to each other in space and time, seismologically, they are not.”

Large earthquakes can trigger other smaller quakes in distant locations and aftershocks, which is what happened in Venezuela.

open image in gallery An aerial view shows an area affected by the collapse of structures after an earthquake in Catia La Mar, Venezuela, earlier this summer. Venezuela saw two back-to-back earthquakes in June ( AFP via Getty Images )

“But there is no evidence for large earthquakes triggering other large earthquakes at global scales,” Eric Dunham, a professor of geophysics at Stanford University, said.

So a large earthquake elsewhere in the world has no impact on whether a damaging earthquake will happen in the U.S., Long and Husker said.

But, that doesn’t mean a major event is off the table - and Southern California’s San Andreas fault is one area being closely monitored. So is the Pacific Northwest Cascadia subduction zone, which runs along the coasts of Oregon and Washington.

These West Coast faults could trigger each other, possibly leading to double the disaster, researchers at Oregon State University warned last October.

“The forecast for the San Andreas Fault is that the fault is overdue for a large earthquake,” Folarin Kolawole, an assistant professor at Columbia University’s Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences, said.

“However, I would also mention that there are many critically stressed faults across the U.S. that can rupture an earthquake if there is significant disturbance around them.”

Earthquakes cannot be predicted, so be prepared. As goes for other major disasters like hurricanes and winter blizzards, having an evacuation plan and emergency supply kit is a good idea.

open image in gallery A tourist takes pictures of broken tiles at the entrance of San Miguel Bajo Church in Spain’s Granada last weekend. Experts stress that everyone should have a response plan in place before an earthquake strikes ( AFP/Getty )

For earthquakes specifically, the early warning apps ShakeAlert and MyShake can give up to a minute’s notice.

During an earthquake, people should drop to the floor, crawl under a protected space away from windows and hold on, the American Red Cross says. People outside should make their way to an open area that is away from buildings and power lines, the USGS advises.

“Large, infrequent earthquakes can be devastating, but so can smaller earthquakes that occur more frequently. Being prepared for how to respond to an earthquake is the best way to handle one when it arrives,” Barnhart said.

News.title: Colombia’s armed groups recruit children and train them in drone warfare, rights group says
News.content:

Drug gangs and rebel groups in Colombia are increasingly recruiting children and using them to perform potentially lethal tasks that include piloting explosives-laden drones, Human Rights Watch said in a report published Monday.

The international watchdog said criminal organizations in the South American country often use social media to recruit children as they try to assert control over rural areas where they profit from the drug trade, extortion and illegal mining.

“Armed groups in Colombia are recruiting children with impunity,” said Juanita Goebertus, Americas director at Human Rights Watch. “Protection systems are failing, and social media platforms have become a more effective recruiting ground."

Child recruitment is on the rise again

According to Colombia’s Human Rights Defenders' Office, at least 1,500 children have been recruited by armed groups since 2021, with 625 cases reported in 2024.

In 1999, during the peak of the conflict between Colombia’s military and the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia, or FARC, an estimated 1,320 children were recruited into the fighting, according to a report by a national truth commission.

A 2016 peace deal between Colombia’s government and the FARC rebels reduced violence in many parts of the country and slowed the recruitment of children by armed groups.

But child recruitment is picking up again as smaller rebel groups and other criminal organizations fight over control of rural areas abandoned by FARC guerrillas following the peace deal, where law enforcement and social services continue to be weak.

In Colombia, rebel groups have long used children to perform tasks that include serving as messengers, gathering intelligence, cooking or engaging with the enemy — while girls are sometimes forced into sexual acts with commanders.

The Human Rights Watch report says children are now also being trained in drone warfare, as rebel groups increasingly use drones outfitted with explosives to strike at rival groups or launch attacks on police and army bases.

Human Rights Watch verified videos published on social media that show children using explosives-laden drones, and interviewed family protection officers who work with children who have escaped from armed groups or have been allowed to demobilize.

“Released children who report having operated drones say that armed groups describe the activity as a game rather than as participation in armed fighting,” the report said.

Colombia’s Human Rights Defenders’ office said in a separate report published Monday that armed groups conducted 121 attacks with drones in the first five months of this year, in which 21 people were killed and 145 were injured.

Social media accounts ‘glorify’ life with rebels

Human Rights Watch identified dozens of social media accounts that “glorify” life in rebel groups, echoing a concern previously voiced by the United Nations.

The watchdog group said in some cases, the algorithms of platforms like Meta and TikTok “appear to have actively promoted” such content that encourages children to join rebel groups.

Meta and TikTok replied to Human Rights Watch saying they prohibit content that promotes violence, and that they had taken down accounts flagged by the organization.

Human Rights Watch also said a FARC holdout group led by a commander known as Ivan Mordisco is involved in most cases of child recruitment and is recruiting heavily in Colombia's Cauca region.

Nearly half of all recruiting cases reported by Colombian authorities since 2021 involved Indigenous children, according to data analysis by Human Rights Watch, despite Indigenous people making up just 4% of the population.

The watchdog group also said girls made up 40% of all recruited children.

Human Rights Watch called on the Colombian government to devote more resources to prosecuting members of armed groups who recruit children, while stepping up efforts to prevent recruitment in rural areas.

There was no immediate government response to the report.

The organization also called on social media platforms to establish channels where users can easily report content that’s related to the recruitment of children, and preserve evidence that can be made available to prosecutors.

A federal judge will decide whether to hold Donald Trump’s administration in contempt after immigration agents violated court orders barring them from entering places of worship.

In February, Massachusetts District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV blocked a Trump administration policy giving agents permission to make arrests inside places of worship, calling the potential consequences of such an operation “profoundly troubling.”

On Monday, the judge sided with church groups who successfully sued the government and agreed to hold a hearing next month to determine why the Trump administration “should not be held in contempt for violating the preliminary injunction.” The government must respond by August 28.

Court filings revealed that undercover Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers spied on people who attended church meetings and ran license plate numbers of worshippers’ cars, part of a recently unveiled surveillance campaign that sought to crack down on protests after a surge of federal agents in Minneapolis earlier this year.

An undercover ICE agent infiltrated and covertly recorded a class inside the University Baptist Church gymnasium in May, according to recent filings from the Department of Homeland Security. Other agents spent hours outside the church, noting when people entered and exited, and ran registration checks on license plates — on including cars parked in a library parking lot next door.

open image in gallery Federal agents who went undercover inside a Minneapolis church and surveilled attendees during Sunday service violated court orders blocking officers from enforcement actions at places of worship, a judge said August 24 ( Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved )

Those actions “constitute clear and egregious violations” of a judge’s preliminary injunction that bars enforcement actions on church grounds, lawyers for several faith groups wrote.

Faith leaders and churchgoers in Minneapolis were “shocked and upset that ICE not only was monitoring the church, and doing so on Sundays, a holy day of worship, but even entered the church itself,” lawyers wrote last week.

“This is a complete violation of our sacred space,” former church president Jean E. Lubke wrote in court documents. “The Church is meant to be a place of sanctuary and safety — not infiltration by government agents.”

Homeland Security Investigations, ICE’s investigative arm, launched “Operation Puppet Master” on January 28 in the days after federal agents fatally shot Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis.

ICE revealed the plan in court documents defending the government’s prosecution of 15 Minneapolis activists that has expanded to include investigations into left-leaning organizations, including collecting financial records for labor unions and nonprofit groups Sunrise Movement and Voices for Racial Justice.

According to an officer’s report submitted in court documents, an undercover agent attending what the government described as a left-wing martial arts group in University Baptist Church’s gymnasium on May 28.

The agent sparred with attendees and interviewed them with a “concealed body-worn audio recorder” — which she dropped at the end of the meeting. Three minutes after leaving the gym, and after realizing she left it behind, she returned to the gym to pick it up.

Agents also spied on people coming and going from the church on two Sundays in April, taking pictures and running license plates for several hours each day, filings revealed.

“We have been shocked and upset to discover that DHS not only has been watching people coming and going from the church and not only has been doing so on Sundays, but has even entered the church building itself in order to make recordings and surveil people inside,” Lubke wrote in a sworn statement in the Minneapolis case. “This is a complete violation of our sacred space.”

open image in gallery The Trump administration recently revealed that agents infiltrated left-wing groups and spied on churchgoers as part of a surveillance campaign targeting protesters in Minneapolis after the killings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good ( Getty )

The federal investigation targeted “an organized network of conspirators operating through online and in person who are providing material support to violent opportunists and agitators involved in impeding federal law enforcement, rioting, destruction of Federal property and assaults on Federal agents and Officers,” according to court filings.

The Department of Justice has tied the investigation to Trump’s National Security Presidential Memorandum-7, titled “Countering Domestic Terrorism and Organized Political Violence,” which civil rights scholars and legal groups have labeled a far-reaching attempt to crush dissent and silence political and ideological opponents.

Homeland Security argues that its “Operation Puppet Master” surveillance scheme did not violate court orders barring federal agents on church groups, stating that the actions didn’t qualify as “immigration enforcement” and “were not planned nor undertaken to enforce” immigration laws.

“The use of the church on that day” was not “central” to the church’s “mission,” according to the government.

Church groups fired back on Sunday, stating that Homeland Security “cannot short-circuit the process the court established in its order by unilaterally deciding that a protected area does not deserve protection, taking an enforcement action there, and then suggesting afterwards that the location should not have been on the list.”

After Trump entered office, the administration rescinded previous ICE policy that prohibited enforcement actions in sensitive locations such as places of worship, as well as schools and hospitals.

Religious groups representing thousands of congregants filed several lawsuits arguing that the Trump administration is infringing on their religious freedoms by threatening their ministry to vulnerable immigrant congregations.

In his February injunction, Judge Saylor said that “the prospect that a street-level law-enforcement agent — acting without a judicial warrant and with little or no supervisory control — could conduct a raid during a church service, or lie in wait to interrogate or seize congregants as they seek to enter a church, is profoundly troubling.”

“Indeed, according to the new policy, agents could conduct a raid, with weapons drawn, at any type of church proceeding — including a regular Sunday service, a wedding, a baptism, a christening, or a funeral — subject only to the exercise of their ‘discretion’ and ‘common sense,’” he added.

The Independent has requested comment from Homeland Security.
