A Chicago woman was hospitalized with a severe gastrointestinal infection after eating a Wendy’s double cheeseburger she claims was “contaminated with Campylobacter and other illness producing bacteria,” according to a federal lawsuit reviewed by The Independent.

In her complaint, Roxie Ellis Douglas, 68, says the campylobacteriosis she contracted, which usually comes from exposure to, or cross-contamination with, raw or undercooked poultry, further led to acute infectious colitis, leukocytosis, dehydration, gastroenteritis and hypokalemia “secondary to diarrhea.”

Douglas trusted that the chain’s food had been safely prepared and “was not adulterated with a deadly pathogen,” the complaint states. However, it contends, “Defendant’s double cheeseburger meal was not fit for the uses and purposes intended – human consumption – and was therefore in breach of the implied warranty of wholesomeness.”

Campylobacter can be extremely risky to people over 65, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Douglas has thus far spent nearly $100,000 on medical bills since the meal last year, court exhibits show.

open image in gallery Campylobacter can be extremely risky to people over 65, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Roxie Ellis Douglas, 68, is suing Wendy's over claims she contracted campylobacteriosis from a double cheeseburger she ordered from the chain ( Creative Commons )

The suit by Douglas comes amid a nationwide outbreak of cyclosporiasis, a parasitic infection that causes explosive diarrhea, that the CDC says has been traced to tainted iceberg lettuce grown by produce giant Taylor Farms and served at Taco Bell restaurants spanning the U.S. The first case emerged in May, and has so far resulted in nearly 14,000 confirmed cases across 47 states, with at least two deaths reported.

A Wendy’s spokesperson did not respond to a request for comment.

On August 5, 2025, Douglas went online and ordered a double cheeseburger and a baked potato from a Wendy’s located on Chicago’s South Stony Island Avenue, her complaint begins.

The meal was delivered to Douglas at home, arriving in a “sealed, unopened bag by Doordash,” according to the complaint, which was initially filed in state court July 30 in state court and removed to Chicago federal court on August 20.

But while the food may have looked perfectly fine, the complaint claims it was in fact “contaminated with Campylobacter and other illness producing bacteria when it left Defendant’s control.”

A summary of medical expenses filed alongside the complaint shows Douglas has spent $93,578.24 on healthcare bills since August 6, 2025 – the day after she ate the Wendy’s double cheeseburger meal. The costs included $2,848.50 for EMS transport to Advocate Trinity Hospital; $24,434 for three days of inpatient treatment; $42,857 for a second, five-day stay at Advocate Trinity a week later; and nearly $13,000 for a colonoscopy in January 2026.

Douglas’s complaint accuses Wendy’s of failing to “properly operate, maintain and/or control the sanitary conditions in the kitchen,” failing to “use ingredients, supplies and other constituent materials that were reasonably safe, wholesome, free of defects, clean… and/or safe for human consumption,” and failing to provide “adequate warning to consumers… of the dangers of hazards inherent in the consumption of double cheeseburger meal.”

Wendy’s, for its part, has not yet filed a formal response to the allegations. At the same time, the chain proudly trumpets its food handling and sourcing practices.

Food safety is “foundational to who we are and how we operate,” the chain’s corporate site tells consumers.

open image in gallery The Wendy's in Chicago where Douglas says she was sickened by a double cheeseburger meal ( Google Maps )

“We take a preventive, risk-based approach to food safety that focuses on stopping issues before they occur,” it says, adding that all suppliers are subject to “regular food safety testing protocols and audits.”

More specifically, Wendy’s also touts its commitment to the safety and sustainability of its beef supply.

“The beef community has a long-standing commitment to caring for their animals and providing families with the safest, highest-quality beef possible,” Wendy’s explains on its site. “Beef Quality Assurance is a program that trains farmers and ranchers on best practice cattle management techniques to ensure their animals and the environment are cared for within a standard set of guidelines and regulations across the U.S. beef industry.”

It goes on to say that Wendy’s, since 2018, “has sourced 100 percent of its beef from Beef Quality Assurance certified sources.”

Wendy’s has been associated with occasional outbreaks of foodborne illness over the past quarter-century. In 2000, an E. coli outbreak was tied to a Wendy’s restaurant in Marion County, Oregon; a 2006 E. coli outbreak reportedly stemmed from food prepared at a Wendy’s in Ogden, Utah; and in 2022, more than 100 people in six states were infected with E. coli after eating at Wendy’s.

Douglas’s lawsuit lays out three separate causes of action: strict product liability, negligence and breach of warranty of wholesomeness.

She is now seeking a money judgment to be determined in court.

Josh Brolin has confirmed he is set to return for a third film in Taylor Sheridan’s blood-drenched Sicario franchise.

Sheridan’s script for the original 2015 film Sicario helped launched his Hollywood career. He went on to be Oscar-nominated for his 2016 follow-up Hell or High Water before creating the hit series Yellowstone which debuted in 2018.

That same year, Sheridan penned sequel Sicario: Day of the Soldado which saw Brolin and Benicio del Toro reprise their roles from the first movie.

A third film in the franchise has been rumored for a decade. Back in 2016, Day of the Soldado director Stefano Sollima told The Independent: “The idea is to make three anthology movies with some of the core actors and [set] in the same world.”

Now Brolin has confirmed that the much-delayed film is finally imminent, telling ScreenRant that it “is happening” and that production will begin “soon.”

'Yellowstone' creator Taylor Sheridan and 'Sicario' star Josh Brolin, who says another sequel is on the way ( Getty )

Brolin stars in the film series as Matt Graver, a CIA agent who leads a ruthless task force charged with combatting Mexican cartels.

No director or cast has yet been announced for the upcoming third installment, and it has not been confirmed whether Sheridan will return to write the script.

The first film was directed by Denis Villeneuve, who went on to direct the Dune series and will helm the next James Bond movie.

Sollima took charge for the second movie, which he told The Independent was “not a real sequel.”

He explained: “It's absolutely a standalone movie - a completely different story with just two of the characters that you met in Sicario. The reason that I love [Day of the Soldado] is because it's not exactly a sequel; it's something you can catch and enjoy even if you haven't watched the first one.”

In a four-star review, The Independent’s Jacob Stolworthy wrote that Day of the Soldado was a “brutal equal to its predecessor.”

He added that the film ends with a final scene “that's so shamelessly tacked on it almost dares you to denounce the already-confirmed third Sicario film despite your better efforts.”

The review concluded: “When Soldado works, though, it soars, holding your breath hostage in a way most films yearn to pull off. It’s hard to gauge how appealing Sicario films would be without the allure of del Toro but it’s to his credit alongside the promisingly talented Sollima that they have made something so brutal so watchable.”

Costco’s North American customers renew their memberships 92 percent of the time, and a lot of it has to do with chocolate chips.

The Kirkland, Washington-based wholesale club’s Kirkland Signature store-brand semi-sweet chocolate chips disappeared from its shelves in 2024 after cocoa prices soared.

Reddit was aflame with comments about the end of what many customers considered a sweet-tooth staple of their pantries.

“Man this sucks,” BornWithAnAK wrote. “I was just telling my partner yesterday that the Kirkland chocolate chips are easily my favorite.”

“They are seriously the best chocolate chip ever,” Incognito816 wrote. “I use them for chocolate fondue, chocolate pudding, brownies, cc cookies, drinking chocolate. Anything chocolate - it’s my only go-to! Nothing else compares, and I tried to find something as good when they discontinued them a few years back.”

open image in gallery Experts say Costco’s Kirkland Signature house brand provides the quality and value that customers have grown to love, but products under the brand can disappear as quickly as they arrive ( Getty )

Kirkland Signature chocolate chips came in multiple variations, including a dairy-free option that would be sorely missed.

“This is the worst news,” user 86VFR wrote. “I own an allergy-friendly bakery and the blue Kirkland chocolate chips are what I buy to make cookies because they are dairy-free. Looks like I need to make a trip and load up my freezer.”

The lengthy laments reflected customers' love for the combination of quality and value that the wholesale club’s products provide. But it’s that exact pursuit of value that can make beloved items disappear from shelves if production costs are too high.

It’s that fine line between disappointment and delight that contributes to Costco’s success, said Alex Hennick, president of supply-chain consultancy AD Hennick and Associates.

“Costco’s strategy is interesting because … part of the business model is built around the ‘treasure hunt’ and ‘while supplies last’ mentality,” Hennick said in an email to The Independent. “It creates a sense of urgency. So, when customers find something they like at a great price, they know they may not see it again, which encourages them to stock up.”

The company’s goal is to sell its Kirkland Signature products – which include everything from coffee and pizza to toilet paper and dishwasher detergent – for at least 20 percent less than a similar national brand, the company noted in a 2024 third-quarter earnings call.

If a product meets the company’s requirements for the Kirkland Signature brand, it has a chance to get on the shelf.

open image in gallery ‘Things you might find near the milk one trip are suddenly near the registers or entrance on the next. This makes the experience a little like a treasure hunt and keeps customers exploring the store,’ one expert said ( Getty )

But if costs are too high or the quality isn’t there, it can doom an item from making a home in the wholesale club’s cavernous stores or eliminate the product from shelves, as was the case with Kirkland Signature chocolate chips.

While the death of a popular Kirkland Signature product brings disappointment, it’s a risk that members take, said Chris Ribeiro, an assistant professor at Rutgers Business School and owner of retail and consumer strategy firm Starlight Analytics.

“Members trade off (unknowingly) on their mix stability for greater price reliability,” Ribeiro told The Independent in an email. “Customers know this, so they stock up or spend more knowing it might go away.”

Reddit certainly has the receipts for Costco customers’ rush to stock up on Kirkland chocolate chips – multiple users had plans to stock up on the morsels and one user posted a photo of three hulking red bags of the product crammed into their freezer.

Another inventory quirk that draws customers to Costco is that the company moves its inventory around the store – Kirkland Signature olive oil could be next to the freezer section one day and five aisles away the next.

“Things you might find near the milk one trip are suddenly near the registers or entrance on the next,” Ribeiro said. “This makes the experience a little like a treasure hunt and keeps customers exploring the store.”

Costco’s handling of Kirkland Signature items may seem like an exercise in retail smoke and mirrors, but it’s not – even if there’s no telling how long a product will be available in stores, Ribeiro said. Why? Customers have bought into the in-store brand’s quality.

open image in gallery ‘Costco is laser-focused on making sure Kirkland is as good or better as the national brand it competes with,’ one expert said ( AFP/Getty )

“Costco is laser-focused on making sure Kirkland is as good or better as the national brand it competes with,” he said. “In cases where other store brands may seem like a 'trade down' to customers…people have come to expect [Kirkland Signature] to be 'as good' over time.”

As an example, Costco’s Kirkland Signature Helles Lager won a bronze medal in the Munich-Style Helles category at The World Beer Cup, “arguably the most prestigious beer competition in the world,” Forbes wrote.

Fittingly, Costco announced in July that it was discontinuing the award-winning beer, food site TastingTable reported. A communal lament made up of lager fans and chocolate chip devotees won’t be around for long, though.

Cooking site Allrecipes reported this month that Costco’s chocolate chips are starting to appear at wholesale clubs across the country again.

News.title: This summer’s wildfire epidemic is one of the worst in decades – so why are deaths so low?
News.content:
Wildfires in Britain and Europe this year are among the worst in decades, yet direct deaths are at some of the lowest levels, according to a Telegraph analysis.

As of early August, 505,683 hectares of land have burned across Europe, forcing the evacuation of more than 360,000 people as uncontrollable flames reach major cities, towns, and villages.

The problem is global – in the US, Nevada declared a state of emergency over the weekend after a wildfire caused more than 42,000 people to evacuate their homes.

But what sets 2026 apart isn’t just the vast areas of land burned, but how few deaths have been caused by the fires.

This summer, just 14 people are reported to have died in European wildfires, the vast majority in a single blaze in Almería, southern Spain.

By comparison, more than 130 people were killed in the summer of 2017 – a toll driven largely by the Pedrógão Grande disaster in Portugal, where more than 60 people died on a single stretch of road.

In 2018, at least 100 others died in a single afternoon in the Mati disaster near Athens, despite total hectares burned that year being roughly a third of current levels.

Since the modern phenomenon of summer wildfires exploded in Europe a decade ago, the direct death toll has broadly trended downward, as the chart below shows.

News.title: Swine flu outbreak in Delhi swamps clinics and hospitals
News.content:
India is battling a surge in H1N1 flu infections, prompting the federal health ministry to step up surveillance and hospital preparedness.

The national capital New Delhi has recorded 1,777 cases this year, almost eight times the number (229) reported during the same period in 2025.

Dr Randeep Guleria, a senior pulmonologist and director of Medanta Medical School, Gurugram, says the H1N1 cases are much higher than reported.

“It’s quite likely that the reported numbers are an underestimate because they depend on how many people are tested,” Guleria said. “If you speak to patients admitted to hospital who test positive for H1N1, you often find that other members of their family have similar symptoms, although they have not been tested.”

“There is a surge and we are seeing a lot of patients. We are testing only those who come to hospital and are more seriously ill,” Guleria said.

H1N1, commonly known as swine flu, is a subtype of influenza A. It is a contagious respiratory infection that can cause fever and cough and in severe cases it can lead to pneumonia and respiratory failure.

Officials at the Indian Council of Medical Research said the rise did not mean the emergence of a new strain of the virus.

The surge comes during India’s rainy season, when seasonal influenza and other respiratory infections typically increase.

Doctors in Delhi say they are seeing more patients with high fevers, persistent coughs and flu-like symptoms, although most cases remain mild.

The H1N1 cases have been reported beyond New Delhi. The metro cities like Mumbai, Chennai and Bangaluru have reported a high number of cases, although the pattern is not uniform across the country.

Doctors in Bangaluru have reported more influenza A infections among children, with some developing pneumonia and respiratory distress.

India’s health minister JP Nadda said there was a need for continued vigilance and robust surveillance. He has asked officials to monitor unusual increases and clusters of cases and ensure hospitals could respond quickly.

“Swine flu (H1N1) can show up through symptoms such as fever, cough, sore throat, headache, runny nose, body aches and fatigue… If you experience these symptoms, seek medical advice at your nearest healthcare centre,” the health ministry said on X.

Delhi’s health minister, Pankaj Kumar Singh, said the capital had enough beds, doctors, medicines and medical equipment to manage the increase. “Delhi is fully prepared to deal with the present health situation,” Singh said.

India has had several waves of H1N1 since the virus emerged globally in 2009.

The infection, commonly called swine flu, became a recurring seasonal respiratory illness after the 2009 pandemic rather than disappearing from circulation.

India recorded 3,320 H1N1 cases and 14 deaths in 2025, according to Ministry of Health data.

News.title: Newcastle and Liverpool serve up thrilling tribute to Kevin Keegan
News.content:
It is fitting that Newcastle United vs Liverpool is a Premier League opening weekend fixture following the death of Kevin Keegan at the age of 75 last month.

All corners of St James’ Park will pay tribute and show their appreciation for the former player and manager who means a great deal to both sets of supporters.

Fans will find a printed message from the Keegan family on the back of black and white cards on their seat, which they will hold up to display a mural before kick-off.

As well as playing for both clubs, Keegan was Newcastle’s manager when they were beaten by a last-gasp Stan Collymore goal at Anfield in April 1996, a 4-3 defeat remembered as one of the great Premier League games.

This fixture usually delivers entertainment, and with new managers Matthias Jaissle and Andoni Iraola promising front-footed, ‘vertical’ football, there should be goals. That was certainly the case last August, when Newcastle fought back from two down with 10 men, before Rio Ngumoha scored a memorable winner.

It has been a summer of tumult for Newcastle, losing manager Eddie Howe, as well as key players Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and captain Bruno Guimaraes. There has been bullish talk of “Newcastle 2.0” from David Hopkinson, the club’s chief executive, and the club believe they have found a promising coach, but fans have understandably revised expectations downwards.

Liverpool are a difficult team to read; champions only 18 months ago but brittle last season, which resulted in Arne Slot’s dismissal. Iraola’s appointment is a shift back towards Jurgen Klopp’s style. That will be music to the ears of Anfield regulars, but holes remain in the squad. Central midfield has not been replenished; they need a Mohamed Salah replacement, and their strength at full-back is questionable. Much will depend on how 21-year-old central defender Jérémy Jacquet fares alongside Vigin van Dijk but he impressed in pre-season.



Full team news on the way shortly.

News.title: Frustrated Russell fails to make up ground as Norris wins incident-packed Dutch GP
News.content:
George Russell had another frustrating Sunday as the Dutch Grand Prix weekend slipped by with him failing to reduce his deficit to leader Kimi Antonelli. In a thrilling finale to the 72-lap race at the Dutch seaside, Lando Norris took his second victory in a row with two bold overtakes in one lap.

Yet compatriot Russell was irritated by Mercedes team orders for him to let Antonelli through into second place in the closing stages. It was a decision he believed risked a double podium for the team and threatened to put him even further behind his team-mate in the standings, with two charging Ferraris close behind. It was a race that, once again, fell away, despite Russell doing little wrong.

“Is he [Antonelli] fighting for the win or is he planning to catch Norris?” he asked, when the McLaren driver was 11 seconds down the road – the margin he would win by. “Yeah – we just lost a double podium here, mate,” was his response after moving aside.

Whilst Norris, who lost his lead from pole to Antonelli on the first lap, sealed the victory with two superb overtakes on lap 54 – first the Italian and then Lewis Hamilton – Russell had to mount a stout defence from Hamilton to secure third. It was against the odds, as both Ferraris, like Antonelli, were on fresh rubber after pitting under a late virtual safety car. Like Russell, Hamilton was critical of his team for their strategy choices.

Russell’s first podium finish since Silverstone – with his sprint victory on Saturday – means he at least retakes second place in the championship from Hamilton, but trails Antonelli by the same 59 point-gap he had after Hungary. That is despite him looking the faster and more comfortable Mercedes driver on Friday and Saturday.

News.title: Enzo Maresca tinkers his way to nervy Man City win
News.content:
Few in elite sport have the luxury of managing their own endings as Pep Guardiola did at Manchester City, yet no one can ever fully control a beginning. Enzo Maresca’s City started their Premier League season with a win, in the end, but three points masked the scale of the job he faces.

The narrative focus has been the impossibility of filling the personality void Guardiola leaves at a club sculpted in his image. That macro reading overlooks the number of distinct issues with City that Maresca must fix. A new midfield has to be recruited then blooded, a jittery defence needs settling down, and Phil Foden clearly requires help to recover the form which made him Premier League player of the year as recently as 2024.

All of that can wait after this victory against Bournemouth, which quietened some of the alarms from last weekend’s 3-0 defeat by Arsenal in Cardiff. Josko Gvardiol scored an injury-time winner after City had trailed for most of the match, much of it a sloppy slog for the home side, who went behind in the 26th minute. The introduction of Rayan Cherki for Nico O’Reilly revived some familiar attacking effusiveness.

A lesser-spotted VAR-aided double celebration capped a tense but ultimately joyful day for Maresca. Marc Guéhi equalised from Cherki’s well-taken corner in the final minutes, then the expanded Etihad Stadium rapturously celebrated Gvardiol’s apparent winner, only to see it flagged offside. Video assistant Paul Howard intervened to show Gvardiol was onside from Cherki’s pass, before City’s fans, players and staff shouted twice as loud for twice as long to salute a morale-boosting victory.

News.title: How to spend a weekend in Lake Garda
News.content:
Lake Garda’s glittering wind-swept waters have long attracted poets, artists, writers and politicians, from DH Lawrence to Wolfgang Goethe – not least Mussolini, who ran the Italian Socialist Republic from the lakefront town of Salò on the western shore.

Fringed by the Dolomites to the north, Italy’s largest lake is Mediterranean both in feel and in flavour, with a mild, temperate climate and a decidedly slow pace of life. Hills are carpeted in olive trees and vineyards, while citrus groves are thick with plump, juicy lemons. In lakefront villages, restaurant tables spill out onto pretty waterfront squares, while boats zip across glimmering waters.

The lower basin is punctuated with sandy coves and gentle rolling hills, while travelling north, the lake takes on a new appearance, with hills replaced by sheer jagged cliffs that plunge into the waters. The northern shore is swept by mountain winds that create the perfect conditions for watersports, with windsailing, kitesurfing, and flyboarding making this a premier destination for outdoor enthusiasts.

News.title: How to spend a perfect weekend in Lake Como
News.content:
An hour drive north of Milan, Lake Como is the most glamorous of Italy’s lakes, hemmed in by the snow-capped Alps with picture-perfect villages on the water. Milanesi pop here for the day for a breath of fresh air and to soak up the fabulous vistas, while international visitors – the Clooneys, the Kennedys – have long been drawn by the grand lakefront hotels and the elegant mahogany Riva boats that zip along the lake’s deep blue waters.

Smart hotels and expensive boats aside, Lake Como is rich in culture, with opulent villas that once belonged to artists, writers, opera singers and explorers. Pliny the Elder, author of the first encyclopaedia, was born here, while 19th-century soprano Giuditta Pasta is known to have entertained composers Bellini and Donizetti in her lakefront residence on the eastern shore.

Though famous spots such as pretty Bellagio still pull in the majority of visitors, the lake has retained its authenticity, with plenty of sleepy fishing villages, such as Laglio, Torno and Nesso, home to rustic, family-run trattorias serving up traditional hearty fare, including risotto al pesce persico (risotto with perch).

News.title: Erling Haaland cuts off his trademark blond hair
News.content:
It is a new-look City in more ways than one this term with head coach Enzo Maresca looking to kickstart a new era following Pep Guardiola’s exit.

Maresca is hoping for an immediate return to form in City’s Premier League opener after a chastening 3-0 defeat by Arsenal in the Community Shield last week.

So far, only Elliot Anderson has arrived but Maresca is hopeful the club will be active in the transfer market. Rodri has left for Barcelona while Savinho is closing in on a move to Tottenham.

“I’ll try to find a new Rodri – it is what it is,” the former Chelsea manager said. “Rodri, before he arrived here, he didn’t win the Ballon d’Or, he didn’t win the Champions League, he didn’t win the Club World Cup. Then he joined the club and then after he achieved many important things. Now the target for us is to try to find the new Rodri.

“When David Silva was here, everyone was worried - Kevin [De Bruyne] arrived. When Sergio Agüero was here, everyone was worried – Erling [Haaland] arrived. When Ferdinando left, Rodri arrived. It’s just about this.

“When they leave, you need to be good and recruit the next one. They are all similar – David, Kevin, Fernandinho, Rodri, Agüero, Erling. It’s just normal, it’s a change. It’s not a problem, just go again and try to do the right things.”

Sports.title: Is £130m Alvarez an upgrade on Gyokeres? In many ways yes, but Arsenal will miss parts of their current striker’s game
Sports.content:
JULIAN ALVAREZ could be the final piece of Mikel Arteta’s Arsenal jigsaw, but the stats suggest Viktor Gyokeres would leave some pretty big boots to fill.

The Gunners are ready to make a move for the Atletico Madrid and Argentina star in the final week of the transfer window if they get encouragement from either the player or his club that a deal can actually be done.



Although Alvarez is said to prefer a move to Barcelona, Atletico have strongly resisted the idea of selling him to their La Liga rivals – report The Athletic.

That potentially leaves the door open for a move to Arsenal, with some reports suggesting that they could even throw Gyokeres in as part of a sensational player plus cash offer.



The Gunners are prepared to go beyond their club-record £105million fee that they paid to sign Declan Rice from West Ham in 2023, with Atletico reportedly wanting as much as £130m to even consider selling their star man.

Alvarez was booed yesterday when his name was read out before Atletico’s 2-2 draw with Villarreal and was jeered again when he came on as a 66th-minute substitute.



That backlash could yet force Atletico to soften their stance – particularly with reports in Spain suggesting Alvarez’s position on only wanting Barcelona is beginning to change.

The former Manchester City man is still hoping for that dream move, but crucially, he is no longer thought to be completely closing the door on a return to the Premier League.

Gary Neville certainly believes Alvarez would take the Gunners, and indeed captain Martin Odegaard‘s game, to another level.

After Arsenal’s 3-0 win against Coventry on Friday night, eight-time Premier League winner Neville told Sky Sports: “What a squad [Mikel Arteta] has built. If he puts another forward into that, if they could get Julian Alvarez somehow, that would light this place up as you’d have a world-class striker to go with all the world-class defenders and midfielders.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“They wouldn’t just become Premier League title winners they’d go the next step and win a Champions League. He needs a bit of magic up front – someone that can win a game for you when you don’t play well.

“Odegaard is exceptional. If there was an Ian Wright-type player up front for Arsenal who makes those short runs he’d be even better.

“As [Kai] Havertz and [Viktor] Gyokeres always come to the ball, Odegaard has to play possession rather than playing the slip passes. If Arsenal were to sign Julian Alvarez then he’d go up a level as it would be perfect for the style of play.”

There is certainly an argument for that as Alvarez is more creative than Gyokeres, registering ten assists last season compared with the Swede’s three.



His 127 minutes per goal or assist also beats Gyokeres’ 145, but that is where the idea of Alvarez being a straightforward upgrade starts to become a little more complicated.

Gyokeres scored 21 goals in 3,481 minutes, while Alvarez managed 20 in 3,549 minutes – meaning the Arsenal man was more prolific in terms of minutes per goal — 165.7 compared with Alvarez’s 190.5.

Gyokeres, who only signed for Arsenal last summer for £55m from Sporting Lisbon, also had a superior shot conversion rate, scoring with 22.6 per cent of his efforts compared with Alvarez’s 15.9 per cent.

There was a period between December and February when Alvarez went 11 games without scoring – something which clearly damaged his goals-per-minute and conversion rate numbers.



The idea that Alvarez simply lives in the space behind defenders is also not quite the complete picture.

Although he can make clever runs in behind, Alvarez also likes to come towards the ball and get involved in build-up play – something he showed with Argentina at the World Cup when he often dropped deeper to allow Lionel Messi to stay higher up the pitch.

That helps explain why his passing accuracy is a whopping 82.8 per cent compared with Gyokeres’ 63.8 per cent.

In that sense, Alvarez can be more of a Harry Kane-style striker – dropping deep, linking play and dragging defenders around, while having the ability to get on the end of things too.

His low centre of gravity also makes him incredibly difficult to knock off the ball and helps explain why he completed 65 dribbles last season compared with just 13 for Gyokeres.



But if Alvarez does come with Gyokeres heading in the other direction, what Arsenal would lose is equally important.

Gyokeres is 6ft 2in, while Alvarez is only 5ft 7in – a physical difference that is reflected in their aerial numbers.

Gyokeres won 44 aerial duels compared with just 13 for Alvarez.

The Swede also won considerably more fouls – 54 to 32 – as his power and physicality makes him a nightmare for defenders.



Perhaps the biggest surprise is possession won in the final third.

Alvarez has a reputation as a pressing monster, but Gyokeres actually won more possession in the final third last season – 34 times compared with Alvarez’s 31.

Gyokeres also recorded more touches in the opposition box – 219 to Alvarez’s 198.

Alvarez did, however, take more shots – 126 to Gyokeres’ 93 – largely because of the way he becomes involved in more phases of the attack by dropping deep.

So, Neville’s prediction that Alvarez would be the perfect fit is not necessarily wrong.



However, the statistics suggest it isn’t quite as simple as swapping one striker for another and watching Arsenal improve across the board.

Arteta could give Alvarez a slightly different role, asking him to prioritise making more runs beyond the defence.

If that happens, Alvarez’s movement could indeed take the Gunners up another level – as Neville eluded to.

But it would also mean sacrificing the aerial threat, physical presence and penalty-box dominance that Gyokeres brings.



Arteta’s caveat to that could be that he also has Havertz, who brings the same qualities.

Alvarez, on the other hand, would give Arsenal something different – a more rounded footballer who offers more creativity.

But Gyokeres was the more efficient goalscorer last season and provides qualities Alvarez simply does not possess.

The numbers, therefore, suggest Alvarez is an upgrade in some ways, rather than the complete upgrade many expect.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

For Arsenal, the question is whether Arteta values what Alvarez adds more than what he would lose by replacing Gyokeres.



With just eight days of the transfer window left, that could be the £130m question which decides whether the Gunners make one final blockbuster move.

Sports.title: Erling Haaland will be ‘VULNERABLE’ after cutting his hair – this is the reason ‘Viking warrior’ made drastic change
Sports.content:
FLOWING blonde locks might be more readily associated with Disney princesses than centre-forwards.

But there is nothing dainty about the Herculean striker who grew the most feared ponytail in the Premier League.



Since landing at Manchester City in 2022, the sight of Erling Haaland‘s tied-up trim streaking into the distance has been nightmare fuel for defenders.

The fact he is quicker, stronger and taller than just about any opponent feeds perfectly into the Norwegian’s “Viking warrior” image.

And the iconic hair-do draped over his 6ft 5in frame completed the look.



That is, until he decided to lop it all off.

Haaland, 26, debuted his brand new buzz cut in City’s 2-1 comeback win over Bournemouth on Sunday.

Pals like Noel Gallagher and Pep Guardiola were among the first to see it when Haaland shocked them on a video call.

They seemed to be having a good laugh about it over the phone, but – as barmy as it sounds – might Haaland’s fortunes be affected by his radical new look?

Might opposition players be less intimidated by a fair buzz cut than a rugged head of Scandinavian hair?



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

And might this new start hamper Haaland, who usually hits the ground running but has stumbled out of the blocks with two goalless appearances so far this season?

Behavioural expert Darren Stanton reckons the towering striker has sent a clear message by going wild with the clippers.

He told SunSport: “He’s got this sort of Viking warrior look, which made him quite intimidating. I think his hair, for him, was almost like body armour, it was his strength.

“He’s either gone through some kind of epiphany in his own career, in his own mind, or he’s been given advice.

“It’s a new season, a new manager, a new reinvention of himself.



“Maybe he wants to kind of return to his roots and not rely so much on his reputation and his experience and just wants to kind of reconnect with the game.

“He probably wants to step back from all the bling and PR buzz and just get back to the thick of it.

“Internally, what he’s saying is, I’ve got a brand new image, there’s a brand new version of me that you’re all going to see.”

There is no biological backing for the ‘Samson effect’ – a concept born out of a Bible story in which Samson loses his supernatural powers after his hair is shaved in his sleep.

That is not to say Haaland’s extreme makeover won’t affect him in any way, shape or form.



Stanton continued: “It’s part of your identity, it’s part of who you are.

“It’s like when people are in a job for 30 years, and they retire, they lose a part of themselves.

“So on some levels he’ll be feeling quite vulnerable because he, or maybe his image, has attributed his long hair to his success.”



But the season is long. And with an average of over 40 goals a year in City blue, the chances are Haaland will find a way to return to his destructive best, even if his ‘Viking warrior’ feats are no longer matched by his haircut.

Stanton said: “He is seeing it as a renewal. A statement that he’s getting rid of the old, and now he’s looking forward to reinventing himself and trying different things.”

*Darren Stanton spoke to SunSport in association with OLBG

Sports.title: Don't panic! Why Man Utd and Carrick get a pass after flat Hull defeat
Sports.content:
I was at the game on Saturday and it was clear early on in the game that Manchester United were not at the races against Hull City.

Words will be bandied towards Michael Carrick's side this week until their home game against Ipswich on Sunday; for example, a lack of intensity, aggression and intent on display.

But when I left Hull, I just felt it was a bit more nuanced than that.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the Premier League match between Hull and Manchester United

It was a bad performance, for sure. Carrick's side didn't perform, and only he will truly know why, but from the off it was quite clear some of his main players are not quite up to match sharpness compared to where they will be in a few weeks.

Six of Carrick's first-team players did have a full pre-season. But Carrick also had a new midfield duo playing together in Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos.

Manchester United

Ipswich Town Sunday 30th August 4:00pm Kick off 4:30pm

Off the bench, he had players nowhere near full fitness in Benjamin Sesko (has not played a minute of pre-season), as well as Kobbie Mainoo and Marcus Rashford, who have had limited minutes since returning from England duty in the summer.

Hull also deserve enormous credit for being a well-drilled outfit for their first Premier League game in nine years while also having a squad who have experienced a full pre-season to prepare for their opener.

Also, allow me a moment to myth-bust something I have seen across social media over the last few days since the defeat.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Michael Carrick promises improvements in his Manchester United side following their surprise opening-day defeat to Hull City, but insists that he won't change the way he does things

'Four defeats out of five under Michael Carrick have come against sides who have played a back five'

Not having it. Look at the games!

Two of them were pre-season games, including United's first of the summer against Wrexham and their last against Ruben Amorim's AC Milan. If anyone is using these as barometers of a side struggling against a formation, it is simply not right.

Hull was bad. Leeds at Old Trafford last season was also bad. These two performances share a lot of similarities but I would argue the most common denominator is that I left both games thinking they were seriously lacking from a physical point of view and that will be Carrick's most pressing thought.

I am more than willing, and Carrick has more than deserved, somewhat of a pass for the Hull result, and I would be extremely surprised if United were not considerably improved against Ipswich Town on Sunday.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Danyal Khan gives us his three things to take away from Manchester United's loss to Hull City on the opening day of the season

So what are Man Utd's plans for the remainder of the transfer window?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look as Sky Sports' William Bitibiri explains exactly what Carlos Baleba might bring to Manchester United's midfield

The midfield was Manchester United's priority going into the season and they have gone some way to addressing it by spending over £150m in reinforcements, with Carlos Baleba the latest addition to their ranks.

But United find themselves in a similar situation to last summer - reinforcing your greatest need just highlights your next biggest gap within the squad.

Rewind back to 2025: the club had finally addressed their inefficiency up front by adding Benjamin Sesko, Matheus Cunha and Bryan Mbeumo but having sorted the attacking weaponry, it became even more obvious the midfield needed strengthening.

United waited 12 months as they did not want to sign a stop-gap midfielder for the sake of addressing the area and believed they would have a better run at the midfield market the following summer.

There is a similar feeling now when it comes to left-back. Now United have signed their three midfielders, the need for a left-back is a must.

The club have long admired Myles Lewis-Skelly and Lewis Hall and my feeling is they are top of United's list in that position.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Danyal Khan looks at whether Manchester United are better off waiting until next year to ensure they sign a No 1 target at left-back

Both seem unattainable at this moment in time, with managers of both clubs dismissing any chances of their players leaving. In addition to Bruno Guimaraes' injury, which especially seems to all but rule out a potential departure for Lewis-Skelly.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mikel Arteta says he is '100 per cent' sure that Myles Lewis-Skelly will be staying at Arsenal after the transfer window closes and is unsure if Bruno Guimaraes will be available against Coventry

My feeling is that with United having focused on attack and midfield over the last two summer windows, they are willing to wait until next summer to address their defence - including a first-choice left-back when Luke Shaw's contract expires next summer.

Things could change of course, and I would not completely rule out United getting creative in terms of potentially adding a left-back in the last week of the window but at the moment, it seems unlikely.

Barcelona's Alejandro Balde has been the latest player linked with United at left-back but from what I understand, although United are aware of his situation in Catalonia, it is not a name they are strongly pursuing at this time.

All in all, it is a lot of pressure on Luke Shaw to stay fit all season, and some reliance will need to be put on Patrick Dorgu at left-back. The club see his long-term future in that position.

Noussair Mazraoui and Diogo Dalot can also both deputise in that position too.

In terms of departures at United, at the time of writing, it seems unlikely any first-team players will leave the club before the deadline.

One potential departure this window was Dutch forward Joshua Zirzkee but interest from Italy has yet to materialise into anything concrete and he is expected to stay at the club.

Sports.title: England's Carse unavailable for Lord's Test after nightclub incident
Sports.content:
England fast bowler Brydon Carse has been withdrawn from the squad for the second Test against Pakistan at Lord's from Thursday following an incident outside a Derby nightclub that is being investigated by the Cricket Regulator.

Video footage emerged of a handcuffed Carse being led away by police on Saturday night after Durham's players had gone out to celebrate their win at Derbyshire in the County Championship.

Carse was seen talking to team-mate Matthew Potts with former England captain Ben Stokes also pictured in the background.

England squad for second Test against Pakistan at Lord's Joe Root (captain), Gus Atkinson, Jofra Archer, Sonny Baker, Shoaib Bashir, Harry Brook, Jordan Cox, Ben Duckett, Matthew Fisher, Emilio Gay, Dan Lawrence, Ollie Pope, Ollie Robinson, Jamie Smith, Josh Tongue. The second Test is live on Sky Sports Cricket and Sky Sports Main Event from 10am on Thursday (11am first ball).

A Derbyshire Police statement read: "A man in his 30s was arrested on suspicion of being drunk and disorderly in Derby city centre on Saturday night (August 22).

"However the man was de-arrested shortly afterwards having agreed to leave the area."

An ECB statement read: "Following a referral from the ECB, the Cricket Regulator have confirmed that they will investigate events on Saturday night in Derby.

"Brydon Carse will no longer be available for selection for the second men's Rothesay Test match while this investigation is ongoing and the full facts are obtained."

Sonny Baker - who made his Test debut against New Zealand at The Kia Oval in June - replaces fellow seamer Carse in England's squad.

The Carse situation comes less than two weeks after new England captain Joe Root removed the midnight curfew that had been installed following a number of drink-related issues across the winter tours of New Zealand and Australia.

Image: Carse was seen in handcuffs outside a nightclub in Derby on Saturday night

Carse did not make the England XI for the thumping three-day win over Pakistan in the series-opening Test at Headingley and was subsequently released to play for Durham against Derbyshire, a game in which he took two wickets and scored 26 runs.

Carse was England's leading wicket-taker during their 4-1 Ashes hammering but has not played for his country since due to injury.

Another off-field issue for England to manage

The paceman's nightclub incident is another off-field episode for England to negotiate.

Image: Carse (pictured) has been replaced by Sonny Baker in England's squad

White-ball captain Harry Brook was punched by a bouncer while out the evening before a one-day international in New Zealand last autumn.

Then, during The Ashes, an unverified video appeared to show batter Ben Duckett drunk while the team were on a mid-series break in the beach resort of Noosa.

Stokes and fast bowler Gus Atkinson missed the second Test of the 2-1 home defeat to New Zealand earlier this summer after breaking the curfew to attend a Chelsea nightclub as they celebrated victory in the first game of the series at Lord's.

Stokes and Atkinson were cleared of violent conduct but hit with written warnings after "breaching specific contractual obligations".

Root had called for his players to "be adults" while announcing the removal of the curfew, so the Carse situation will raise further questions about the side's relationship with alcohol.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player England Test captain Joe Root explains why he has removed the curfew that was previously imposed on his England team

Broad: Carse 'pretty daft' to be caught up in nightclub incident

Speaking on his For the Love of Cricket podcast, before Carse's withdrawal from the squad for the second Test was announced, former England bowler turned Sky Sports pundit Stuart Broad said: "We can't really make a judgement apart from it being, whatever's happened, pretty daft.

"We'll wait and see. We don't know, it could have been 10 o'clock in the evening, it could have been two o'clock, but whatever.

"This is not really anything that anybody wants to be talking about any more, to be brutally honest."

Sports.title: What has gone wrong for Pakistan cricket with 'alarm bells ringing'?
Sports.content:
It must be hard being a Pakistan cricket fan right now.

Those supporters have seen the side suffer 14 defeats in their last 19 Tests after last week's three-day, innings-and-103-run drubbing by England in the series opener at Headingley.

The tourists were loose and ineffective with the ball, poor with the bat and awful in the field - a damaging cocktail.

Ahead of the second game at Lord's from Thursday - live on Sky Sports Cricket (10am on air, 11am first ball) - Osman Samiuddin, a senior editor at Cricinfo and Pakistan cricket expert, joined Michael Atherton and Nasser Hussain on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast.

Samiuddin explained where he thinks things have gone wrong for Pakistan as cricket in the country reaches an "alarm bells stage" with fans "fed up" at how the game is being run…

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the day three of the first Test between England and Pakistan as Joe Root's side cruised to an innings victory at Headingley.

Too much change with domestic structure

OSMAN SAYS: "Whichever structure you choose - there has been a great battle in Pakistan over the last 50 years, really, about whether you should have departmental or regional sides - I would pick one and stick with it, say this structure stays for the next 10, 12 years.

"They have changed structure almost every single season since the first first-class season in 1953. There has been no stability.

"We cut from 16 to six teams in 2019-20, then expanded to 16 teams with four first-class tournaments and three white-ball tournaments.

Image: Pakistan have lost 14 of their last 19 Test matches

"When they cut down in 2019, they literally lost half their first-class cricketer pool. There were stories of players taking up driving taxis as, overnight, they didn't have a career.

"That drastic change every season has impacted the quality of domestic cricket, which is where you get your talent from.

"Domestic tournaments used to be played across 16 first-class grounds. For the last few years, they have been at about four or five.

"How are batters like Abdullah Shafique and Imam-ul-Haq supposed to work out how to play in different conditions playing at four grounds?"

More Tests needed? Samiuddin also said Pakistan do not play enough Test matches. The side have not had a double-figure number of Tests in a calendar year since 2017, while only Sri Lanka (4), Ireland (3) and Afghanistan (2) played fewer than their five matches in 2025. They are scheduled to play nine games in 2026.

Issues with administration and management of players

OSMAN SAYS: "A lot of it is self-inflicted.

"Since 2021, we have had four chairmen - Ramiz Raja, Najam Sethi, Zaka Ashraf and now Mohsin Naqvi - with very different views and very different levels of involvement in the game.

"The current chairman is also the interior minister of the country. Pakistan has a lot of interior-minister issues on any given day so he is fairly busy with his day job. You wonder how much time he has for cricket?

"Shaheen Shah Afridi, Babar Azam, Abdullah Shafique, Naseem Shah...

"So many of these players have burst onto the scene and then regressed. There is a feeling that golden talents have not hit the heights we are expecting them to hit and maybe never will.

Image: Captain Babar Azam could return for Pakistan at Lord's after missing the Leeds Test with a hand injury

"There is only one reason, really, for that regression and that is how the PCB manages their careers.

"They haven't managed them well enough whether through injury or basic player development stuff. There has been a succession of managements that haven't brought their best players on.

"There is no reason Shaheen and Naseem should not be leading Pakistan's pace attack but Naseem has not played a Test since December 2024 and Shaheen has played nine of 27 Tests since coming back from a knee injury.

"Shaheen injured his knee in a Test in Sri Lanka in 2022 fielding. There was a lot of confusion over the rehab and he was maybe rushed back.

Image: Pakistan are missing left-arm seamer Pakistan Shaheen Shah Afridi's x-factor in this series

"He has been hit by constant changes in the coaching set-up, never knowing who his coach is, who the bowling coach is, for example.

"He has hardly played a first-class game in three years and a fast bowler, you would think, would need to keep bowling to build your body up. Same for Naseem.

"What has become acute over the last five, six years is how wasteful Pakistan is of its talent. There has always been a certain amount of waste - it is not efficient - but that waste has increased more and more rapidly."

Samiuddin also noted how Naseem and Shaheen - not part of this Test squad - have been unceremoniously dropped at times without explanation, saying that "messes with a player's career."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports' Urooj Mumtaz was disappointed with Pakistan's performance in Leeds, saying the tourists lacked discipline and skill

Can fans be won back?

It was noticeable in Leeds how sparse the Pakistan support was and Samiuddin says patience with the governance is wearing thin.

He added: "I have heard more from fans anecdotally, not that they are angry at the team or because they are losing, but that they are fed up with how Pakistan cricket is being run. I suspect people will still turn up at Lord's to watch them.

"But it is dwindling and I think we are at an alarm-bells-ringing danger-point where if it goes on like this then you may think cricket will go the way hockey has gone in Pakistan and the way cricket is going in the West Indies, for example."

Sports.title: Is Norris now Antonelli's biggest title threat?
Sports.content:
While he won neither of the race formats across the Zandvoort Sprint weekend, Kimi Antonelli increased his overall world championship lead at the Dutch Grand Prix as Formula 1 returned from its summer break.

The Mercedes driver now leads both team-mate George Russell and Ferrari rival Lewis Hamilton by 59 points, the second-largest advantage Antonelli has enjoyed at the top of the Drivers' Championship so far this season.

But Antonelli's advantage over the driver now occupying fourth place in the standings was cut by a further eight points, following reigning champion Lando Norris' second successive Grand Prix victory, which moved him to within 83 points of the championship lead.

Norris became just the second driver after Antonelli to claim consecutive wins this season, with the McLaren driver's Zandvoort triumph coming after he overtook the championship leader on track. Antonelli had initially reclaimed the lead from Norris at the restart following the red flag triggered by Max Verstappen's heavy lap-one crash.

Yet does the result mean that Norris' hopes of retaining his world title, which seemed all-but over just a few races ago before McLaren brought a notable car upgrade to Budapest, are firmly back on?

To view this content you can use the button below to allow Monterosa cookies for this session only. Enable Cookies Allow Cookies Once

Just how well is Norris driving?

Four weeks on from a supreme showing at the Hungarian Grand Prix, when he claimed the first Grand Prix pole and win of his world title defence, Norris was impressive again throughout the Zandvoort weekend on the sport's return to action.

But he was initially left frustrated on Saturday after finishing third in the Sprint.

Norris' concern centred on McLaren's long-run pace after Charles Leclerc overtook him with six laps remaining in the shorter-form race. The Ferrari driver was running on soft tyres that even he had expected to be past their best by that stage, making his ability to pull clear of Norris' medium-shod McLaren all the more concerning.

Norris later confirmed McLaren's single-lap pace was certainly strong by taking pole position for the main Grand Prix, but his 'celebrations' in parc ferme were noticeably muted.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Charles Leclerc overtakes Lando Norris in a 'beautiful' move to take second place.

Saturday's frustration made the nature of his win on Sunday all the sweeter.

Asked how highly he rated his 13th career triumph, Norris said: "Pretty high just from a point of just very well fought in many ways.

"More than that is, you know, the turnaround from yesterday to today. I was pretty disappointed yesterday. It kind of took a little bit of the fire out of me, seeing how much we struggled in the Sprint.

"I know it's just a Sprint, but, you know, every point matters and we just really didn't have the pace. I didn't have that something that gave me life inside the car.

"Last night we worked very, very hard. I spent a lot of time with my engineers to kind of understand what we could do better today, how to push more, save the tyres more, how to do everything in a better way than I've done and better than everyone else. And I certainly believe I did that today."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from the 2026 Dutch Grand Prix.

Having taken time to adapt to the complexities of F1's new regulations, and for McLaren to get on top of car and power-unit performance, Norris now feels back in a place to "make a difference".

"Of course I'm never one to over-talk about myself, normally always the complete opposite," he said.

"But for once I would give myself a little bit of credit that I feel like I'm doing a better job than everyone, and I think that can also make a difference."

Team principal Andrea Stella said after Sunday's race that Norris is "driving and operating at a very high level in absolute sense in relation to a Formula 1 world champion".

Stella added: "Lando is definitely now expressing a higher level of assertiveness as he drives. The manoeuvre on Antonelli is a really good demonstration of that.

"He's demonstrating more self confidence and the self-confidence sometimes is not demonstrated by being the most aggressive.

"Sometimes you are self-confident when you think like, 'you know what, I'm not going to have a fight now because I may lose in this fight, it's a very long race. See you at the end of the race'."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Kimi Antonelli storms past Lando Norris to take the lead in the Dutch Grand Prix on the restart.

Does Norris now have the quickest car?

Although Antonelli, who turns 20 on Tuesday, has continued to barely put a foot wrong in the championship-leading Mercedes despite his inexperience, the team's early-season advantage over McLaren and Ferrari has been steadily eroded. Mercedes' relative lack of recent upgrades has allowed both rivals to close the gap, with McLaren in particular making significant gains in recent races.

Sky Sports F1's Nico Rosberg believes Zandvoort showed that the Norris-McLaren combination is now the one to beat on track.

"A world champion's drive by Lando," said Rosberg, the 2016 world champion.

"Who would have thought, in Melbourne McLaren were nine tenths behind Mercedes and now Lando is the guy to beat?

"What a rest of the season we have ahead of us now."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player The Ferrari team-mates nearly came together in the final stages of the race as Lando Norris took the Dutch GP victory.

Antonelli, whose Mercedes team have won only two of the last six races having won all of the year's first six, concurred: "We're clearly not the fastest car anymore on the grid.

"We're probably second or third, at least in today's race, and McLaren has taken a huge step, especially since Hungary, since the big upgrade package they brought."

Norris, though, who speaks openly and now with the experience of knowing what it takes to win a title, said that while McLaren had clearly improved significantly, in his view the MCL40 was not yet on ready to take another crown.

He told Sky Sports F1: "We are doing everything we can. I can only ask for so much. I clearly have a very, very strong car and it's been amazing and I'm very pleased and happy for the team to see how much progress we have made.

"We have improved by over a second to the beginning of the year comparing to our competitors. We have probably brought even more performance to ourselves this year. So I'm very happy with the car. If you want me to be confident and if you want me to say 'yeah, I can still fight for a championship' I need more than what I have now.

"And that's not to say I'm not pleased that I can win a race here and win in Budapest, but I know what's needed in a season. I know what kind of a car I need; I know to the level I need to perform at."

Is a Norris title comeback truly on?

At 83 points back - and with three drivers to catch ahead of him in the standings - Norris is clearly still a championship outsider at this stage of a campaign which features a scheduled 11 races left.

He would arguably perhaps not even be yet considered to be really in the mix from so far back had Verstappen effectively not redefined the meaning of a championship comeback last year.

Drivers' Championship - Top 5 Driver Points 1) Kimi Antonelli 242 2) George Russell 183 (+59) 3) Lewis Hamilton 183 (+59) 4) Lando Norris 159 (+83) 5) Charles Leclerc 155 (+87)

It was this week last year that Verstappen fell 104 points behind then-leader Oscar Piastri with nine races to go at the Dutch GP. The Dutchman had not won for eight grands prix and Red Bull appeared to be struggling to get on top of their 2025 car.

But a breakthrough in car performance, coupled with some scintillating and relentless driving from Verstappen, sparked an almighty fightback against the McLarens over the closing months of the season. He moved ahead of Piastri in the standings at the season's penultimate round in Qatar, but ultimately fell just two points short of Norris in the title race at the Abu Dhabi finale, having trailed the Brit by 70 points after Zandvoort.

Norris admitted Verstappen's feat served as encouragement for him a year on, although quipped that he would also need some of the late-season good fortune that Verstappen enjoyed at McLaren's expense.

"Obviously, we were on the not-so-good end of it last year," said Norris of being the title leaders. "But there's no point thinking about it.

"I honestly don't care what I'm doing next weekend or the weekend after. It's nice to know that it's a possibility, and of course I'm hoping both Mercedes get a double DSQ in Vegas like we did and decide not to box in Qatar for a free pit stop. So as long as they make the same mistakes, it'll probably be just as easy!"

Verstappen's winning run started at the Italian Grand Prix, when he unexpectedly beat the McLarens to victory, and F1's return to Monza next week could again serve as a pivotal weekend in this year's title battle.

It is already known that Antonelli will be compromised by a grid penalty for engine usage, meaning rivals should have a greater chance than normal of take more points out of the Italian's title lead than they could normally hope to.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Mercedes team-mates Kimi Antonelli and George Russell reflect on their Dutch Grand Prix race.

Stella admitted high-speed Monza would truly show how competitive McLaren's car was for the run-in.

"If we think about the demand of Zandvoort and Hungary, and then we think about the demand of Monza, we are in a completely different regime," he said.

"If we can confirm our improvements in Monza, I would say, yes, we can look with some optimism for the remainder of the season."

For Norris, who has yet to achieve three race wins on the spin in F1, a big result in the back yard of both Antonelli and Ferrari would certainly give credence to early talk of his own version of Verstappen's 2025 fightback.

Sports.title: Saints skipper Hastings gets three-game ban for punch
Sports.content:
St Helens captain Jackson Hastings' season could be over after being handed a three-match ban for violent conduct following his sending off in their win over Castleford Tigers on Saturday.

Hastings was dismissed in the first half of the 36-12 victory after punching Castleford's Tyler Dupree, who was sin-binned for the same incident.

Commenting on Hastings' dismissal, Castleford director of rugby Chris Chester told Sky Sports: "Scott Murrell just jumped (in the way of Dupree). We all know the rules, you can't punch people in the face."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Super League clash between St Helens and Castleford Tigers.

The win keeps Saints' play-off hopes alive, though they are currently on 28 points and seventh in the standings, one place outside of the play-off positions with three games to go.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player There were jubilant scenes at the full-time whistle as St Helens kept their play-off hopes alive with victory over Wakefield Trinity, with players and supporters celebrating together in the stands.

It means that should they fail to leapfrog one of Hull KR (sixth, 30 points), Leigh Leopards (fifth, 32 points) or Wakefield Trinity (fourth, 32 points) down the stretch, Hastings will have played his last match of the season.

Current Super League leaders Leeds Rhinos, as well as Wigan Warriors - tied on 38 points but with an inferior point differential - and Warrington Wolves, two back in third, have already qualified for the play-offs.
