Sports.title: Julián Alvarez walks alone at Atlético in transfer saga with no end – and no winners | Sid Lowe
Sports.content:
Julián Alvarez entered a long, dark tunnel on his own. “We’re stronger together,” Giuliano Simeone said but that wasn’t the way it went. At the end of their first home game of the season, a 2-2 draw with Villarreal, all of Atlético Madrid’s players gathered by the centre circle, shook hands with their opponents and each other, then headed towards the south end of the Metropolitano. Almost all of them did, anyway: one was left behind. Somebody in a suit had a quiet word then the press officer came, pointing in the other direction. So, while his teammates turned to the supporters who had turned on him, the man wearing No 19 went west, to the exit.

Alvarez walked alone. Head down in silence, as he had been all afternoon and beyond, he set off slowly across the pitch accompanied only by his thoughts and the whistles that followed him. Not offered a hand to shake or a nod of acknowledgment, he stepped past the Atlético badge on the touchline where the mouth of the tunnel opens. Either side, supporters hung over the void, whistling and shouting. Way off to his left, Atlético’s other players paused, seemingly waiting for him to slip out of sight before approaching the stand, but none turned back. A scarf was thrown, landing at Alvarez’s feet and left lying there. And then he disappeared into the dark, a portrait of the place he is in.

No one was waiting for him on the other side. Alvarez went up the stairs, past a couple of security guards and turned left to an empty dressing room, not lifting his gaze and not invited to either. Four minutes would pass before his teammates came up the stairs together. But at least it was quiet now, for a little while. The noise had been loud; no one could recall supporters turning on their own player quite like this. Atlético’s fans, still his fans, had whistled him when his name was read out, whistled him when he had warmed up, whistled him when he came on wearing red and white there for the first time since April and since he declared it his “dream” to leave, and they had whistled him out of there too, for good.

Good? “Unhappily, this situation isn’t comfortable for anyone,” Jan Oblak said, and amid the damage done, the mutual accusations, the hurt pride and spited faces, nor is it easy to see a solution. The situation, in short, is this: Julián Alvarez wants to leave for Barcelona. Barcelona want to sign him. But he has a contract until June 2030, a €500m buyout clause, and Atlético won’t sell him. And definitely not to them. And so, here they are. Stuck.

View image in fullscreen Julián Alvarez trudges off the pitch alone as his Atlético Madrid teammates applaud the fans. Photograph: Manu Reino/DeFodi Images/Shutterstock

The first time Alvarez hinted he may not continue was after facing Tottenham in the Champions League last March. The timing seemed odd then: it hadn’t been an easy season, the feeling that something was wrong growing and about to be confirmed, but he had just scored twice and Atlético had won 5-2. It seemed odder still when he chose the moments after Argentina beat Austria at the World Cup to announce he wanted to go. “It’s not the time to talk about this but nor can I hide,” he said. “I spoke with the people I needed to [at Atlético] and the best thing for everyone is a transfer. I want to fulfil my dream.”

There had been a “bid” that wasn’t really a bid at all from Real Madrid but the dream was Barcelona and they were the ones who had been speaking to Alvarez, planning how to make it happen. Which was one of the reasons why Atlético were so determined it wouldn’t, deciding to take a stand instead, make this a cause. This was not about him wanting to go, or not only, but about the way it had been done.

From New York, Joan Laporta claimed that Barcelona had made an “important” offer. “If Atlético are prepared to accept, fantastic,” he said, but they weren’t and they didn’t think much of the offer either. Atlético’s chief executive, Miguel Ángel Gil Marín, insisted they would not sell at any price: they had told Alvarez, his agent and Barcelona that. “I know Joan: he’s always acting up for the media, fans, his own personal circus,” Gil Marín said. “I told him: ‘Leave it, please. We don’t want to sell and won’t sell, stop insisting’. He loves to play the part but he knows perfectly well that Julián won’t play for Barcelona next season.”

Barcelona insisted that they had approached a potential transfer the right way, with “respect”, but Atlético reported them to the RFEF (Spanish Football Federation) and refused to budge, a statement made, territory defended. This had become a point of principle, examples to be made of them. The noise though refused to go away. When Alvarez arrived for pre-season, still wanting out, he cut an isolated figure. If every silence and furrowed brow was analysed to death, it was true that there was an absence about him. This weekend Jorge Valdano took a line from Julio Cortázar to explain it: “When someone says they’re going, they’re already gone.”

Even if they’re not going. While Atlético quietly investigated other options, Gil Marín gave a statement again insisting that Alvarez was staying. “We can’t allow other clubs and media to dictate our policy and disrespect us,” he said. “We have values.” He attacked Alvarez’s agent too, saying that Alvarez had been poorly advised. To which Fernando Hidalgo – whose version has Atlético promising that if Alvarez publicly said he wanted to go, taking responsibility, they would allow him to – replied with a post: “Never ask a liar to explain why he lied; he would only have to lie again.”

As for the coach, watching his superiors take the lead, he was ready to put Alvarez back in the team. “You can’t be clearer than the club’s been. It’s like when the judge says: ‘Denied!’,” Simeone said. As if it was that simple, the case so easily dismissed. While Atlético said they would “look after” him, while accusing Barcelona and Hidalgo lifted some blame from his shoulders, Alvarez’s return instead underlined that coming back from this might be even harder than anticipated, redemption more of a reach than imagined.

View image in fullscreen Diego Simeone left Julián Alvarez (bottom right) on the bench to start with. Photograph: Sheng Cheng/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

Sunday did not suggest a solution, a moment for the healing to start. Instead, it felt unsustainable, the case eclipsing all else, pressure building to find a proper conclusion. This was a fun match, but it was all about one man, the bad guy, and the verdict against him – and that affects everyone, maybe no winners any more. After the game there was a moment when, hands raised in front of him, the press officer asked journalists if there were any more questions, pausing to add … about the game … and the hands went down again. Before it, every photographer gathered in front of the bench as Alvarez took up his place to the left of Juan Musso and José María Gimenez, staring at the floor, the only movement his clenching jaw, while 60,000 people whistled his name. That, it turned out, was just the beginning.

Quick Guide La Liga results Show Rayo Vallecano 1-1 Alavés, Real Betis 1-0 Real Sociedad, Espanyol 1-2 Real Madrid, Valencia 0-0 Celta Vigo, Athletic Club 1-3 Sevilla, Elche 0-5 Barcelona, Getafe 1-0 Racing de Santander, Atlético Madrid 2-2 Villarreal Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

When he went to warm up on 51 minutes, they whistled again. From the south end, there were chants of “Fuck Barcelona! Fuck Catalonia!” They sang: “We are Atlético”. And “Atlético yes, mercenaries no!” Another one ran: “Tell him to go, once and for fucking all!” (To which Alvarez might have thought: yeah, that’s what I’m trying to do). As Atlético’s players came to the touchline after their first goal, the fitness coach said Alvarez was about to go on. “Careful, eh,” Marc Pubill replied. The noise when he did was deafening and didn’t relent. There weren’t many touches but with every one the angry volume rose, the rejection not receding all the way to the final whistle, which was not the final whistle at all: that too was for Alvarez. With eight days left in the window, it could still have been a good riddance, but … if it’s not?

“Julián is with us in the team and for as long as he is, we’re going to support him,” Oblak said. “All I know is that if Atlético want to win titles we have to be together, we need strikers and we need important strikers,” Simeone noted, admitting he had apologised to Ademola Lookman for making him play there in the absence of Alvarez and the injured Alex Sørloth. They do have strikers, the coach said the second time he turned to that line, but they would have to “take care” of them, the coach confirming that the club had told him it was their decision that he shouldn’t greet the fans, not Julián’s.

Yet if it had been designed to protect Alvarez and if this statement had too, absolving him of having chosen to turn his back on them, it also exposed him. Leaving first without the others, none joining him, served as an expression of his isolation, his othering, of how broken the situation had become. “Together we’re stronger, that’s always characterised us, made Atlético Madrid different. He is our player so we will die for him on the pitch,” Giuliano said, but when the time came, Alvarez went alone.

Sports.title: Liverpool are still haunted by the mess of last summer | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
The good news for Liverpool is that, Arsenal aside, every other team with vague title aspirations who played over the weekend looked undercooked, and that Andoni Iraola’s men did, in the end, come away from Newcastle with a point. But the vulnerability to the counter that undermined them so often last season has not gone away, and nor have they suddenly found a new creativity under Iraola.

The main theme of the first three days of the new season was the value of stability. Manchester City under a new manager were poor and fortunate to overcome Bournemouth. Aston Villa, after big changes of players and backroom staff, were hammered at Brighton. Tottenham, midway through yet another overhaul, were dismal in losing at Brentford. Manchester United at least provided a degree of stability by looking very much like the United of the past decade in their defeat to Hull.

Liverpool, for much of the first 96 minutes of their fixture at St James’ Park, looked like joining the list of challengers struggling to emerge from a summer of churn. Arne Slot spent much of last season complaining about how opponents always scored with their first chance and about Liverpool’s inability to deal with direct attacks, and as Anthony Elanga put Newcastle ahead, it seemed that not much had changed. Joe Willock’s goal to restore the Newcastle lead was much the same: opponents running at pace through vacant space.

What is odd is how pressing the need for a replacement for Fabinho has been since the defensive midfielder left in 2023. Even as Liverpool won the league under Slot in 2024-25, the discussion was of how the squad needed of an overhaul, and how a dedicated holding player to operate alongside Ryan Gravenberch was a priority. Which was what made the spending spree of last summer so surprising: it wasn’t so much who came in as who didn’t.

Without a holding midfielder, the flaws of the centre of defence, where Virgil van Dijk’s lack of pace on the turn is becoming increasingly obvious, are magnified. Liverpool could perhaps get away with it were he prepared to operate 10 yards higher in possession but the 35-year-old, aware of his ageing legs and worried about balls played in behind him, instinctively drops deeper, giving opponents just the sort of opportunities that Yoane Wissa kept exploiting on Sunday.

Iraola insisted it wasn’t “just about personnel” – which itself seemed an implicit acknowledgment that it is in part about personnel. Had he scored, Iraola said, everybody would have praised Gravenberch, who had advanced to the edge of the Newcastle box in the attack that led to the first Liverpool concession. “I don’t want us to take that from his game but we have to adapt as a team to these situations,” said Iraola. “We have to know these situations can happen.”

Of Newcastle’s second goal, he said: “It wasn’t like they caught us by surprise. We should compete for the first ball and probably make a foul – be a bit more aggressive against the ball carrier. There were different reasons for both the goals which happened in transition. We have been preparing in the week for these transitions but there’s a reason why Newcastle are so good at them. It’s not just because one person is playing there. It’s something we have to correct between a lot of players.”

But conceding on the break isn’t the only familiar issue for Liverpool. Their full-backs, Jeremie Frimpong and Milos Kerkez, were unconvincing. Alexander Isak, booed throughout by the home fans, rarely looked dangerous in the first full 90 minutes he has completed since his British record transfer from Newcastle last summer. Florian Wirtz produced a characteristic performance full of neat touches and little incision.

Iraola’s career suggests it often takes him time to instil his ideas at clubs. There is no reason for panic. Liverpool at least had the resilience to come back and pinch the draw. It’s not like any side other than Arsenal has looked particularly impressive. But perhaps there does need to be a reconsideration of what has gone before.

The familiar narrative is that Slot drove the car that Jürgen Klopp had put together to a league title and was then found wanting. But while the Dutchman cannot escape blame for last season, an equally valid interpretation might be that Slot coaxed an ageing team to an unexpected league title. Then, with an overhaul badly needed – Jamie Carragher wasn’t alone in speaking towards the end of that season of Liverpool needing half a dozen new players – he was let down by those charged with recruitment.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Michael Edwards left his role as chief executive for football at Fenway Sports Group, which owns Liverpool, in July, but the mess caused by last summer’s spree endures. Of the six most expensive signings of last summer for a combined fee of around £410m (about $560m), the only one who has looked remotely impressive, Hugo Ekitike, is still out for months with a ruptured achilles. Rarely has so much been spent in football to such destructive effect.

Sports.title: Rennes push PSG all the way to show they are the best of the rest in Ligue 1
Sports.content:
On the scale of expressions of prowess and power, Paris Saint-Germain bringing almost €150m worth of attacking talent off the bench – including the man who scored the winning goal in the World Cup final last month – ranks only a couple of rungs below the level of the extravagant aggression of a military parade. Imposing, dominating, reasserting, this wasn’t about expression but necessity as the reigning European champions initially floundered against a Rennes team that lived up to their billing as the best of the rest in Ligue 1.

PSG were forced into rolling out their new attacking arsenal early. For 45 minutes, Rennes’ incessant pressing and fluidity in transition had Luis Enrique’s side under duress. Sebastien Szymanski opened the scoring with a sliced effort from outside the box that clipped in off the inside of a post.

PSG had territorial dominance but could not equalise. Two former Rennes players – Désiré Doué and Ousmane Dembélé – had the best chances, the latter particularly wasteful with a skied first-time effort from inside the box. Esteban Lepaul, the top scorer in Ligue 1 last season, picked up where he left off, beating Matvey Safonov with a first-time effort towards the near post to double Rennes’ lead.

A reaction was needed, and it drew a very strong one from Luis Enrique. Off came perhaps the two most talented players in the league, Dembélé and Khvicha Kvaratskhelia. On came Ferran Torres and Mika Godts, signed for a combined fee of nearly €100m, at half-time. The former hauled PSG back into the game.

In the meantime, the €50m signing Maghnes Akliouche had come on for his Ligue 1 debut for the champions, as had Fabián Ruiz and it was the Spanish connection that ensured a point for PSG. Ruiz teed up both of Torres’ goals, the first after an exquisitely timed run in behind from the former Barcelona forward and the second a close-range header. Willian Pacho was called upon in the dying moments, making a goalline clearance to secure the draw.

“If you think about what you’ve won, you won’t win anything else. You have to show every day that you are ready,” said Luis Enrique when asked about his decision to replace Dembélé and Kvaratskhelia. He added that there had been a “a big difference in rhythm” between Rennes and PSG.

View image in fullscreen Ferran Torres scored twice for PSG in their 2-2 draw against Lens. Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/Reuters

PSG’s lethargy is no surprise; it was only the nature of their opponents – Nantes and Angers – that prevented them from slipping up at the start of last season, once again after limited preparation time. “We have to be more ready,” said Luis Enrique. The same applies to the groundstaff at the Parc des Princes. The state of PSG’s pitch meant this game moved last minute to Roazhon Park; it suited Rennes, especially if, as they argue should be the case, the second game is also played at their home ground.

There is a burgeoning positivity around Roazhon Park. While the prospects of other challengers have dwindled, Rennes’ have multiplied. The wealth of the Breton club’s owners, the Pinault family, has bought them a form of immunity to the financial crisis that has now struck down Marseille and Monaco; other challengers: Lille, Lyon, Strasbourg and Lens are consigned to stagnation, for now.

Rennes approached the season looking second-best on paper, and after Sunday night, that perception now aligns with reality. Rennes fended off competition from the Premier League to sign the England youth international Charlie Cresswell from Toulouse. One of the best defenders in Ligue 1 last season, he was excellent against PSG; in Adrien Thomasson, Rennes also acquired the most valuable piece of Lens’ success last season, arguably the best midfielder in the division, and on a free, no less. And in Lepaul, they have a prolific striker who is very much in contention to be in Zinedine Zidane’s first France squad next month.

They have a strong spine and a brilliant manager. Franck Haise began his managerial career as a youth coach at Rennes, and they were only too happy to bring him back in February after things turned sour at Nice. There has always been the perception that there has been a missing piece in the puzzle at Rennes. Despite their means, their talented squad, their renowned academy, they had reached a ceiling. Questionable managerial appointments played their part. Haise may well be the right man, the missing part.

“There is more positive than negative,” he said after the 2-2 draw. The negative is the way the two points were ceded, a laxness creeping in, particularly from Abdelhamid Aït-Boudlal, who is nonetheless another exciting prospect. The positive is that Rennes did not look second-best on the night, but they could be come the end of the season, and for all clubs in Ligue 1, that has to be the aspiration. PSG flexed their muscles, but only because Rennes made them.

Quick Guide Ligue 1 results Show Ligue 1 results Angers 0-2 Lille Le Havre 0-1 Monaco Rennes 2-2 PSG Lens 5-2 Auxerre Le Mans 2-2 Brest Nice 0-0 Lorient Toulouse 0-2 Lyon Troyes 0-0 Paris FC Marseille 4-0 Strasbourg Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Talking points

Strasbourg should be worried after their 4-0 defeat to Marseille. They had to replace Gary O’Neil in the summer when he moved to Ipswich but there are doubts about Hugo Oliveira. This is not a vintage Marseille side, but they looked it as they put four past goalkeeper Filip Jörgensen, who is on loan from Chelsea. Strasbourg’s cause was not aided by a petulant Samir El Mourabet kick on Pierre-Emile Højbjerg, which rightly earned the Morocco international a red card on the hour mark. Conceding 21 goals in seven friendlies can be dismissed as “just pre-season”, but when that form carries into the campaign, there may be a problem for a club with European ambitions.

Despite losing Pierre Sage and the spine of their side, Lens did not look any weaker as they swept aside Auxerre on Will Still’s return to the Beaujoire, winning 5-2. The former Lens manager, who is back in Ligue 1 after a failed stint at Southampton, saw his side comprehensively beaten thanks in part to an inspired Florian Thauvin. Now wearing the captain’s armband, he scored twice and set up another as Dino Toppmöller got off to a roaring start as Lens manager. European football will provide a fresh challenge once it arrives in September, but this emphatic win eases fears that last season was a flash in the pan.

The matches in Marseille, Le Mans and Nice were preceded by tributes to Éric Roy, who was still in his post as Brest manager when he died from pancreatic cancer in June. Roy led Brest in the club’s first ever European campaign in the 2024-25 season. “We have him in our thoughts,” said Julien Lachuer, an internal appointment at the club over the summer. The new era at Brest began with a draw against Le Mans on Saturday.

Sports.title: Amorim’s Milan live up to billing as teenage star Cissè upstages signings | Nicky Bandini
Sports.content:
“I love Cissè. I love Cissè.” Ruben Amorim had not yet taken charge of his first competitive game as Milan head coach but already he was furnishing journalists with soundbites and supporters with memes, clippable moments that you just knew we were destined to revisit.

Alphadjo Cissè is a 19-year-old attacking midfielder who signed for Milan from Verona in February but only joined up with them this summer, after completing the season-long loan he had already begun at Catanzaro in Serie B. He scored six goals in 22 games there, missing the second half of the campaign with a thigh injury. Previously he had played a combined 14 minutes for Verona across three substitute appearances in the top flight.

Yet Amorim spoke of Cissè like a man who knew something that the rest of the world doesn’t. More than his words, it was the body language: hands rubbing together in anticipation, lip curled at one corner into an emoji-like version of a smirk.

Cissè would start away to Torino the following evening. Within 75 seconds of kick-off, he had taken the first shot of the game: racing forward to hook a Ruben Loftus-Cheek cross into the side netting from an acute angle beyond the far post.

For an Italian teenager to make Milan’s first XI on the opening weekend was already a significant detail. The scarce opportunities afforded to young domestic talent in Serie A has been a national talking point ever since the Azzurri failed to qualify for a third consecutive men’s World Cup.

Data compiled by Football Benchmark found that Italians who qualified for the under-21 category accounted for only 3.9% of minutes played last season, while foreign players in that age group took 8.2%: “In other words, young foreign players receive more than twice as many opportunities as their Italian counterparts.”

There were signs of a possible shift this weekend. The season began with 21-year-old Pio Esposito delivering a man-of-the-match performance for the champions, Inter, in their 4-1 win over Monza, but he was the exception who stood apart already last year.

More surprising were the new faces popping up elsewhere. Cissè, born in Treviso to Guinean parents, was one of three Italian teenagers on the pitch at the Olympic stadium in Turin, with Diego Mascardi and Alessio Cacciamani, both 19, lining up at goalkeeper and left wing-back for the Granata.

View image in fullscreen Ruben Amorim won his first Serie A match in charge against Ignazio Abate’s Torino. Photograph: Daniele Mascolo/Reuters

The 18-year-olds Matteo Palma (an Italian-German dual national) and Simone Lontani started for Udinese and Parma respectively, and the 19-year-old Mathis Mout for Monza. Even Como, whose project has been criticised for relying almost exclusively on foreign talent, gave Mattia Liberali, 19, some minutes off the bench. It is far too soon to draw conclusions, but certainly a trend worth tracking.

In any case, putting your faith in untested young talent can feel like a greater gamble for a club with Milan’s expectations. After a disappointing fifth-place finish last season under Massimiliano Allegri, the Rossoneri have spent big – appointing Amorim and then dropping a club-record €74m to sign Gonçalo Ramos from Paris Saint-Germain, as well as another €50m on the midfielder Diego Moreira from Strasbourg and €30m on the defender Mario Gila from Lazio.

Amorim has not shied away from ambition, saying his goal is to win the Scudetto, even while acknowledging it may take time to bridge the gap to Inter. More than that, he has won over fans with the promise of a front-footed team who will seek to set the tempo and dictate how games are played – a welcome change from the caution and reactivity of Allegri.

There were promising performances in pre-season – not least the 4-2 win over Amorim’s last club, Manchester United, with Cissè on the scoresheet. But friendlies are not the real thing. Sunday’s visit to a Torino side undergoing a renewal of their own under a new head coach, and former Milan player, Ignazio Abate, was always going to be a fascinating first challenge.

Ramos and Gila started, at centre-forward and on the right of defence. Moreira, who only completed his move on 19 August, stayed on the bench. Cissè was the other truly new face, playing to the left of Ramos in a 3-4-2-1, though Yunus Musah and the right wing-back Samuel Chukwueze were also returning after spending last season out on loan.

Amorim’s approach lived up to billing. From the start, Milan dominated the ball and the pitch – claiming more than 70% of first-half possession while outshooting their opponents by 11 to one. And yet, they struggled to break Torino down in the final third. Aside from one solo effort by Chukwueze, who dribbled in from the right and forced a save from Mascardi, they had rarely looked like scoring.

Quick Guide Serie A results Show Parma 0-1 Cagliari, Genoa 0-2 Napoli, Udinese 1-1 Como, Inter 4-1 Monza, Torino 1-2 Milan, Atalanta 2-1 Sassuolo, Venezia 0-2 Lecce, Frosinone 0-1 Juventus Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

Cissè thought he had earned Milan a penalty after the interval, when his cross struck the arm of Nikola Vlasic. That the VAR booth did not call the referee, Luca Zufferli, to take a second look may be an early indicator – together with incidents from other games – of a shift in approach under the new refereeing designator, Daniele Orsato. He has stated a desire to “put referees back at the centre of the match” and return to the idea that technology should only be used for those elusive “clear and obvious” mistakes.

Torino were growing into the game. But that might also have been their undoing. In the 64th minute, Musah turned his man in midfield, surging into space left open by the home team’s press. He fed Adrien Rabiot, a second-half substitute, on the right. The Frenchman crossed to Cissè, who brought the ball down with his waist and curled a half volley into the far corner. The teenager slid to his knees as he celebrated in front of the away fans.

Within moments it was 2-0, Rabiot himself converting a Chukwueze delivery. Torino kept battling, and Scotland’s Ché Adams scored the best goal of the game in injury time, an outrageously nonchalant right-foot volley over his own left shoulder. But the three points went to Milan.

Cissè laughed when the interviewer from Dazn asked him at full time what he thought about Amorim’s professions of love. “It makes me happy,” he said. “But I didn’t hear the press conference. All my friends told me about it instead.”

View image in fullscreen Alphadjo Cissè’s half volley gives Milan the lead in Turin. Photograph: Valerio Pennicino/Getty Images

He was still recovering from injury when he first joined up with Milan this summer. Cissè said he had tried to watch training as closely as possible, getting to know what the head coach wanted. Still, he acknowledged, it was “beyond a dream” to get to start, and score, in the season opener.

The numbers say he is the youngest Italian to score for Milan since Patrick Cutrone in 2017, as well as the first Italian to score for them on a debut Serie A start since Daniel Maldini in 2021. Those names should remind everyone not to get ahead of themselves. Cutrone, now 28, was a substitute for Monza this weekend and has only reached double figures for goals once in a top-flight season. Maldini, 24, has played for seven clubs since 2022, and begins this campaign with Cagliari.

But Amorim clearly thinks highly of Cissè, who has represented Italy at various age categories up to under-21, saying he looked at times in the first-half like the most experienced player on the pitch.

The head coach, conducting his interviews mostly in English, said Milan have “a lot to improve”, acknowledging both their struggles to break Torino down early on and the way they faded at the end. “[But] the first thing is also win. That is the most important thing. We talk about ways of playing, but there is one goal in calcio. Vincere.”

Sports.title: Football Daily | The Premier League soap opera is back – and Spurs are already hogging the narrative
Sports.content:
STUNG BY THE BEES

While the opening round of Premier League fixtures hasn’t yet concluded, Football Daily can’t be alone in having jerked both knees to the point of dislocation based on the evidence of what little we’ve seen thus far. Newly-promoted Hull City look the most likely contenders to challenge Arsenal for the title. Ipswich Town’s Julio Enciso already looks a shoo-in for the Ballon d’Or. Eddie Howe will be head coach of Manchester United by the end of the next international break – if Aston Villa don’t nab him first. And judging by James Trafford’s endearingly heartfelt post-match soliloquy on Match of the Day, Leeds United’s gain is very much the Royal Shakespeare Company’s loss.

“Who cares, just enjoy it … just have a right go,” exhorted the Leeds keeper in plummy tones, channelling his inner Kenneth Branagh as he pondered the futility of folk getting too bent out of shape over the occasional setback during a meandering top-flight campaign. Of course while Trafford is correct in his assertion that things don’t always go swimmingly for even the best of teams, Tottenham fans were genuinely buoyed by optimism going into their curtain-raiser after two seasons of watching their under-performing club circling the drain. Excited by the sight of their owners hosing a bazillion pounds upon a Supermarket Sweep-style summer transfer market trolley-dash that shows little or no sign of abating, even the most pessimistic among them couldn’t have envisaged the absolute monstering their team would endure at the hands of Brentford.

“Bad game,” sniffed a crestfallen Roberto De Zerbi, after witnessing a textbook ‘Lads, it’s Tottenham’ performance in which his side were 3-0 down after just 49 minutes. “Our physical condition was not in the right level for all players because many came later after the [Geopolitics] World Cup and there were many new players in the squad and first XI.” While Andy Robertson, Marcos Senesi and Jan Paul van Hecke were the debutants who probably deserve a pass having returned late from their summer exertions, the same cannot be said for Spurs’ spanking new £100m midfielder Sandro Tonali, whose country hasn’t troubled a World Cup since he was 14. The Italian was completely overshadowed by his Brentford counterpart Mamadou Sangaré, who was immeasurably more effective than Tonali for considerably less than half the transfer fee.

“It’s been really nice working with him and I think the club deserves a lot of credit for getting that deal done,” buzzed Bees boss Keith Andrews following the Malian’s bravura debut performance in the Premier League. “We [want to] be relentless, we want to approach the game in as aggressive a way as you can and as positive a way as you can but you can’t always do that because you’ve got to take backwards steps at times. Football’s a soap opera, that’s the reality of it – stories within the narrative. There’s goodies, there’s baddies and you need to live with that, whatever you’re dealt.” And of course, every ongoing soap needs its comic relief and for the third consecutive season, despite stiff opening weekend competition, that role already looks destined for Spurs.

Sports.title: EFL and Scottish league pushing to stop illegal broadcast of matches in Russia
Sports.content:
The English Football League and Scottish Professional Football League have launched investigations and are considering legal action after discovering that television coverage of their matches has been broadcast in Russia this season.

Football TV, a Russian subscription and streaming service, has broadcast numerous games from the opening two rounds of the EFL, as well as Scottish Premiership matches featuring Celtic, Rangers and Hearts.

The EFL and SPFL stopped broadcasting in Russia in March 2022 after the previous month’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and have not sold rights packages in the country since, so the live footage of games appears to have been obtained and televised illegally.

Quick Guide How do I 

Until Russia’s full-scale invasion the EFL had a rights contract with Football TV, and the Scottish Premiership was broadcast on Match TV.

The Premier League suspended its broadcasts in Russia at the same time, with its rights held by Okko Sport.

The EFL contacted Football TV last week after being alerted that several games, including Cardiff’s 1-1 draw with Wrexham last Monday and Watford’s 2-1 win over Southampton the previous day, were shown in Russia, but despite this complaint the broadcaster also aired live coverage of West Ham v Charlton and West Brom v Burnley this past weekend.

Those matches were listed as test events, raising concerns that Football TV may also plan to show illegal content from the Premier League.

Several Scottish Premiership matches were shown over the past two weekends, with the broadcasts promoted on Football TV’s Telegram channel.

The EFL and the SPFL’s priority is to ensure the broadcasts stop, which is being pursued, and they are seeking to discover the source of the pirated content.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Both organisations are understood to reserve the right to take legal action against Football TV and whoever is supplying it with access to their matches.

An SPFL source said the league was investigating the matter in conjunction with its broadcasting distribution rights holder, Infront.

The EFL and SPFL declined to comment.

Sports.title: Women’s Super League 2026-27 preview No 3: Birmingham City
Sports.content:
Guardian writers’ predicted position: 12th (NB: this is not necessarily Tom Garry’s prediction but the average of our writers’ tips)

Last season’s position: 1st (WSL2)

Prospects

Founding members of the Women’s Super League when it launched in 2011, Birmingham are back in the top flight after four years in the second tier, having won promotion as WSL2 champions on the final day of last season. After a decent summer transfer window, Birmingham look to have a fighting chance of staying up, and perhaps even surprising a few teams, while off the pitch they are the best-equipped of the three promoted sides to cement themselves in the top division.

Forwards Lily Crosthwaite and Wilma Leidhammar and defender Neve Herron, are all 23-years-old and likely to continue improving. Birmingham have also added players with WSL experience, such as the former Brighton goalkeeper Sophie Baggaley and the centre-back Millie Turner.

Inconsistency was nearly their downfall last season; they won the most games in WSL2, but also lost six times. They delivered under pressure, boosted by the performances of Leidhammar after her club-record arrival in January, ensuring they avoided a repeat of the heartbreak of 12 months earlier when they missed out on promotion on the final day. Nonetheless, Birmingham are still a long way off from the days when they were runners-up in the top tier and their first two away fixtures are against Manchester City and Chelsea. They also host fellow promoted sides Crystal Palace and Charlton relatively early in the campaign and those home fixtures could be key to building confidence.

Off-field picture

Birmingham’s women’s team were sold to the club’s ownership group in February, with Shelby Companies Limited – an affiliate of Knighthead Capital Management – owning 97%. The remaining 3% was purchased by investors including the former England midfielder Karen Carney and the four-time grand slam tennis champion Kim Clijsters. The club appear to be in a relatively healthy position with ambitious owners determined to reestablish the 2012 FA Cup winners as a regular, competitive presence in the WSL. They train at the recently renovated Knighthead Performance Centre, on the same site as the men’s team’s former Wast Hills training base, with a new gym among other extensive refurbishments.

The manager

Amy Merricks has been in charge since April 2024 She holds a Uefa Pro Licence and was 30 years old when she was appointed by Birmingham. She has previously coached within the England youth setup as well as at Gillingham, Millwall and Brighton, where was stepped up to be interim manager three times.

Star signing

View image in fullscreen Lisa Naalsund arrives from Manchester United to boost Birmingham’s midfield. Photograph: DeFodi Images/Getty Images

Birmingham have recruited players with international experience, including the Canada defender Marie Levasseur from Montpellier, but their two most eyebrow-raising additions are Turner and Lisa Naalsund from Manchester United. They were starting members of United’s FA Cup-winning side of 2024 and played in a Women’s Champions League quarter-final as recently as April. Naalsund will be an influential force in the midfield – she has won 39 caps and was part of Norway’s squad at last year’s Euros.

Stat attack

Birmingham topped WSL2 last season despite not scoring the most goals or conceding the fewest. One stat they led was big chances, Opta’s metric for opportunities where it is reasonable to expect the attacker to score. While their tally will be much harder to repeat in the top flight, their attacking process looks in good order.

Set for a breakthrough

There is plenty of excitement at Birmingham about another of their new signings, the 19-year-old France youth forward Chancelle Effa Effa, who arrived from Le Havre for a fee understood to be about €120,000 (£100,000) this month. She broke into Le Havre’s first team at the age of 15 and scored 17 times in 28 games for France’s Under-17 and Under-19 teams, having helped France win 2023’s Under-17 Euros.

What they say …

“We know it’s going to be a massive challenge, but it’s a challenge that, as players, you thrive upon. As long as we can take that togetherness, that relentlessness, into the games, I’m sure we’re going to be just fine” – Chelsea Cornet.

Where are they playing their home games?

Birmingham play their home fixtures at St Andrew’s, which has been the women’s team’s home since 2021. They set a club record attendance for a women’s game there on the final day of the 2024-25 season – 8,749. Long-term, the club have announced plans to build a new women’s team stadium as part of the ‘Sports Quarter’, which also includes the proposed 62,000-seater men’s team Powerhouse Stadium as well as an indoor arena, training ground facilities and a new railway station.

Sports.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from opening weekend of the season
Sports.content:
1 Wright laments Martinelli treatment

Arsenal’s treatment of Gabriel Martinelli has been questioned by Ian Wright after the Brazil forward was left out of their squad for Friday’s opening game against Coventry. Martinelli turned down a move to Galatasaray last week after Arsenal had agreed a fee with the Turkish club and the former striker Wright revealed on Sky Sports after the Coventry game that no one at the club has spoken to the 25-year-old to discuss his future. “I know they might want him out, and a lot of people might say: ‘Yeah, it’s time for him to move him on.’ But there’s ways of doing that and it should suit him as well, how he wants to leave,” said Wright. “He’s done enough with this squad to be treated with a little bit more respect than he’s being treated with at the moment.” Ed Aarons

Quick Guide Play our football trivia game, On the ball Show The Guardian's daily football game, On the ball, is now live in the app for both iOS and Android. Can you identify the Premier League star from the clues? Was this helpful? Thank you for your feedback.

2 Has Watkins tarnished legacy?

It was only one game after 278 for Aston Villa, accumulated over the previous six seasons – a period in which Ollie Watkins has scored 108 goals and made himself one of the most popular players in the club’s Premier League history. But the rules are the rules. Nobody can refuse to play and emerge without a mark against their character. This is the charge against Watkins, brought in none-too-subtle fashion by Unai Emery after Villa’s 4-0 defeat at Brighton – a match that Watkins missed as he considers an approach from Al-Hilal. We do not yet have Watkins’s side of the story. Or that of his agent. But given Emery had no other available No 9, it feels pretty clear the manager did not choose to omit Watkins. Villa claim they are not close to any agreement with Al-Hilal, having rejected more than one offer from them. Perish the thought that this could drag on. Villa have one more game before the window shuts – against Arsenal at home next Monday night. David Hytner

View image in fullscreen Unai Emery did nothing to deny that Ollie Watkins had refused to play for Villa in their sobering defeat. Photograph: Glyn Kirk/AFP/Getty Images

3 United falter as No 9 options look thin

Michael Carrick was limited in his options during Manchester United’s opener because Benjamin Sesko was unable to feature at any point in pre-season but Matheus Cunha was completely ineffective as a false 9. Hull’s back three enjoyed a very quiet lunchtime as they returned to the Premier League. Cunha did not embrace the physical battle and went missing, leaving United with barely any presence in the final third as they failed to threaten their opponents. Sesko was brought on to change the dynamic but was equally ineffectual, while his fellow striker Joshua Zirkzee was left on the bench, implying how little trust the coaches have in him. Carrick needs to get Sesko up to speed and sell Zirkzee soon, freeing up funds to find a better alternative if United are to compete this season, especially with the false 9 tactic looking flawed. Will Unwin

4 Tigers delight in Tzolakis’s debut

Manchester United were impressively unthreatening in their approach to losing at Hull. There was the odd half-baked attempt at scoring or putting a cross into a dangerous area but nothing that made the highlights reel. This was unfortunate for the Hull goalkeeper Konstantinos Tzolakis, who had an impressive, if somewhat uncomplicated, debut between the sticks. United should have made a greater effort to test the £20m signing from Olympiakos. What duties the Greek international was forced to do were carried out with ease, instilling confidence in the defence in front of him. If he continues to look so calm and assured, Tzolakis could prove himself one of the smartest signings of the season. “We bought him and we spent some money there,” Sergej Jakirovic said. “He’s a national-team player of Greece, an Olympiakos player. If you’re following Greek football, Olympiakos, it’s a huge stress, huge pressure there, and he’s used to it. For him, I think this is like a cup of tea.” WU

5 Cherki’s crucial cameo after disquiet

Rayan Cherki wrested the three points in a cameo that consisted of the corner for Marc Guéhi’s equaliser and the cute pass for Josko Gvardiol’s winner. Enzo Maresca gave an insight into the Frenchman’s disquiet at not starting. “Rayan is quite a nice and clear boy, if he is not happy he wants to show it. If he’s next to me and he’s not happy, you all realise that he is not happy because he is doing anything just to show that he is not happy. I know that he was not happy today but at the end I had to take a decision,” said the manager. Jamie Jackson

6 Sangaré shines against big spenders

At a time when some Premier League are willing to spend more than £100m on midfielders there is unlikely to be a better bargain than Mamadou Sangaré. Brentford’s new signing was excellent for Lens last season and was outstanding on his debut against Tottenham. Sangaré dominated midfield, even with Spurs able to field upwards of £175m worth of talent in Sandro Tonali and Mateus Fernandes, and his performance raised the question of why the league’s bigger clubs are not willing to look further afield for signings. Brentford, after all, paid only £39m for Sangaré. Yet it seems inevitable there will be clubs willing to pay double the price if he has a good first season in England. Jacob Steinberg

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

7 Isak struggles on return to Newcastle

As gut-wrenching as it must have been for Newcastle fans to see their side concede a stoppage-time penalty to Liverpool, at least they can take comfort that it wasn’t Alexander Isak that scored the Reds’ dramatic equaliser from 12 yards. The former Newcastle striker had a torrid time on his return to St James’ Park – booed at every touch, crunched by Lewis Hall in the tackle and sending his only real chance of note into orbit – but he would surely have fancied taking his revenge with the last kick of the game before Dominik Szoboszlai converted the 99th-minute spot-kick. Worryingly, Isak is lacking the fluency that convinced Liverpool to spend £125m last summer and with Hugo Ekitiké still sidelined with a long-term injury, Andoni Iraola doesn’t have a natural replacement at No 9. If Liverpool are to be successful this season, Isak has to turn it on. Michael Butler

View image in fullscreen Alexander Isak watches the ball during his return to Tyneside. Photograph: Molly Darlington/Getty Images

8 Ipswich combat set pieces with O’Shea

A defensive tactical shift from the Ipswich Town manager, Gary O’Neil, demonstrated the changing nature of the Premier League. O’Neil, an astute reader of the game, chose to play the tall centre-back Dara O’Shea at right-back to counter the threat of set pieces that have become so prevalent, in Ipswich’s surprise win against Sunderland. “Aerially the Premier League is such a test now, from long throws and set pieces,” O’Neil said. “To have three centre-half types in your back four helps us from set pieces, size-wise.” In the first season since Pep Guardiola departed, the top flight is already shifting away from his neat, passing football to a different beast. Sam Cunningham

9 Dewsbury-Hall on path to complete midfielder

David Moyes felt his young Everton team might have been uncomfortable chasing the game against Crystal Palace and were therefore indebted to Jordan Pickford’s save from Eddie Nketiah, plus Jean-Philippe Mateta’s finishing, for not having to do so. Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall’s guidance was instrumental too. The performance of both teams altered once the midfielder imposed himself, while his superb strike beyond Dean Henderson underlined the quality of a player who will be crucial to Everton’s aspirations. “I want to be better than last season,” said Dewsbury-Hall, who delivered eight goals and four assists in his first Premier League campaign at Everton. “That’s not just goals and assists, it’s my overall play. A couple of years ago I probably wasn’t getting goals and assists but was influential in play. I want to mix that together and when you do that that’s when you become a complete midfielder. I know I have the ability to do it so fingers crossed I do.” Andy Hunter

10 Farke hopes Leeds can cement status

Optimism abounds at Leeds. An encouraging opening-day victory at Nottingham Forest gave credence to the idea that Daniel Farke’s side are capable of cementing their place in the league. Last season, survival was the aim but after investing about £80m to sign James Trafford, Tarik Muharemovic and Nico Elvedi, plus Harry Wilson on a free, they are seeking to build on a 14th-placed finish. Leeds and Forest, who meet again in the Carabao Cup on Tuesday, have both been linked with a move for Chelsea’s Liam Delap; a striker to share the load with Dominic Calvert-Lewin would surely elevate Farke’s side. “If we want to establish ourselves and after a few years perhaps speak about something else, then we need to add individual quality,” Farke said. “The last time this club was able to have two solid seasons at this level, you will perhaps find it in black-and-white photos.” Ben Fisher

Sports.title: Why Julian Alvarez's war with Atletico Madrid could push him into Arsenal's arms: Striker shocked by fan backlash, Barcelona move NOT an option and how Viktor Gyokeres and Andrea Berta could get £130m deal done
Sports.content:
Julian Alvarez was left so stunned by the hostility he faced from Atletico Madrid fans on Sunday, that the option of moving to Arsenal is no longer completely off the table.

It remains the unsettled striker's absolute priority to move to Barcelona, but Atletico’s point-blank refusal to negotiate with their Catalan rivals could set up a deadline day emergency resolution to what is now a completely unsustainable situation.

Alvarez expected a harsh welcome on Sunday having said during the World Cup that it was his dream to move to Barcelona. His name was whistled by over 60,000 fans ahead of the game, and there was more of the same when he warmed up and when he came on as a 66th-minute substitute.

But the intensity of the reaction shocked him and what followed was even worse. At the end of the game when his team-mates went to supporters behind one of the goals the 26-year-old Argentinian walked off down the tunnel alone, stepping over an Atletico scarf, thrown his way, as he went.

It seemed the defining image of what looks like an irreversible divorce but there are still huge obstacles to be passed if the former Manchester City Treble winner is to return to England.

He has until now been adamant about keeping his young family in Spain. Arsenal are also understood to have some reservations over a player who has made such a big play for Barcelona.

Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez's relationship with the club is broken after he declared during the summer that he wants to move to Barcelona

The Argentine striker was booed on and off the pitch at the Metropolitano on Sunday - and now needs a way out of the club with Arsenal interested

I was commentating on Atletico’s draw on Sunday and along with every commentary team inside the stadium concluded - as he walked away from fans and team-mates - that he had done that on his own accord. But Atletico Madrid coach Diego Simeone said after the match that the club had decided he should not join the rest of the players. ‘The decision was not his,’ said Simeone.

Whoever made the call – and an Atletico Madrid press officer had approached Alvarez and spoken to him before he turned and left the pitch – it only served to further open the wounds that have been festering since the World Cup when he admitted: ‘I can’t hide it, I think the best thing is a transfer so I can fulfill my dream.’

Barcelona have so far only made one offer, two months ago, of £77million plus £8.6million in add-ons to be paid over six years, which Atletico Madrid have dismissed as derisory.

Barcelona could make a second offer this week but they do not have the financial muscle to get close to Atletico’s £130million price tag, and regardless, Atletico are adamant they will not sell to them.

Atletico Madrid’s sporting director Mateu Alemany was in London last week to negotiate a possible move for Chelsea’s Nicolas Jackson, that trip doubled up as an opportunity to speak to his opposite number at Arsenal, and predecessor at Atletico, Andrea Berta.

Berta’s Atletico connections would grease the wheels if the two clubs were to try to come to an agreement on how a move to sign Alverez would be structured.

The inclusion of Viktor Gyokeres in any deal would remedy Simeone’s demands for a top-class replacement, though the Sweden striker would not be his first choice in less-rushed circumstances. Simeone is a fan of Jackson and in such a chaotic scenario Chelsea emerging as surprise suitors for Alvarez cannot be ruled out - but it’s Arsenal who have been his long-term admirers.

Just how committed Arsenal would be to the deal if they were encouraged by the player’s camp remains to be seen.

Arsenal are also understood to have some reservations over a player who has made such a big play for Barcelona

Atletico Madrid coach Diego Simeone said after the match on Sunday that the club had decided Alvarez should not join the rest of the players in applauding the fans

Alvarez has not had a good pre-season, evidenced by a pedestrian 25 minutes on the pitch on Sunday. They would also be signing a player who has made no secret of his desire to be at another club.

One precedent that might allay some of those concerns is that of Sergio Aguero. He wanted to move to Real Madrid in 2011 and Atletico were so adamant that it would not happen they sold him for £42million to Manchester City, where he became a club legend.

Atletico’s determination that Aguero would not join Real Madrid pales into insignificance when compared to their refusal to sell Alvarez now to Barcelona. They have reported Barcelona to FIFA over what they believe was completely inappropriate behaviour during key moments of last season.

The versions of Alvarez's camp and Atletico’s differ wildly but what they agree on is that at the end of last year the player communicated to the club that he was unhappy.

Atletico felt they had gone out of their way to give him the support he and his young family needed. The player became a father in January 2026.

At first they continued to assure him they wanted the team to be built around him. But his response was that he felt Atletico’s style of football did not fit with his and he wanted to move on.

The club have briefed that they then told Alvarez’s agent, Fernando Hidalgo, that they were not going to retain the player against his will but that he would need to come up with the right offer and in the correct manner for them to facilitate his departure.

They wanted nothing to happen that would disrupt their season. They believe that in spite of that condition being set, conversations between Alvarez’s agent and Barcelona took place during the campaign and spiked around the time the two teams met in both the Spanish Cup and Champions League.

Arsenal's Viktor Gyokeres was an unused substitute for Friday night's victory over Coventry

Arsenal's sporting director Andrea Berta used to work for Atletico Madrid and his connections would help grease the wheels of any possible transfer

Bad blood continued to run right up to the start of the Spanish season when Atletico’s CEO, Miguel Angel Gil Marin, said Alvarez had been ‘badly advised’ by Hidalgo and the agent responded by posting on social media: ‘Don’t ask a liar to explain why he lied because he’ll just tell you another lie.’

The player’s £220,000-a-week wages would need to be matched at the Emirates, but Arsenal were prepared to pay far more to Vinicius Junior earlier this summer, while Bukayo Saka is also thought to be on more than £300,000 a week in north London. Real Madrid star Vinicius opted to stay put, such was his commitment to the club that had brought him to Europe.

This is a very different case. It’s difficult to think of another example of such animosity between a club and a player on such a long contract. Alvarez’s deal with Atletico runs until 2030.

The next six days will decide if that animosity has reached such a level that Arsenal becomes not just Alvarez's reluctant alternative but his only escape route from an unsalvageable situation.

Sports.title: Boxing legend's accusations of Trump's 'unbelievable' cheating on the golf course resurface weeks after President's latest win
Sports.content:
Accusations of Donald Trump's penchant for cheating at golf resurfaced weeks after he claimed a pair of victories in a championship.

Earlier this month, the President won the senior and super senior contests at his course in New Jersey.

'The Winning Shot in the Bedminster Club Championship!' he wrote alongside a video on Truth Social on August 2.

'Thank you very much to all of those who participated. I won with a score of 70, and am so honored in that, unlike the rest of the field, I'm given very little time to practice, because I'm focused on many other things.

'It's called TALENT, and I have it, and they don't!' Trump added before signing off with his name.

But in the wake of the victories, multiple quotes from many previous journalists and former associates have resurfaced.

Oscar De La Hoya, above with Donald Trump in 2009, claimed the President is a cheat at golf

He alleged the President wouldn't count shots in the water and improved his lie illegally

Oscar De La Hoya has claimed the President repeatedly bent the rules in his favor during a round they played.

The former professional boxer, who won belts at the super featherweight, lightweight, light welterweight, light middleweight and middleweight classes, recalled Trump moving his ball from the rough and onto the fairway. He also says the President did not count shots that landed in the water.

'It was unbelievable,' De La Hoya told the Associated Press in 2016, adding, 'It shows something about his character.'

'Golf is a gentleman's sport. You don't lie about your score; you don't lie about moving your ball. It goes to show what we're dealing with.'

De La Hoya is one of multiple people, including Barack Obama, to hint at the President's golfing dishonesty. Trump has repeatedly denied any claims of cheating.

Veteran sports writer Rick Reilly penned a book diving into the President's alleged history of cheating in the sport.

Reilly once described a pattern of behavior he saw firsthand. Among these were claims that Trump drove a modified golf cart that went faster than others so he could speed ahead of the rest of his group to move his ball into a better position.

The writer, like De La Hoya, claimed Trump would move his ball into better lies. But Reilly also claims the President would kick opponents' balls into sand traps.

Multiple sports writers who have played with Trump have also accused him of cheating

In the book, published in 2019, Reilly recalled a round in Los Angeles where Trump hit a shot into a pond – only for the ball to magically end up in the fairway. When asked to explain what happened, Reilly claims that Trump replied, 'Must've been the tide.'

Reilly is not the only journalist to have made claims about the questionable integrity of Trump's golf game.

British golf writer Kevin Brown recalled an incident in 2012 during a round at Trump's Balmedie course in Scotland. He described the President as impatient and eager to move quickly, telling a playing partner to 'get a move on' at one point in the round while Brown was admiring the scenery.

Trump previously claimed he has 'too much integrity' to cheat at the sport.

Sports.title: Why Andoni Iraola should be concerned after Newcastle draw: The key problem Liverpool must solve, the player they desperately need in the transfer window and a worrying lack of depth in attack
Sports.content:
Nearly a year to the day that Rio Ngumoha scored a 100th-minute winner at St James's Park, Liverpool fans were again toasting a last-second goal as they descended the many steps down from the away end up in the skies.

Last August, they were singing and dancing as they left the stadium. They were doing the same here but with a nagging worry in the backs of their minds.

When the pulses and emotions lowered as they trudged back down the A1(M), everyone connected to Liverpool would know that, despite the drama and joy that came from the last-gasp equaliser, there are a lot more issues than this time last year.

Back then, remember, the Reds were the reigning champions and had started the defence on fire. Many observers, like they do now with Arsenal, expected this team to win the league at a canter. Now, there are hints of optimism but that is overridden by uncertainty.

Twelve months on and a change of manager later, this opening performance prompted more questions than answers. The issues that ultimately led to Arne Slot losing his job were still evident and, despite the late celebrations, fans might be worried for the season ahead.

The chief problem for new boss Andoni Iraola was the midfield – or lack thereof. Both goals were accomplished counter-attacks from Newcastle but both were highly preventable as Liverpool were cut through at ease.

Dominik Szoboszlai salvaged a point for Liverpool at Newcastle with a last-gasp penalty

Ryan Gravenberch, Florian Wirtz and late hero Dominik Szoboszlai are all incredibly talented footballers. But do they work as a midfield three? They are all more naturally inclined to be attack-minded and the back door is left ajar to let teams punish them.

This summer has been all about replacing Mohamed Salah, who scored on his Trabzonspor league debut on Sunday, but why has there been no attempts to sign a midfielder?

It is not like this is a new problem. Alexis Mac Allister and Gravenberch were both poor for the entirety of last season and Liverpool have needed a deep-lying player since Fabinho left in the summer of 2023.

'The team needs a defensive midfielder, we have been talking about this at Liverpool for three years,' said Daniel Sturridge on Sky Sports. 'Gravenberch changed that philosophy but if you analyse the midfield, they are all naturally more attacking players.

'You look at Mamadou Sangare at Brentford, the stats jump off the page, he was only £39million which is not a load of money.'

Both of Newcastle's goals came from Gravenberch having possession on the edge of the home penalty area. Before they knew it, Liverpool were chasing back, there was no midfield enforcer to stop the counter-attack, the defence was stretched and they conceded.

Think of some of the great Premier League teams, they have always had someone happy to sit in and break up the play: Claude Makelele, Ngolo Kante, Rodri, Fernandinho, some of the greats at Manchester United.

Gravenberch was adept in 2024-25, when Liverpool won the title, but has not reached that same level since. Mac Allister likewise. Szoboszlai is a mercurial footballer but better further forward, as is Wirtz who was anonymous again here at the start of a defining season for him.

Ryan Gravenberch was at fault for both of Newcastle's goal and Liverpool should focus on signing a No6

Dominik Szoboszlai is far too attacking of a midfielder to fill the need deeper in the middle

Liverpool remain hopeful of signing Paris Saint-Germain's Bradley Barcola this week and are weighing up whether to make a third bid for Brighton's Yankuba Minteh. Those will be crucial additions, given the wide options are limited at present.

But signing a deep-lying midfielder is just as important. They could have the best front three in the world yet they will win no trophies if they are so vulnerable and exposed to the counter-attack like they were here.

Lionel Messi, Xavi and Andres Iniesta took the headlines in Pep Guardiola's Barcelona super-team, but No 6 Sergio Busquets was the most important cog in that machine.

Iraola thought Liverpool were the better team here but might be delighted with the point given, for most of the match, they looked likely to leave with nothing.

At Bournemouth, he played with an energetic and dynamic double-pivot of Tyler Adams and Lewis Cook. So far, the Basque boss seems unsure about the make-up of his top-heavy midfield. How to get the best of Wirtz and Szoboszlai but also keep the team solid?

It is now over to those upstairs to ensure the impressive Iraola has the tools to thrive this season, as the bench looked weak.

A winger or two would be great but a new holding midfielder should join the wide forwards at the top of that shopping list.

Isak's day to forget

We cannot repeat the words used by Newcastle fans but you can have a good guess at the sentiments expressed towards Alexander Isak, once of this parish.

Most words were four letters long and let us just say that they were not kind.

Isak, all £125m of him, saw his every touch jeered and booed by the hostile, raucous crowd at St James'.

This was a day to forget for the Swede, who has looked sharp in pre-season but failed to translate that form to when it really matters.

He had a couple of chances but fluffed his lines, much to the delight of the home fans. If Liverpool are to succeed this season, they need a lot more from Isak and Wirtz.

A returning Alexander Isak was booed with every touch and struggled against his former side

Lack of depth in attack is a real worry

Lewis Koumas has been impressive in pre-season, is a talented player who can play across the front three and the manager has taken a shine to the Welshman in training.

But the sight of him coming on as a substitute to try to salvage a point might worry some Liverpool fans.

Koumas, son of former Premier League midfielder Jason, spent the second half of last season at Hull City – and was an unused substitute in the play-off final despite scoring some important goals on the way to promotion for the Tigers.

He has deserved his top-flight debut but fans are right to ask why Iraola was left to rely on a player who has spent the last few years in the second tier, with loans also at Birmingham and Stoke.

The other wingers had mixed afternoons. Victor Munoz looked bright off the bench, asking constant questions and winning the foul that led to the decisive penalty.

Cody Gakpo took his goal incredibly well with a fine hit from distance and was Liverpool's most effective attacker – yet he has question-marks over his future given Tottenham have shown interest in signing him this summer.

Ngumoha is an exciting talent and has all the tools to be a future world-beater but failed to make a serious impression here, with just 21 touches. The 17-year-old is better on the left flank and was largely ineffective on the right flank.

All this came as, 2,000 miles south-east, Salah was scoring on his Turkish Superlig debut for Trabzonspor. With little over a week left of the window to go, the Egyptian King has still not been replaced.

Sports.title: Newcastle edge closer to signing Nico Gonzalez from Man City - as Newcastle rekindle interest in Lille forward Matias-Fernandez Pardo and Coventry agree £6m deal for Ethan Pinnock: WINDOW WATCH
Sports.content:

Ethan Pinnock is set for a move to promoted Coventry Gonzalez edges closer to Toon move Newcastle United are continuing to edge closer to agreement with Manchester City over a deal for Nico Gonzalez. The 24-year-old was an unused substitute in City’s win over Bournemouth on Sunday with Marc Guehi playing in midfield and it is clear that a move away may now be in his best interests. Nico Gonzalez is closing in on a move to Newcastle after falling out of favour at Man City Matthias Jaissle wants to add a midfielder with Premier League experience before the window closes. City agreed an £86m deal with Lille for midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi yesterday and want another before the window closes. Imps land Wheatley Manchester United striker Ethan Wheatley has joined Championship side Lincoln City. Wheatley, who had a spell at Bradford last season, joins on loan for the rest of this campaign.
