World.title: High-intensity sprints can trigger molecular changes in the bloodstream
World.content:
High-intensity sprints can trigger molecular changes in the bloodstream

Jesussanz/Getty Images

We all know a sprint feels different than a longer, take-it-slow kind of workout.

Your heart is pounding. You gasp for air. Maybe your muscles burn.

Now, new research reveals this kind of high-intensity training provokes a remarkably robust response throughout the bloodstream. The training substantially mobilizes more proteins and other molecules in the hours after exercising.

The findings were published by a team of scientists in the U.S., Australia and Sweden. The results do not mean that sprint workouts and other forms of high-intensity interval training, or HIIT, are better than moderate exercise where your heart rate remains at a steady level.

Sponsor Message

But the data does suggest that pushing yourself in these all-out, short bursts of effort may yield unique benefits for health and fitness, according to Dr. Paul Cohen, whose lab at Rockefeller University led the study, which recently appeared in the journal Cell Reports Medicine.

In a series of experiments, Cohen and his colleagues collected blood from young, healthy adults before and after they exercised, and combed their blood for thousands of proteins and other metabolites.

For example, participants were divided into two opposing camps: One completed six sets of a 30-second maximum effort on the bike, each spaced by 4 minutes of rest.

The others did a 90-minute moderate-paced ride.

When they ran their analysis, it was clear the sprint group had "many, many more changes," explains Cohen. "What we can conclude is that sprinting does have a greater effect on remodeling the molecules in the bloodstream."

Want the latest stories on the science of healthy living? Subscribe to NPR's Health newsletter.

The practical implications of those changes need to be teased apart in future trials; however, the study did find some initial clues. They overlaid the results from their study participants with a massive database of 50,000 people, collected from the U.K. Biobank.

Sponsor Message

That evaluation showed the proteins that were altered in the sprinters were associated with improved cardiovascular and metabolic health.

In another part of the study, the research team saw that fat cells behaved differently when drenched with blood collected from the HIIT folks, including changes involved in many genes that regulate fat and whole-body metabolism.

"That's further evidence and much more causal evidence that something in the blood following sprint training can remodel the molecular landscape of other tissues, like fat tissue," Cohen says.

This latest work reflects a broader effort in the field of precision medicine to unpack all the ways molecules — in blood vessels, muscles, the liver and other organs — respond to exercise, including different intensities.

"We know now there's very orchestrated events happening under the hood during exercise," says Scott Trappe, director of the Human Performance Lab at Ball State University. "All these organs are communicating, it's like a super highway and the circulation is that highway."

Trappe is also an investigator in a National Institutes of Health initiative to uncover the molecular inner workings of physical activity. He says this new data clearly shows that "there are some potential benefits you're leaving on the table if you don't do high-intensity exercise."

Though he and other experts emphasize that HIIT may not be practical, or even safe, for everyone.

"I don't view this in the light of high intensity versus moderate," he says. "There's a continuum and all of this stuff is good."

In the study, the participants were young, physically fit, and predominantly males, and that limits how much you can extrapolate to other groups, especially those who are older and less conditioned.

The cycling protocol itself — six sets of 30-second maximum sprints — could prove enormously taxing for the average person, he notes.

Overall, the human studies comparing high- and moderate-intensity exercise suggest they're largely comparable to each other when you look at measures of fitness and other areas of health, says Todd Astorino, an exercise physiologist at California State University, San Marcos. He has spent almost two decades studying HIIT.

The real upside with high-intensity training — assuming you're healthy enough to do it — is how much you benefit from a small investment of time, he explains.

Sponsor Message

"Sometimes, I think people worry too much about time, or frequency," he says. "If you amp up the intensity, you can do a hell of a lot less of that and still get meaningful adaptations and responses."

For example, Astorino says new data from a grant he's involved in shows two sprints a day totaling less than 40 seconds can lead to meaningful improvement in VO₂ max – a measure of cardiorespiratory fitness – within just 6 to 8 weeks.

The work from Cohen's lab and others is all driving at the goal of eventually developing nuanced exercise prescriptions — and possibly drugs — that can be tailored to the individual.

"Perhaps some individuals have a greater response to sprint training, whereas others might do better with moderate intensity training," he says. "This is just the first step towards providing those kinds of recommendations."

World.title: Thousands forced to evacuate parts of Reno, Nevada, as new wildfire rages
World.content:
Thousands forced to evacuate parts of Reno, Nevada, as new wildfire rages

toggle caption Haven Daley/AP

Some 42,000 people in Reno, Nev. have been forced to evacuate, and another 45,000 have been told to prepare to leave, as a fast-growing wildfire spread toward neighborhoods in the northern part of the city on Sunday.

The blaze, known as the Hawk Fire, has grown to more than 15,000 acres since it began Saturday in the foothills of the Sierra Nevada mountains, according to data posted by the National Interagency Fire Center's Inciweb late Sunday.

"We can confirm that the fire was human caused," Shane Akerson, a battalion chief with the Truckee Meadows Fire Protection District and one of three incident commanders for the Hawk Fire, said at a press conference late Sunday morning. "However, that is still undergoing active investigation."

Sponsor Message

He said at least six people, including three first responders and three civilians, have been injured, and several properties have been destroyed. Some 800 emergency responders are battling the blaze.

The zone of people urged to "go now" reached the edge of the University of Nevada on Sunday. Officials say people evacuating should be prepared to stay away from home for several days, as unpredictable winds have complicated the fight to contain the blaze.

Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo has activated the National Guard and declared a state of emergency in Washoe County, which includes Reno and parts of Lake Tahoe. This releases federal resources needed to help contain the fire.

"This is an active and rapidly evolving situation, and I urge everyone in the affected areas to remain vigilant and follow the direction of local officials," Lombardo said Saturday in a statement posted on social media.

As the fire moves into more heavily urban areas, authorities said tens of thousands of people in areas with "be ready to evacuate" status should stay alert and have "go bags" prepared in case they have to leave suddenly. Sheriff Darin Balaam of Washoe County also urged residents to keep tabs on Watch Duty, an app and website that provides real-time data on nearby wildfires and other natural disasters.

Sponsor Message

"If you can get out now, I would ask you please to do that," Balaam said, saying that would make it easier for firefighters and first responders to do their job.

The Reno-Sparks Convention Center is receiving evacuees, and hundreds of people spent Saturday night there, NPR member station KUNR reports .

Officials first received reports of the Hawk Fire just after 11 a.m. Pacific Time on Saturday. "Red flag" fire conditions – warm temperatures, low humidity and strong winds – helped fuel the blaze, according to Richard Edwards, fire chief at Truckee Meadows Fire and Rescue, one of the teams combating the wildfire.

"The Hawk Fire is a very dynamic incident for us, as it's being driven by the winds," Edwards said in a video posted to social media Saturday.

"The wind-driven fires move very rapidly into our residential areas, creating a lot of challenges for our firefighters to save homes and protect lives," he said.

toggle caption Noah Berger/AP

Balaam noted that the Hawk Fire is the third major wildfire to hit northern Nevada in the last few weeks. The Bug Fire, which began Aug. 8 just north of the Hawk Fire, has burned nearly 94,000 acres and is now around 94% contained. The Stallion Fire, which started two days later, is now 98% contained after claiming just over 40,000 acres.

World.title: Trump threatens new 50% tariffs on Canadian cars, trucks and steel. Follow live updates
World.content:
U.S. president promises new tariffs on Jan. 1, on top of taxes that came into effect early Saturday

Canada-U.S. trade: Trump threatens new tariffs after talks fall apart LIVE

U.S. President Donald Trump threatened yet another batch of tariffs on Monday after trade talks between Canada and the U.S. fell apart. Ontario Premier Doug Ford, an outspoken critic of Trump's tariffs, is expected to speak on the issue, while Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre is set to appear at a manufacturing facility in Windsor, Ont.

World.title: 'Kiss my ass,' Ford tells Trump as he readies to speak in Hamilton amid Canada-U.S. trade war
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford and members of his cabinet will be holding a news conference in Hamilton Monday, as the fallout from the Canada-U.S. trade war continues.

Ontario Premier Doug Ford and members of his cabinet will be holding a news conference in Hamilton Monday after Canada-U.S. trade talks failed, with the premier saying Trump can "kiss my ass" as the fallout from the trade war continues.

Fifty per cent U.S. tariffs on about $28-billion worth of Canadians goods came into effect early Saturday. Prime Minister Mark Carney said retaliatory, dollar-for-dollar tariffs will hit the U.S. Sept. 8.

Trump further escalated the trade war in a post to Truth Social Monday, slamming Canada for "ripping off the United States" and announcing that starting Jan. 1, 2027, the U.S. will increase tariffs on Canadian automobiles, car parts and steel to 50 per cent.

Currently, the levy on Canadian steel is already 50 per cent, while the levy on car parts and automobiles is 25, according to the Canadian government's website.

Ford is expected to speak at 1:30 p.m. CBC will live stream the conference here.

In response to Trump's latest tariff threats, Ford told Toronto radio station Newstalk 1010 the U.S. president can "kiss my ass."

"We need to throw everything in the kitchen sink at them. He's arrogant. He's cocky," he said in the interview.

Ford and other premiers have largely backed Carney's decision to reject the trade deal.

The premier will be joined by Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli and Finance Minister Peter Bethlenfalvy. They are expected to share their remarks at 1:30 p.m. ET, according to an advisory from the premier's office.

WATCH | Ford voices support for Carney's decision to walk away from trade deal: Premier Ford says suspended trade talks avoided a 'bad deal' for steel, auto sectors | Duration 1:49 Ontario Premier Doug Ford slammed the proposed trade agreement with the United States as a 'bad deal' for the province's steel and auto sectors. Ford said he supports Prime Minister Mark Carney's decision to suspend negotiations and that the province will help workers and businesses who now face a 50% tariff from the U.S.

Canada negotiated in good faith: expert

Daniel Tisch, CEO of the Ontario Chamber of Commerce, said tariff retaliation from Canada has to be "surgical," such as targeting American products that have a clear Canadian alternative readily available.

"The reality is the Canadian government negotiated with a good faith that was not returned," Tisch told CBC Radio's Metro Morning Monday.

"We're dealing with somebody in the White House who doesn't believe in win-win outcomes. But at the same time, that's the foundation, as we know, of every business relationship," he said.

Despite the failed trade deal, Tisch said he is optimistic Canada will "get through this dark time," noting that Canada, including Ontario, has led the U.S. in job growth and unlike some dire predictions, the country's economy didn't enter a recession.

"I still like our odds and I still believe that with the right collaboration between business and government we can actually make a positive difference."

World.title: Yellowknife woman diagnosed with ALS in Alberta after spending thousands to leave territory for specialist treatment
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Mary Rose Blackduck started feeling like she would stumble and fall every time she walked, she knew she had to see a doctor.

The Yellowknife woman ended up spending thousands of dollars out of pocket to travel south in order to learn that she had a fatal disease.

Blackduck, 69, is a former Tłı̨chǫ broadcaster for CKLB radio and CBC North. She says she visited doctors in Yellowknife five times and told them she had painful muscle spasms, cramps and weakness to the point where she fell and broke a foot, and that the right side of her body stopped working.

"I knew I was in trouble," she recalled.

After multiple X-rays and blood tests, she says doctors in Yellowknife told her she was healthy and prescribed her sleeping pills.

“That is when I lost confidence and I lost faith in our medical community here in Yellowknife and right across the Northwest Territories,” she said.

Blackduck then spent nearly $6,000 to visit the University of Alberta Hospital, where she was diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), also known as Lou Gehrig's disease, which is a rare nervous system disease that leads to damaged muscles. The typical life expectancy after diagnosis is two to five years.

Blackduck says she went into shock when she heard the diagnosis. She describes ALS as "a very dreadful, cruel disease.”

Blackduck says ALS is 'a very dreadful, cruel disease.' An estimated 4,000 Canadians are living with the disease at any time, according the ALS Society of Canada. (Elliot Pope/CBC)

The Northwest Territories Health and Social Services Authority (NTHSSA) says it can't comment on individual cases. However, in an emailed statement to CBC News, the authority said diagnosing ALS is complex because there isn't a definitive test and early symptoms can vary.

"We recognize that the journey to diagnosing ALS can be difficult and include periods of uncertainty," the statement reads.

The ALS Society of Canada says at any given time, there are about 4,000 Canadians living with ALS and approximately 1,000 die from the disease each year.

The N.W.T. health department said it does not track cases in the territory.

The territory also does not have a full-time neurologist to diagnose people who might have the disease. The NTHSSA said that's because neurology is not a funded core specialist service in the territory.

The authority said it works with a group of private neurologists in Alberta who provide visiting services in Yellowknife "with varying frequency."

'I dread that time when I have to face it'

Since her diagnosis, Blackduck has been researching the disease and watching interviews of others who have ALS to prepare herself for what’s to come.

“I won't be able to talk anymore … I won't be able to eat salads because my muscles are dying,” she said.

“I'm going to need some oxygen and then feeding tubes, wheelchairs. I won't be able to move, not even my fingers. Everything will just be a complete vegetable.

“I dread that time when I have to face it,” she said.

The N.W.T. health department would not say whether Blackduck would be reimbursed for her trip to Alberta for a diagnosis. The department says it cannot comment on individual cases, and that patients need a medical referral under the territory's medical travel policy.

“Should a resident require medical travel, we recommend that they work with their health care provider to submit a request,” the department said in an emailed statement to CBC News.

Blackduck says she is now considering a move to Edmonton where there are more supports for people living with ALS. (Elliot Pope/CBC)

Blackduck says she doesn't expect to be reimbursed.

“I don't think I'll get a refund in my lifetime,” she said.

After living in the N.W.T. all her life, she is now considering moving to Edmonton where she hopes to join a support group.

There isn’t a support group for people with ALS in the N.W.T., the health department said. The department says patients can reach out to ALS Canada or the ALS Society of Alberta for more resources.

For now, Blackduck is focusing on giving away her clothes, sewing machine and other belongings.

“I am relieved to find out what disease I have. I'm also grateful for the time that I have now, so I can sort out my affairs,” she said.

World.title: Documents reveal Ambassador Bridge owner's private meeting with Ottawa ahead of Gordie Howe opening
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The American owner of the Ambassador Bridge, Matthew Moroun, sought a meeting with senior Canadian government officials about the new Gordie Howe International Bridge three and a half months before the rival crossing opened — but what was discussed at that meeting remains largely a secret.

CBC News learned of the April 7 meeting through federal briefing notes obtained under the Access to Information Act. The 17-page release package is available for public view at the bottom of this story.

According to the documents, Moroun, who's based in Michigan, was accompanied by Kevin Kalczynski, a senior lawyer with the family's companies, and Brennan Lee, a senior financial executive and Moroun's son-in-law.

On the Canadian side were Housing Infrastructure and Communities Canada deputy minister Paul Halucha, assistant deputy minister Marco Presutti and Jesse Tracey, a senior federal government lawyer.

'You are here to listen'

The records show Moroun requested the meeting with Canadian officials, but portions of the agenda, as well as the government's account and analysis of the meeting, were redacted.

The Gordie Howe International Bridge connects Windsor, Ont., and Detroit, adding publicly owned competition to the privately owned Ambassador Bridge. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

CBC News contacted the Ambassador Bridge seeking Moroun's account of the meeting and what he wanted from Canadian officials, but did not receive a response before publication.

The stakes were enormous. Moroun had a lot on the line financially — the new bridge was expected to take almost half the Ambassador Bridge's traffic, according to U.S. government estimates.

By itself, the Ambassador Bridge is a vital link between both countries, and in 2021 it handled more than $140 billion in merchandise trade — about $390 million a day and 26 per cent of Canada's exports by road, according to Transport Canada.

The Canadian government had its own interests going into the meeting. Officials were trying to get the $6.4 billion Gordie Howe bridge open under intense political pressure from the White House to stop.

Briefing materials prepared for Halucha describe his role in the meeting with Moroun this way:

"Note you are here to listen and look forward to hearing Mr. Moroun's perspective and better understand his views on corridor operations as the new bridge prepares to come into service, as well as views he may have on resolution of outstanding issues."

Much of the material detailing those issues and portions of the government's subsequent account of the meeting are redacted.

Behind closed doors

Laurie Trautman, director of the Border Policy Research Institute at Western Washington University in Bellingham, Wash., said the involvement of a private owner adds a dimension that would not ordinarily be present in the management of an international border crossing.

The Ambassador Bridge is seen on July 28, the day after the opening of the Gordie Howe International Bridge, which ended nearly a century of private monopoly over commercial bridge traffic between Windsor, Ont., and Detroit. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

"It's not necessarily about better accessibility or more efficiency of trade flows. It's about profits," she said.

The arrangement itself may also be unique: Trautman said she knows of no comparable example of a fully privately owned international crossing operating alongside a publicly owned competitor.

She said the unusual relationship, with the inclusion of a private business, adds another layer to diplomacy, raising questions about transparency at a time when relations between Canada and the United States are strained.

"Those government-to-government channels are only as strong as the government-to-government relations," she said. "I think Canada and the U.S. are becoming a little bit more transactional in their diplomacy."

WATCH | A look at the Gordie Howe bridge deal: What's inside the new Gordie Howe bridge deal? | Duration 1:38 The Canadian government has released the text of a new pact with the U.S. to open the long-awaited Gordie Howe International Bridge connecting Michigan and Ontario. CBC Windsor's Emma Loop breaks down what's inside the controversial agreement.

Housing Infrastructure and Communities Canada wrote in an email that discussions with private bridge owners are not unusual.

"Discussions with international bridge owners who facilitate trade and commerce to Canada are continuous and occur through various channels," the department said.

The department would not discuss the outstanding litigation, but said it continues to work with stakeholders to "strengthen a vital trade corridor that generates billions of dollars in economic activity on both sides of the border."

From monopoly to competition

A federal briefing note written after the meeting dated April 24 and included in the package obtained by CBC News said, "Mr. Moroun acknowledged that GHIB will proceed to opening," referring to the Gordie Howe bridge. The note said that acknowledgement came a day after the April 7 meeting with senior Canadian officials.

The Gordie Howe International Bridge is seen from the air on July 27, its opening day. The event brought a second major bridge crossing to the Windsor-Detroit corridor. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

Whatever was discussed behind closed doors, the competitive landscape changed soon afterward.

The same briefing note said 11 days after the meeting "the Ambassador Bridge announced reductions to toll rates for some of its users, positioning them slightly below those planned for the GHIB."

John Sutcliffe, a political science professor at the University of Windsor, has studied the Moroun family's decades-long efforts to protect the Ambassador Bridge from a competing crossing.

"You have a classic case of moving from a monopoly situation to one where there's competition, and therefore prices come down in those situations usually," he said.

New rival, new strategy

Sutcliffe said for the smaller, older and less accessible Ambassador Bridge, the new, publicly owned competition presents a significant challenge.

Trucks funnel through the Ambassador Bridge's customs facilities on July 28. The new six-lane Gordie Howe bridge offers modern border infrastructure and a direct highway-to-highway connection. (Patrick Morrell/CBC)

"Having a new competitor that is much larger, has state-the-art infrastructure and the capacity to handle traffic and deal with it more quickly is a huge problem," he said.

Sutcliffe said the tactics may have changed as the Gordie Howe bridge moved from proposal to reality, but the objective has remained the same: protect the family business.

Since 2014, that campaign has included strategic land purchases whenever a route for a rival bridge was identified and political lobbying on both sides of the border, Sutcliffe said. The briefing notes also identify 22 separate legal challenges launched by the Marouns over the past two decades.

Strange political bedfellows

"Trying to secure political support is sort of a long-standing part of the Ambassador Bridge's operation," Sutcliffe said.

U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, left, and Moroun, right, are seen in the composite image. The Trump administration's 'America First' agenda makes for an unusual alignment with a family whose business depends on cross-border trade. (Alex Brandon and Carlos Osorio/The Associated Press)

Sutcliffe said the Trump administration may also represent a unusually receptive audience. He said he sees similarities between Trump's preference for private enterprise and the Moroun family's long-standing opposition to a publicly owned competitor.

"Moroun's position sort of fits with Trump's view of the world and so you have that political dynamic, the view that it's about what's in it for us and what's in it for the United States," Sutcliffe said.

Sutcliffe said the Morouns found themselves aligned with Trump's "America First" approach, even though disrupting cross-border trade could ultimately hurt the Ambassador Bridge itself.

World.title: WNBA star Natasha Cloud confronts Enes Kanter Freedom over anti-trans shirt at Fever-Sky game
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Former NBA centre Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected from Sunday night’s Indiana-Chicago WNBA game after he was confronted by Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.

Freedom was sitting along the baseline. He had on a black shirt that read “WOMAN noun. adult human female.”

The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then did a chest bump with teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning around and walking in Kanter’s direction.

Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Kanter, also 34, as she approached him. A standing Kanter held his arms out and took one step on the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved in between the two.

“There was just a fan incident and the security handled it, and we’re just going to focus on the game,” Chicago forward Azura Stevens said after the Sky’s 113-90 loss.

Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom greets a friend before the game between the Indiana Fever and the Chicago Sky on Sunday. (Nam Y. Huh/The Associated Press)

Chicago coach Tyler Marsh said Cloud was concerned about being a distraction for the team.

“I told her she wasn’t,” Marsh said. “I told her that we all embrace her as someone that protects our team and protects people that need to be protected, and so Tash is always going to stand on that, and we stand for Tash.”

Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.

He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.

“I didn’t see it, we were talking about the next play in our huddle,” Indiana star Caitlin Clark said, “so I think that’s probably a question for Chicago.”

Cloud met with team and league security after the game. She did not speak with the media.

WNBA subject of debate on transgender women

The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been a trans woman player in the WNBA.

Los Angeles Sparks guard Layshia Clarendon, who was the WNBA’s first openly transgender and non-binary player, retired in 2024. Clarendon was assigned female at birth.

Although the league’s collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.

In an ESPN profile published last month, Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls’ and women’s sports.

Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, have mockingly declared themselves eligible for the WNBA draft, saying they now identify as women.

Kanter joined a small rally in support of Cunningham outside the arena before the game.

Asked if he had a message for Kanter, Marsh praised the league and its players.

“If you come to a game, you should probably come to enjoy the basketball,” he said. “That seems pretty simple to me. I think these players deserve that and have earned that. Being a former basketball player, you should probably understand and feel that, too.”

World.title: London is famous for its great trees. More than 70% are at risk due to climate change, research finds
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

In the middle of a heat wave and severe drought this summer, Divya Hariramani was pruning a plum tree in south London when she noticed something wrong with one of the tree's branches.

The branch was beginning to split completely from the tree. The workers at Mitcham Community Orchard told her it was because the fruit tree was stressed.

"Because of the heat essentially. Like, when the trees can't provide enough water to its parts and like some parts will just drop," said Hariramani, who documents fruit trees and the people who tend to them across the city on a social media account called Fruity Walks .

While London’s stone architecture may be more famous to some tourists, the 2,000-year-old city is also renowned for its mature urban forest, which has been called the largest in the world.

Divya Hariramani documents fruit trees and the people who tend to them across London on her social media account Fruity Walks. (Submitted by Divya Hariramani)

This year has proven difficult for the normally lush canopy, though, as five successive heat waves and a serious lack of rain have strained plants and wildlife.

And it’s projected to get much worse for the city’s eight million trees.

By the end of the century, according to a recent report from Royal Botanic Gardens Kew forecasting the vulnerability of London’s urban forest, some 73 per cent of the city’s trees could be at risk of dying due to climate change.

Driest July on record

The Kew Gardens tree collections and arboriculture team worked with the Greater London Authority to assess a sample of over a million public trees and found that 62 per cent of them already have "low suitability" to the climate conditions that can be expected by 2090 without action to reduce emissions. On top of that, nearly 11 per cent are “vulnerable."

It’s not just a future problem. In 2022, 400 of Kew's 11,000 trees died amid extreme heat and drought conditions. The gardens have left the skeleton of one red oak standing, and painted it red as a symbol of what climate change is already doing to London's trees.

Kevin Martin, head of tree collections at Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, views a willow beech tree suffering from drought dieback in 2024. Martin led a recent report from Kew Gardens estimating how much of London's urban tree canopy is at risk due to climate change. (Toby Melville/Reuters)

Kew highlighted the findings and unveiled the red tree ahead of Climate Action Week in June, when Britain and Europe were already in the throes of a second heat wave. By August, there had been two more and a major drought was declared in much of England and Wales. Virtually no rain fell in July, resulting in the driest July on record in Britain.

Farmers lost crops, warned of food shortages and had to dip into winter feed reserves for cattle. Wildfires in parts of the country prompted an emergency cellphone alert in August. In the city, park grass turned yellow and brittle; tree branches and leaves looked droopier than usual. In some places, trees lost their leaves altogether, giving an autumnal look to the ground in the middle of summer.

The week in June when Kew publicized its report, Hariramani, in an ironic twist of fate, had to cancel a group walk she had organized in light of Climate Action Week due to the heat.

"Literally one of the most important walks in a way, for such an important situation and we couldn't even do it," said Hariramani, whose day job is in sustainable design.

More like Barcelona?

With a London that’s getting warmer than its current trees can handle, botanists are exploring whether they should start planting different trees.

"From most projections, we're expecting the climate in London in 2050 to look more like Barcelona's is now," Joe Richomme, a botanical horticulturist at Kew Gardens, told CBC on a recent visit to Kew’s Carbon Garden, where 35 trees and 6,500 plants have been selected to show how different species respond to changing conditions.

The Carbon Garden in London's Kew Gardens is meant to raise awareness about climate change through its wide range of plants showing how biodiversity can remain resilient amid warming temperatures. (Lyza Sale/CBC)

Richomme explained that Kew has been exploring what types of tree species could fare better in hotter, drier weather, while also being able to withstand England’s notorious wetter winters.

For example, English oak, which are native to Britain, have struggled in the heat, but have also adapted to grow in warmer places, such as the southern United States.

'They’re irreplaceable’

Paul Wood has written four books and two maps about London's trees, which he attributes to growing up playing in the forests of southern England — and also, his name.

"It's called nominative determinism," Wood said over the phone in mid-August with a chuckle, referring to the idea that people gravitate toward work that suits their name.

Paul Wood is the author of a blog and several books about London's trees. (Submitted by Paul Wood)

He too has made a career of writing about the British capital's storied tree canopy, and the cooling and relaxing benefits it brings to residents and visitors.

But these days he worries about what could happen to London's leafy streets and pockets of ancient woodland in the future as he sees the city struggling in record extreme heat and drought.

"Places like Highgate Woods and Sydenham Hill Woods, Oxleas Woods, Hampstead Heath, where there is native woodland which is really struggling in the current climate," Wood said.

Trees as old as 1,000 years live in some of those places, meaning they’ve stood through the Norman conquest, the Magna Carta and Shakespeare. They saw Victorian railways being built and felt the first rumblings of the London Underground.

"That would be really devastating to lose," Wood said, noting it's not just the trees' history that's valuable but the biodiversity they support as well.

"They're irreplaceable."

World.title: U.S. couple selling isle off Cape Breton for $7M to someone who will keep it wild
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

William F. Baker and his wife have owned Henry Island for the past 35 years, but now at 84 years old he wants to sell the nearly 90-hectare island to someone who will preserve it.

Henry Island is a 20-minute boat ride from Port Hood, N.S. It features a four-bedroom family home and a fully functioning lighthouse installed on the island in 1901.

The Bakers bought it in 1991 and use the island as a getaway from their busy lives in New York City.

WATCH | See the N.S. island and lighthouse listed for $6.9M: This Cape Breton island is listed for $6.9M. We went for a tour | Duration 3:32 Henry Island comes with a four-bedroom home, a working lighthouse and decades of history. CBC's Ethan Hunt stepped ashore to see what the sellers are looking for.

Baker built an acclaimed career as a broadcaster in the U.S. He was the president of the PBS flagship station in New York for 20 years. Before that, he was president of Westinghouse Television, where he helped launch Oprah Winfrey's talk show career.

But both he and his wife, Jeannemarie Gelin-Baker, a nurse practitioner, were searching for a more peaceful way of life when they found Henry Island.

Baker was enamoured with lighthouses and wanted to own an island. A colleague suggested he look at Canada's East Coast.

"Lighthouses are pretty special,” Baker says. “They represent the very best of humanity, really selfless, helping others with no payment in return. That's what a lighthouse stands for, and that's what the lighthouse has meant over the centuries. So being part of all that, it's virtually religious."

William F. Baker waves down to his wife and friend, as he stands on the top of his lighthouse on Henry Island. (Ethan Hunt/CBC)

The Bakers fell in love with Henry Island because of its natural beauty and quiet. It's surrounded by beaches and rugged cliffs, and the only inhabitants besides the Bakers are the wildlife that makes their home in the woods.

"For the first time I saw the full Milky Way,” says Gelin-Baker. “It was exotic. It was beautiful."

Baker says repairs were needed on the lighthouse and the home.

With help from local residents, the house is now fully renovated and is run completely off the grid. They use rainwater for drinking water, solar panels for power and an outhouse.

"We'd come every year and spend two or three weeks repairing and fixing and painting and all,” Baker says. “But it was such a powerful distraction. It took my mind off of all my work in New York City and the pressure of the film and TV business."

He eventually wrote a book about his family's experience on the island called Lighthouse Island: Our Family Escape.

Henry Island has changed over the 35 years the Bakers have owned the island. They have done renovations on the house and the lighthouse. (Donald MacDonald)

The Bakers escape to Henry Island in August every year.

It's become a tradition for them to invite people from the Port Hood area to visit their island retreat. Some people like Donald MacDonald have become regular visitors.

MacDonald is the president of the Henry Island Lighthouse Preservation Society, a volunteer group that looks after the lighthouse.

"We're over here a lot on an island. But we enjoyed it,” MacDonald says. “It's kind of a labour of love and doesn't matter what the job is, it's just a nice place to be. It's quiet, we enjoy it."

Looking for a new owner

Baker says owning a remote island is a lot of work, and they spent most of their early years renovating the space. But now the couple is finding it difficult to keep up with the maintenance.

But Baker says it will be difficult to part with his beloved island.

“People say, ‘Well, how often do you get to Henry Island? Only once a year?’ I said ‘I get there every day of my life. I'm thinking about Henry Island,’” Baker says. “And so we don't want to sell it. But I'm going to be 85 years old soon. My children are not available. They love it, but they're just not available to maintain it. "

The view from the top of the lighthouse on to Henry Island's four-bedroom home and out to the Atlantic Ocean. (Ethan Hunt/CBC)

It's been on the market for the last two years for nearly $7 million Cdn.

Their agent, Angie Bryant with Sotheby's International Realty Canada, says there's been interest from people in Ontario, the U.S. and Germany.

"It's actually become quite popular to see islands selling,” Bryant says. “There's a couple of islands that have sold off the coast of Mahone Bay just recently. Over the course of the last year, islands have become a popular topic for buyers."

She says the island will continue to be marketed on their website and will appear in magazines dedicated to preserving lighthouses, hopefully to attract people interested in owning the beacon.

The Bakers want to find a buyer who will keep Henry Island as untouched as possible.

“So something has to be done, and it's too precious just to close the door and let it sit and rot. We're not gonna let that happen.”

World.title: Inside the mainstream media meltdown: Full Comment podcast
World.content:
Article content

Trust in legacy journalism is plummeting, and after years working inside the CBC, Tara Henley has a good idea why. The author of the new book, “The Trust Spiral: Why the Media Needs Objectivity,” discusses with Brian Lilley how broad-mindedness in newsrooms was ruined by the emergence of an urban and elite class of group-thinking journalists combined with a revenue crisis that discouraged the risk of nonconformist perspectives. Making things worse, Henley argues, is that government subsidies have corrupted market signals that could force badly needed discipline on media owners. But the answer isn’t internet outlets that are even more one-sided, she explains: media need to relearn the tools they once used to keep themselves more honest. (Recorded July 10, 2026.)

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.
