World.title: The Jewish-Mexican food traditions hiding in plain sight
World.content:
My friend Jorge Fitz once told me a story about his childhood visits to the town where his grandfather grew up, Juliantla, just outside of Taxco, Mexico. He remembers many particular things about the way the town celebrated festivities and holidays, but one thing that stuck out in his memory was a special braided bread they made called pan de Juliantla.

As an adult, Jorge said he started making Jewish friends, and when he saw pan de Juliantla on their tables, he wondered how they knew about it.

“Jorge, that’s challah bread,” they would respond.

He later learned that Juliantla is believed to be the first Jewish settlement in the Americas, complete with a spiritual cleansing bath known as a mikveh that dates back to the 16th century.

As far as Jorge could tell, a majority of the townspeople didn’t realize where many of their customs and food came from. He and his parents definitely didn’t know about their Jewish ancestry until much later.

Hearing this story illuminated just how deeply rooted Jewish food is in Mexican culture, so much so that even when origins have been forgotten, they remain an integral part of community life.

Waves of migration and a culinary legacy

The first Jews to grace Mexican shores sailed in on the ships of Spanish conquistadors during the 1500s and 1600s. They were fleeing the Catholic Inquisition of the Iberian Peninsula, but found little solace in the New World as the Inquisition migrated across the ocean.

Many of these early Jews “converted” to Catholicism while continuing to practice their own religion in secret. In Spanish, they are called “conversos,” or the converted. In English, we often refer to them as Crypto Jews.

With these Sephardim came cinnamon, grapes, figs, dates, almonds, cherries, apricots, olives and olive oil, nutmeg, ginger, cardamom and mustard, as well as black pepper, thyme, basil, clove, fennel, oregano, cumin and other Mediterranean spices.

They also had a strong tradition of pickling what they brought to the New World. In northern Mexico, cabrito, slow-roasted baby goat, is a traditional dish among the Sephardic Jews of the Iberian Peninsula. Similarly, the region’s dessert bread known as pan de cemita and la capirotada, a kind of bread pudding, are also attributed to those early Iberian Jewish immigrants.

The second wave of Jewish immigrants to Mexico arrived at the end of the 1800s from the failing Ottoman Empire. Jews who were part of the diaspora from Spain and Portugal, now living in the countries of the Levant, came because of economic opportunities in Mexico. They arrived from what is today Lebanon, Syria and Turkey, and because they were not fleeing persecution, their culture, religion and food were much more visible.

Preserving culture in the neighborhood oven

A third wave of Jewish immigrants came to Mexico during and between the two world wars. Some had plans of continuing on to the United States but were turned away at Ellis Island because of the Immigration Act of 1924, which severely limited the numbers of Southern and European immigrants allowed into the country.

These immigrants brought the Ashkenazi dishes of Eastern European countries like Poland, Ukraine and Germany — hearty soups and stews made with root vegetables like borscht, matza ball soup, gefilte fish, schmaltz (rendered chicken fat), tzimmes, gribenes and braised meats like brisket.

Food is paramount for any immigrant community trying to preserve their identity. The Jewish community was no different.

When Syrian Jews moved into Colonia Roma at the beginning of the 20th century, they not only built one of the city’s oldest synagogues but also opened a community oven down the street where special traditional breads were baked and sold to worshipers coming from services. At the local market were kosher butchers, while elderly folks sat in neighborhood cafes sipping thick, Turkish-style coffee and eating the sweets of home.

Unlike some of the immigrant groups I have researched, the diverse Mexican-Jewish community not only preserved the traditional dishes of their culture, but also, over the generations, adapted and innovated with local ingredients and cooking methods, creating a distinct Judeo-Mexican cuisine.

The fusion kitchen and home recipes

“Sabor Judío,” published in 2024, is a recipe collection by two authors whose Jewish grandmothers passed down handwritten recipe books. They gathered together a comprehensive archive of recipes from kitchens across the Mexican-Jewish community. Among the book’s pages are traces of many cuisines — Mexican mestizo, Spanish, Sephardic-Iberian, Sephardic-Middle Eastern and Ashkenazi.

Yiddish blintzes with huitlacoche (Mexican corn smut considered a local delicacy), matza chilaquiles, a variation of shakshuka with poblano peppers and Mexican oregano, and brisket tacos with three-chile salsa are all included in the collection. Irma Appel’s stuffed poblano peppers with guacamole include a smattering of gribenes (often referred to as Jewish bacon), and Pati Jinich, of PBS’s “Pati’s Kitchen,” provided her recipe for jalapeño-mushroom matza ball soup.

Then there are traditional Mexican recipes that the Mexican-Jewish community has adopted as their own, cooking them for high holidays and other festivities. That includes nopal and tomato salad made in advance to eat cold during Shabbat, or ceviche with prepared horseradish on top, supposedly invented during a Passover Seder.

Not everything is kosher, but the community’s many identities are on full display.

Scanning through the menus of Jewish restaurants in Mexico City, however, it’s hard to find the fusion dishes represented in “Sabor Judío.” For whatever reason, these dishes hold sway in family kitchens, but haven’t yet made it to commercial dining rooms.

Where to find Jewish food in Mexico City

Maybe the world isn’t ready for spicy gefilte fish?

That’s not to say that you can’t get glimpses of them — the salami chilaquiles at Klein’s in Polanco is a delicious example. You’ll also find chiles making guest appearances in the Israeli dishes at Merkava, and kosher cafe Guacho Grill has al pastor tacos made with fish and chicken, as opposed to the traditional pork.

So maybe fusion is yet to take off in restaurants, but at places like Klein’s or Niddo, which once described itself in an interview as Jewish-Mexican-Canadian, diners will at least find Jewish and Mexican dishes coexisting on the table.

Plenty of other expressions of Jewish food can be encountered throughout the city — Mendl, for instance, has incredible U.S.-style deli sandwiches and bagels with lox. And at Pat Patz, chef Mijeal Seidel has a labneh recipe that he adds dill to as a shout-out to his Eastern European side, along with tons of other dishes worth exploring.

You may have to make some fusion dishes at home, but a taste of Jewish-Mexican heritage is definitely available across Mexico City.

Lydia Carey is a freelance writer and translator based in Mexico City. She has published extensively both online and in print, sharing her insights about Mexico for over a decade. She lives a double life as a local tour guide and is the author of “Mexico City Streets: La Roma.” Follow her urban adventures on Instagram and see more of her work at mexicocitystreets.com.

World.title: How the Middle East has shaped Mexico for almost 2,000 years
World.content:
I’m sitting in the courtyard of Guanajuato’s Museo Iconográfico del Quijote, admiring the stone arches and columns, waiting for a chamber music concert to begin. I probably walk through at least one courtyard a day in Guanajuato because they’re everywhere in town – not just in museums, but in restaurants, universities, government buildings and parks. Even the classic Mexican colonial home has a courtyard with a fountain in the center, surrounded by rooms.

Mexican courtyards reflect the influence of the Moors, the North African Islamic group that ruled Spain for 800 years and whose ornate tilework, intricate geometric patterns and decorative calligraphy influenced the art and architecture of Spain. After the fall of the Moors in 1492, Spain continued to use Islamic patterns in its designs, creating a unique style that blended Islamic and Christian elements known as mudéjar, which later made its way to Mexico.

But it’s not just courtyards that bear the mark of the Moors. From architecture and folk medicine to crafts and textiles, here’s a quick roundup of the Islamic group’s lasting impact on Mexican culture.

Alhambrismo

This is an architectural style in Spain and Latin America inspired by the decorative Islamic arts of the Alhambra, a palace and fortress complex in Granada, Spain, with Moorish elements such as horseshoe arches, intricate stucco and colorful tilework.

A well-known example of this is the Kiosk of Santa Maria la Ríbera, an ornate octagonal pavilion made of wrought iron with a glass cupola dome on the top, in Mexico City’s Alameda Park.

Churches

In many colonial Mexican churches, you can see echoes of the mudéjar architectural style, including azulejos, blue-glazed tiles that adorn domes, bell towers and facades; intricate geometric carved-wood ceilings resembling inverted ship hulls; and arches and doorways.

Oaxaca’s famous Templo de Santo Domingo de Guzmán, for example, displays these design elements in the intricate geometric arabesque patterns on the ceiling and the genealogical tree of the temple’s namesake saint.

Inward-facing living

I remember when my husband and I first saw the house we bought in Guanajuato. Although one of its assets was a close-up view of the dome atop one of the city’s signature churches, San Francisco, we could barely see it from the tiny window in one of the bedrooms.

Unlike in the U.S. and Canada, traditional Mexican houses face inward, revealing their Moorish and Andalusian roots, with walled enclosures and internal gathering spaces.

Urban layouts

While Spanish colonial urban planning in the Americas officially ordered a strict grid system, some historic Mexican towns like Guanajuato and Taxco have narrow, winding streets, reflecting the medieval and southern Andalusian urban layouts shaped by centuries of Moorish influence.

Tiles, pottery and ceramics

Moorish craftsmen influenced Iberian ceramic styles, including tin-glazed pottery, by integrating geometric patterns and calligraphic bands into their work. When the craft was established in Puebla during the colonial period, artisans carried over these traditional Iberian-Islamic design elements, including abstract script borders and traditional brushstroke motifs.

Puebla’s famous Talavera pottery also blends Indigenous styles with Spanish and Moorish glazed-tile traditions.

Crafts and textiles

Mudéjar geometric inlaid woodworking and carpentry techniques influenced traditional lacquerware and furniture crafts in regions like Michoacán and Guerrero. Precise interlaced framing merged with Indigenous wood-carving and pre-Hispanic lacquering, creating colonial furniture like desks with repetitive geometric paneling and floral touches.

As for weaving, the traditional Mexican sarape displays complex linear, diamond and star-centered layouts that show cross-cultural parallels to Middle Eastern flat-weave blanket traditions.

Curanderismo (folk medicine)

Moorish and Islamic medical practices influenced curanderismo, the herbal medicine still widely practiced in Mexico. Ritual cleansing, petitionary prayers and talismanic magic elements arrived via Spanish traditions that had absorbed Moorish folk customs.

For example, the belief that the “mal de ojo,” or “evil eye,” can cause physical discomfort like fever, crying and restlessness was brought to the New World via Spanish and Moorish folk magic.

Middle Eastern influences beyond the Moors

Influential as the Moors were, they are not the only Middle Eastern influence in modern Mexico.

Following the fall of the Moors, many Sephardic Jews fled from the Middle East to colonial Mexico to escape the Inquisition. Later waves of Sephardic Jews arrived from the crumbling Ottoman Empire in the early 20th century. These communities established synagogues, cultural institutions and social networks, primarily in Mexico City.

While Mexico has seen periods of antisemitism throughout its history, modern Mexico hosts one of the largest and most vibrant Jewish communities in Latin America, mostly in Mexico City.

Meanwhile, the Lebanese diaspora in Mexico — currently standing at more than 500,000 descendants — has shaped the nation’s culture, cuisine and commerce since the late 19th century.

In the 1890s, they left to escape political oppression, heavy taxes, religious conflict and military conscription. At the same time, Mexico’s then-president, Porfirio Díaz, encouraged foreign immigration and trade, offering a welcoming environment and growing business opportunities.

During the period between the 1890s and 1930s, more than 100,000 mostly Lebanese immigrants arrived from Arabic-speaking nations, settling predominantly in the Yucatán, but also in Veracruz, Puebla and Mexico City.

In the early 20th century, the Lebanese community contributed around 50% of the total immigrant input to Mexico’s economy, and it remains one of Mexico’s most successful immigrant groups.

I’ve known for years that words like ¡ojalá!, albañil, and azotea are Arabic in origin, but I had no idea about other enduring Middle Eastern influences. The next time I use the Talavera dish I bought in Puebla, I’ll appreciate its ancient Moorish history, going back almost 2,000 years.

Louisa Rogers and her husband Barry Evans divide their lives between Guanajuato and Eureka, on California’s North Coast. Louisa writes articles and essays about expat life, Mexico, travel, physical and psychological health, retirement and spirituality. Her recent articles are available on her website, authory.com/LouisaRogers.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: Fugitive swaps, a strawberry spat and a stronger peso
World.content:
Mexico and the United States spent the week of Aug. 17 trading shows of security cooperation, from fugitive handovers to a new drone-technology pact, culminating Wednesday in a federal operation in Michoacán that saw nine alleged members of the Jalisco New Generation Cartel arrested and set off narco-blockades at more than 20 points across the state.

That cooperation ran alongside friction on other fronts. Mexico is contesting a proposed U.S. antidumping tariff on strawberry exports and objecting to Washington’s decision to deport some Mexicans to Central America rather than home, as trade uncertainty lingers more than a month after the U.S. declined to renew the USMCA free trade deal in its current form. Domestically, the fallout from the U.S. visa revocation of former president López Obrador’s son continued to shadow the government’s messaging on fuel-smuggling enforcement. Against that backdrop, the peso’s push below 17 to the dollar stood out as a rare point of good economic news, as the central bank held its interest rate steady on lingering inflation concerns.

The week also brought a new Mexico-made electric vehicle, a national debate over kids and social media, and a presidential sick day. Didn’t have time to catch this week’s top stories? Here’s what you missed.

Fugitive returns and a new drone pact mark security cooperation

Mexico and the United States kept up a steady drumbeat of security announcements this week. Ambassador Ronald Johnson said U.S. authorities returned three wanted fugitives to Mexico in a single day — one linked to the CJNG, one wanted for murder in Zacatecas and one for fraud — while separately handing over six more fugitives wanted for crimes including murder and firearms offenses. Jalisco police also captured Antoni Covarrubias, wanted for second-degree murder in California, in Puerto Vallarta, which Johnson called the ninth high-profile U.S.-targeted arrest in the state in recent weeks. At the same time, the U.S. and Mexico conducted a joint security exercise along the El Paso-Ciudad Juárez border, and the two countries signed a declaration of intent on drone technology that will let Mexico’s Defense Ministry access the U.S. Army’s marketplace for unmanned aircraft systems, though no models, quantities or purchases have been agreed.

Security Minister Omar García Harfuch drew public praise from DEA Administrator Terry Cole at the 40th International Drug Enforcement Conference in Buenos Aires, where García Harfuch said U.S. agencies are processing 155 arrest warrants tied to Mexican investigations and reported that Mexico’s Financial Intelligence Unit has frozen more than 8.6 billion pesos in assets. He also cited a more than 50% drop in daily homicides, from 86 to 42, over the past two years, a figure attributed to his ministry’s own count of arrests and seizures.

The Michoacán operation capped the week’s security news: Soldiers and National Guard troops arrested nine people, including two women identified as relatives of CJNG plaza boss Heraclio “Tío Lako” Guerrero Martínez, who evaded capture as the operation set off blockades that were largely cleared by Wednesday afternoon.

That flow of cooperation announcements ran alongside a separate dispute over fuel smuggling and politics. Sheinbaum said at Tuesday’s mañanera that fuel smuggling, or huachicol fiscal, is “practically over” in Mexico thanks to customs interventions and arrests — a claim she offered in the context of defending her government against opposition criticism. That criticism stems partly from the U.S. revocation of the visa of Andrés Manuel López Beltrán, son of former President López Obrador, which Sheinbaum has called a political matter, saying he “was not” ever on authorities’ radar for criminal involvement. The fuel-trafficking case itself advanced this week when Rear Admiral Fernando Farías Laguna, accused of leading a Pemex-linked smuggling ring, was extradited from Argentina and jailed at the Altiplano maximum security prison. The case has damaged the Navy’s reputation and drawn indirect allegations, which Sheinbaum has rejected, involving López Beltrán.

Strawberries, Vietnam imports and a Canada call test trade ties

Mexico is contesting a U.S. Commerce Department finding that could impose antidumping tariffs on Mexican strawberries, which supplies 98% of U.S. strawberry imports. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard called the U.S. criteria “arbitrarily applied” and inconsistent with USMCA provisions; a final ITC ruling isn’t expected until early 2027, and the case could affect roughly 5,000 Mexican producers and 151,000 jobs if it proceeds. Sheinbaum has warned the case could set a precedent for challenging other Mexican agricultural exports.

Separately, Mexico’s imports from Vietnam more than doubled in the first half of 2026 to $18.4 billion, a jump that has raised suspicions — flagged in a recent White House report naming Mexico a “Tier 1” transshipment risk — that Chinese goods are being routed through Vietnam to dodge Mexico’s tariffs on non-free-trade-agreement countries. Mexico has denied being a transshipment hub for Chinese goods bound for the U.S.

Against that backdrop, President Sheinbaum and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney discussed North American trade by phone on Thursday. Carney’s office said the two underscored the importance of renewing the USMCA pact soon, and separately thanked Mexico for deploying more than 400 firefighters to help combat wildfires in British Columbia. The call came as Trump-imposed tariffs on Canadian goods, delayed this week, loomed for Saturday absent a deal. (The U.S. tariffs on Canada ultimately went into effect after trade talks collapsed late Friday night.)

Peso strength collides with a cautious Banxico

The peso dropped below 17 to the U.S. dollar this week, dropping below 16.9 on Friday, largely on dollar weakness following a U.S. Treasury bond buyback announcement. The currency has appreciated nearly 6% in 2026, a gain Banxico credits with helping cool inflation.

Even so, the central bank held its benchmark rate at 6.5% earlier this month. In meeting minutes released this week, four of five board members cited persistent services inflation as a driver of that decision. Headline inflation slowed to 3.12% in July, but Banxico now doesn’t expect it to reach its 3% target until the fourth quarter of 2027. The bank also flagged Middle East tensions as an upside risk to oil prices. Separately, INEGI’s preliminary July data showed the economy growing 2.7% annually, which Rodríguez called “another piece of good news” following 2.1% growth in the second quarter.

Other business and finance news this week:

Mañanera themes: EVs, phone lines and a presidential sick day

On Monday, Sheinbaum said she opposes a social-media ban for minors like Australia’s, calling the idea “very problematic” and noting enforcement challenges, while Education Minister Mario Delgado announced a nationwide teacher consultation on classroom device rules ahead of the Aug. 31 school year.

At Thursday’s press conference, Sheinbaum unveiled a prototype of Olinia Carga, the government’s second domestically developed electric vehicle, a light-cargo EV that can carry 650 kilograms and will sell for around 150,000 pesos starting in late 2027. The same day brought a new arrest in the 2024 kidnapping case of Sinaloa Cartel figure “El Mayo” Zambada.

On Friday, Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez, standing in for an ill Sheinbaum, told U.S. Ambassador Johnson that Mexico disagrees with Washington’s decision to deport some Mexicans to Guatemala, Honduras and Costa Rica rather than to Mexico.

Elsewhere, millions of Mexican cell phone lines were suspended after an Aug. 15 mandatory registration deadline passed, though regulators say most affected users can still recover service. Mexico also abstained from an OAS vote, which passed 29-1, to convene an emergency session on Nicaragua’s move to bar opposition candidates, with representative Alejandro Encinas citing Mexico’s non-intervention principle. Friday’s mañanera, run by Rodríguez after Sheinbaum announced she had the flu, also touched on new archaeological finds in a Chiapas cave tied to Zoque ritual traditions.

Regional news roundup:

And some good news to close out the week:

Looking ahead

Several threads left open this week are likely to develop further: Security cooperation with the U.S. continues to strengthen, while trade friction between the two countries shows no sign of easing. On a practical note, cell phone users facing the next registration deadlines — Aug. 31 for numbers ending in “1” — should act before their lines are suspended.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: From the archive: How to whistle like a true Mexican
World.content:
The goal of our “From the Archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in January 2025 — is a perfect example, offering humorous insight into the fine art of whistling.

I have known no jealousy like the jealousy I feel when I hear Mexicans’ elaborate category of effortless whistles.

Okay fine, they’re not effortless. They just sound that way because they learned how to do it when they were kids. You know, like speaking Spanish.

Indeed, whistling is part of the language in some meaningful ways. There are specific whistles used for getting people’s attention. There are whistles for saying “Hey buddy, what’s up?” from across the street. There are whistles for saying, “But of course, my horse” — okay, maybe not exactly that, but a kind of “You know it!” with that adorable tone. There are whistles to say, “Wowza, nice butt, strange woman I don’t know!” Some whistles say, “Okay, back up your car now, a little more, a little more, a little more, stop!” There are even whistles to tell people where they can stuff it. Careful with those.

And I am going to learn them all.

A realistic goal

Well, I’m going to try. Forget turning my health or finances around; it’s too big a task. I need something I actually stand a chance at being able to bite off. Even though the prospect of practicing them takes me back to the deep humiliation I felt trying to string a four-word sentence together in Spanish while the three-year-old next to me rattled off deep, complex sentence after deep, complete sentence, I’m committed. I did it once, and I can do it again!

I won’t necessarily use them all, or use them frequently. In fact, I’m fairly certain that men whistle much more than women around here, anyway. Like cursing, it falls into a decidedly “male” category of behavior, and is seen as somewhat crass and unladylike.

I’ve also noticed that whistling is more prevalent among lower socio-economic classes than among the more well-to-do. Part of this is simply cultural habit, growing out of the need to communicate at great distances. It’s more pleasant sounding, and clearer, than shouting. If you’re willing to do some digging, there are actually some fascinating examples of whistles-as-language. There’s a cool short video about this below.

But I don’t need to be communicating over great distances in the Oaxaca countryside. I just want to have some fun.

Indigenous Whistle Language In Mexico

Watch this video on YouTube

And I don’t want to go too fast, but I’m also an eager learner. This video is pretty cute, by the way, as an introduction to the meanings of different whistles.

Here are the specific ones that I want to learn:

Learning how to whistle in Mexico (in different styles, for different purposes)

The whistle to get someone’s attention

Say you’re walking along a busy street and you need to get someone’s attention. Maybe it’s a vendor, or maybe a taxi that didn’t notice you! This whistle is perfect for it. It’s also important for me personally, because my voice does not carry at all. My loudest is not very loud, and the strain on my voice physically hurts! This can either be a quick low-high sound, or the more universally recognized high-low-slightly higher.

The ‘you can count on me, buddy’ whistle

I mostly want to learn this one because I think it’s both hilarious and adorable. My partner does this one sometimes, and even though it’s kind of a joke, I am 100% charmed.

‘Hey, friend on the other side of the street!’

Finally, I’ve just got to learn this whistle. It’s short and sweet, and I don’t care that I’ve hardly ever heard it from a woman’s lips.

So those are the three goals. Three distinct whistles — I can kind of do a “pucker” whistle now, but not very well — should be manageable in a year, right?

In the meantime, I’m dying to know: can you whistle? Can you do any specifically Mexican whistles? I especially want to know how many women out there can — please let me know in the comments!

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

Kid Abelha Fortaleza marked the band’s return to the stage after 13 years. They played at the Centro de Formação Olímpica on Saturday 22 August 2026.

The Brazilian pop-rock trio, fronted by Paula Toller, played to a full arena. It was part of their national tour ‘Eu Tive um Sonho’.

The Return of Kid Abelha Fortaleza

Kid Abelha Fortaleza was the band’s first live performance since 2013, ending a 13-year silence. The show took place at the Centro de Formação Olímpica, a sports complex in southern Fortaleza.

The trio of Paula Toller, George Israel and Bruno Fortunato took the stage, as confirmed by Kid Abelha Fortaleza. According to g1, they returned with the tour ‘Eu Tive um Sonho’ through arenas and stadiums.

The concert was held on Saturday 22 August 2026, two days before this report. The band played their first live show in thirteen years, as confirmed by Brazilian outlets.

However, the band had not played live since 2013, making this a significant comeback. The show was part of a ten-date arena tour across Brazil.

A Historic Band Back on Stage

Kid Abelha, meaning ‘Kid Bee’, are icons of Brazilian pop rock of the 1980s and 1990s, according to Terra. Their hits include ‘Como Eu Quero’, ‘Grand’ Hotel’ and ‘Fixação’.

This is a national reference band returning to full-size arenas after a decade away. For a foreign reader, it is not a club-circuit reunion.

The comeback is a major event in Brazilian music. Kid Abelha, meaning ‘Kid Bee’, formed in Rio de Janeiro in the early 1980s.

Their songs are radio standards in Brazil, though largely unknown outside it. In addition, their songs are radio standards in Brazil, though largely unknown outside it.

This return to arenas highlights their enduring popularity.

The Tour Named After a Dream

The tour is called ‘Eu Tive um Sonho’, which means ‘I Had a Dream’. Paula Toller explained the title: after so long away from the stage, she literally had a dream about Kid Abelha playing again.

That became the motto of the tour. In total, the tour will have ten performances, according to Estado de Minas.

The Fortaleza show was the seventh date, with three more to come. The tour title comes from a literal dream Paula Toller had about the band playing again.

The Venue and Its Location

The concert took place at Centro de Formação Olímpica, also known as Arena CFO. It was on Avenida Alberto Craveiro in the Castelão area.

Castelão is the district built around the Arena Castelão football stadium, and the CFO stands beside it. Fortaleza is the capital of Ceará on Brazil’s northeastern coast, a city of roughly 2.4 million and a major beach-tourism destination.

The venue is a publicly built sports and training complex whose arena doubles as a concert hall. The Centro de Formação Olímpica is a publicly built sports complex in the Castelão area.

Show Times and Ticket Prices

The gates opened at 6pm, with the band starting at 9pm, as reported by GCMAIS and O POVO. Tickets were sold through Ticketmaster, the official channel, and at the Barraca Santa Praia kiosk, with no service fee.

The full price list, published by O POVO, ranged from 125 reais (about US$24) for a half-price grandstand ticket. It went up to 920 reais (about US$179) for a full-price VIP package.

Brazilian law reserves half-price ‘meia’ tickets for students, people over 60, teachers and other listed groups. A foreign tourist does not qualify for the half-price rate, so the cheapest full-price ticket was 250 reais (US$49).

Remaining Tour Dates

After Fortaleza, three tour dates remained. Porto Alegre was Saturday 26 September, Curitiba Saturday 10 October, and Florianópolis Saturday 17 October.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Kid Abelha?

Kid Abelha, meaning ‘Kid Bee’, are a Brazilian pop-rock band formed in Rio de Janeiro in the early 1980s. They are fronted by singer Paula Toller and are icons of Brazilian pop rock of the 1980s and 1990s.

Why was the Fortaleza show significant?

The Fortaleza show marked the band’s return to the stage after a 13-year hiatus, their first live performance since 2013. It was part of a ten-show arena tour across Brazil.

What Is the Café Vinilo Festival

The Café Vinilo Festival is a music festival staged by Café Vinilo, a small Buenos Aires music club. It presents a palette of what is happening today in independent music, as the club’s official event page says.

In addition, the programme includes an educational concert for children and performances by La Ferni. Ernesto Snajer, Guillo Espel Cuarteto and others, according to CEMBA.

The festival’s official page says it shows a palette of today’s independent music. However, the press describes it as ten days celebrating independent music in San Cristóbal.

The festival runs from Monday 21 September to Saturday 3 October 2026, with concerts on eight dates. All performances take place at Café Vinilo, located at Estados Unidos 2483, between Alberti and Matheu streets, in the San Cristóbal neighbourhood.

World.title: Chiles en Nogada Season Reaches San Miguel de Allende
World.content:
Mexico · FOOD

Key Facts — What happened Chiles en Nogada season has reached San Miguel de Allende, with two kitchens serving the patriotic dish.

— How big The season runs from July to September, when fresh walnuts and pomegranates peak.

— The real story The dish’s green, white and red colours echo the Mexican flag, symbolizing independence.

— The catch The legend of nuns creating it for Iturbide in 1821 lacks documentary support, historians say.

— On the map Two addresses in San Miguel de Allende, Guanajuato, serve the dish this season.

— What comes next The season ends in September, tied to Mexico’s independence celebrations on 15-16 September.

The dish’s green, white and red colours echo the Mexican flag, and its short season runs from July to September each year.

A chile en nogada under its walnut sauce, pomegranate seeds and parsley — green, white and red.

Chiles en Nogada season has reached San Miguel de Allende, bringing the patriotic dish to the colonial town’s tables. The dish, a fire-roasted poblano chilli stuffed with pork and fruit, is a summer treat that runs from July to September.

What Is Chiles en Nogada?

In short, Chiles en Nogada is a Mexican seasonal dish. It is a fire-roasted poblano chilli stuffed with pork and seasonal fruit.

The filling, called picadillo, mixes meat with local apple, pear and peach, plus dried fruit and nuts. The sauce, nogada, is made from fresh green walnuts, milk or cream, and often fresh cheese.

The dish is served per chilli, called por pieza, as one portion. However, the season runs from July to September when ingredients peak.

The dish is a symbol of Mexican independence, tied to September holidays. Therefore, it is a patriotic plate for the national celebrations.

The Dish Wears the Mexican Flag

The plate carries the three colours of the Mexican flag, which is why Mexicans call it patriotic. The poblano chilli represents the green, the walnut sauce the white, and the red pomegranate seeds the red.

Green also comes from parsley leaves laid on top. Therefore, according to Viva México, the colours represent the national flag, a point echoed across Mexican food writing.

The red pomegranate seeds symbolize the flag’s red stripe. Meanwhile, the green chilli and parsley represent the green, and the white sauce the white.

A Flag Older Than the Modern One

In fact, the colours are older than the modern flag. They come from the banner of the Army of the Three Guarantees, raised in 1821.

In that standard, green meant independence, white meant religion, and red meant union between peoples. Postal de México explains that Iturbide chose these colours for his Three Guarantees standard, and they remain in today’s Mexican flag.

The dish, therefore, carries a historical weight beyond its taste. These colours were chosen by Iturbide for his standard in 1821.

As a result, the dish honors that original banner, not just today’s flag.

The Legend of the Nuns and Iturbide

The popular story says Augustinian nuns at the Santa Mónica convent in Puebla created chiles en Nogada for Iturbide to celebrate independence. Still, Telediario calls this version a legend, not established history.

Specialists note that this account has no documentary support and is a romantic construction, according to El Heraldo de México. The famous date of 28 August 1821 does not fit Iturbide’s whereabouts, the same report says.

The story says nuns made it for Iturbide on 28 August 1821. However, that date does not match his presence in Puebla, specialists note.

What Historians Accept Instead

Historians do accept that the dish came from convent kitchens in colonial Puebla, but not the single banquet story. Research from Mexico’s national university, the UNAM, says the recipe existed long before Iturbide’s visit.

It was an existing convent recipe adapted and perfected for the occasion, drawing on historian Guadalupe Pérez San Vicente. Moreover, La Jornada adds the dish emerged from changes the Spanish conquest brought to cooking, although the inventor remains unknown.

The recipe likely existed before Iturbide’s visit, adapted later. Still, the woman who invented it remains unknown, La Jornada reports.

Why the Season Is So Short

The season is agricultural, not marketing. Even so, Chiles en Nogada can only be enjoyed at its best between July and September.

That is when fresh walnuts and pomegranates are at their peak. Chef Ricardo Muñoz Zurita told El Economista that a real chiles en Nogada can only be made properly in those months.

He adds that his restaurants end the season in September when native fruit and fresh walnut run out. Fresh walnuts and pomegranates are only at their best then.

In addition, chef Muñoz Zurita insists on using native fruit and fresh walnut.

Official Dates and Prices Elsewhere

Meanwhile, in Puebla, the home state, the official season starts on 15 July and runs to early September, according to El Economista. A related fair runs from 15 July to the end of September, Milenio reports.

Prices elsewhere in Mexico vary. Overall, in Mexico City, restaurants charge between 490 and 750 pesos per chilli, about US$29 to US$44.

In the State of Mexico, prices range from 250 to 800 pesos, about US$15 to US$47. Meanwhile, a Mexican hotel group set its own window from 19 August to 24 September.

These prices, however, are not San Miguel de Allende figures.

San Miguel de Allende Joins the Season

San Miguel de Allende, a colonial hill town in Guanajuato, adds two addresses to this seasonal campaign, according to Vinetur. One kitchen serves a poblano stuffed with pork shank, seasonal fruit and artisanal candied cactus, plus a vegetarian option.

By contrast, the other serves a version with beef, fresh and dried fruit, home-made walnut sauce, coriander and pomegranate. However, no verifiable list of restaurants with names, addresses, or prices has been published for the town this season.

Two addresses in the town serve the dish this season, Vinetur reports. Still, no local prices or dates have been published for these kitchens.

A Dish for the September Celebrations

Mexican outlets tie the dish to the September independence holidays, calling it the star of the celebrations. Mexico’s independence is marked on the night of 15 September and the day of 16 September.

A Mexican hotel group describes chiles en Nogada as one of the most representative dishes of Mexican cooking. Its own season runs from 19 August to 24 September, a window that fits the national July-to-September period.

The dish is a symbol of Mexican independence, tied to September holidays. Therefore, it is a patriotic plate for the national celebrations.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is chiles en nogada?

Chiles en Nogada is a Mexican dish made of a fire-roasted poblano chilli stuffed with pork and seasonal fruit. Covered in a walnut sauce and decorated with pomegranate.

Why is chiles en nogada considered patriotic?

The dish carries the three colours of the Mexican flag: green from the chilli and parsley. White from the walnut sauce, and red from pomegranate seeds.

When is chiles en nogada season?

The traditional season runs from July through September, when fresh walnuts and pomegranates are at their peak. In Puebla, the official season starts on 15 July and runs to early September.

Can I find chiles en nogada in San Miguel de Allende?

Yes, two addresses in San Miguel de Allende are serving the dish this season, according to Vinetur. However, no detailed list of restaurants with names, addresses, or prices has been published for the town.

Sources: Vinetur; Viva México; Milenio; El Economista; El Financiero; Cabe Señalar; El Heraldo de México; Telediario; La Jornada; El Mensajero de Puebla; TV Azteca; Postal de México.

World.title: Afya and Yduqs Confirm Merger Talks of Brazil’s Education Giants
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Brazil · BUSINESS

Key Facts — What happened Afya and Yduqs confirmed on 24 August 2026 that they are in early talks over a possible business combination.

— Market reaction Yduqs shares jumped more than 10% in São Paulo, while Afya edged up 0.77% on Nasdaq.

— Who is involved Germany’s Bertelsmann controls Afya, and its top executives met bankers in São Paulo last week.

— The catch Both companies say the talks are early-stage with no binding agreement, so a deal may never happen.

— What is missing No price, no exchange ratio and no deal structure have been published by either side.

— What comes next Both companies must disclose material progress under Brazilian and United States securities rules.

Brazil’s largest education group and its top medical-school network are talking — very carefully.

Afya and Yduqs confirmed on Monday, 24 August 2026, that they are discussing a possible merger. The talks are at an early stage, and both companies stress that nothing binding has been signed.

Students on a Brazilian university campus. A merger of Afya and Yduqs would create the country’s largest education group.

What the companies confirmed

Yduqs went first on Monday, 24 August 2026. Brazil’s largest education group published a material fact, the formal notice listed companies must release under Brazilian law.

In it, Yduqs confirmed negotiations with Afya over a possible business combination. The filing stressed that the talks are at an initial stage.

It added that no agreement, contract or binding commitment exists. Neither the companies nor their shareholders have assumed any obligation.

Afya followed within hours. The medical-education company, listed on the Nasdaq exchange in New York, released its own statement confirming early-stage conversations.

How the market reacted

Yduqs shares moved first and hardest. They were up 10.8% shortly before 11:00 in São Paulo, Valor Econômico reported.

The rally extended through the session. At one point the shares were up 12.1% at 8.82 reais, about US$1.71, per Investing.com data.

The dollar figure uses the central bank’s PTAX rate of 5.1512 reais per dollar, published on 24 August 2026. Afya shares, traded in New York, rose a modest 0.77%.

The gap between the two moves is telling. Investors see Yduqs, the smaller partner, as the bigger winner of any combination.

How the talks surfaced

The first hint came a day earlier, on 23 August. O Globo columnist Lauro Jardim reported that two top Bertelsmann executives had landed in São Paulo the previous week.

Bertelsmann is the German media and services group that controls Afya. According to the column, its executives met at Bank of America with one objective.

That objective was evaluating a merger with Yduqs. The meetings suggest the talks have senior backing on the Afya side.

Neither company has confirmed the São Paulo meetings themselves. Their Monday statements speak only of early conversations between the two education groups.

Who the two companies are

Afya is the largest medical-education network in Brazil. It runs medical schools and related courses, and its shares trade on the Nasdaq.

Its controlling shareholder is Bertelsmann, the German group. That gives Afya deep pockets and an international owner with a long investment horizon.

Yduqs is the country’s largest education group by reach. It serves hundreds of thousands of students across universities and distance learning.

Together, Afya and Yduqs would create an education giant with few rivals in Latin America. That scale is the strategic logic behind the talks.

The financial backdrop

Yduqs arrives at the table under pressure. Its second-quarter profit dropped 54%, as new rules hit its distance-learning business.

The weak quarter helps explain why its shares reacted so strongly on Monday. A combination could offer shareholders a route back to growth.

Afya arrives from a stronger position. Its second-quarter revenue rose, and the company maintained its 2026 revenue guidance, per its August earnings report.

Medical education is the premium end of the Brazilian market. Afya’s margins and Bertelsmann’s backing make it the natural senior partner.

What a combination would mean

A merged group would unite mass-market higher education with elite medical training. That pairing covers nearly every price point in Brazilian private education.

For students, little would change in the short term. Brands, campuses and course offerings typically survive such mergers intact.

For investors, the appeal is scale and cost discipline. Shared technology platforms and marketing budgets can lift margins across a larger student base.

No source has published enrollment or revenue figures for a combined group. Any size estimate would be speculation at this stage.

What has not been decided

Almost everything, in fact. There is no published price, no exchange ratio and no proposed governance structure for a combined company.

The companies have not said whether Afya would absorb Yduqs or whether a new holding company would emerge. Even the deal currency, shares or cash, is unknown.

Antitrust is another open question. Neither statement mentions CADE, Brazil’s competition regulator, which would likely review a combination of this size.

Both companies were explicit about the risk. There can be no assurance, Afya said, that the discussions will result in any agreement at all.

What happens next

Both companies now operate under disclosure obligations. Yduqs must update the market under Brazilian securities law whenever talks reach a material stage.

Afya faces parallel duties under United States securities law and Nasdaq rules. It said it will not comment further unless disclosure is required.

The next signal to watch is a term sheet or a definitive agreement announcement. Bankers involved in the talks may also surface in future filings.

Until then, the story is a courtship, not a wedding. Monday’s share-price jump prices in hope, and hope is not yet a deal.

Frequently Asked Questions

Are Afya and Yduqs merging? Not yet. Both confirmed early-stage talks on 24 August 2026 about a possible business combination. No binding agreement exists, and either side can still walk away. Why did Yduqs shares jump more than 10%? Investors expect a combination to benefit Yduqs, the financially weaker partner. The shares rose as much as 12.1% to 8.82 reais, about US$1.71, on Monday. Who owns Afya? Afya is controlled by Bertelsmann, the German media and services group. O Globo reported that Bertelsmann executives met bankers in São Paulo last week to evaluate the merger. Would the merger need antitrust approval? Very likely, from CADE, Brazil’s competition regulator. Neither company has mentioned a filing yet, and no details have been published. What happens next in the Afya and Yduqs talks? Watch for new material-fact filings from Yduqs or statements from Afya under Nasdaq rules. A term sheet or definitive agreement would be the first hard signal of a real deal.

— Who decides Minority shareholders of Usiminas must still approve any delisting, all three reports stress.

— What comes next A formal filing with Brazil’s securities regulator would be the first hard signal the plan is moving.

A decade-long control war ended in 2023 — now the winner wants the whole company.

Ternium plans to take Usiminas private, Brazilian media reported on Monday, 24 August 2026. Shares of Brazil’s largest flat-steel maker jumped more than 7% on the news.

The Usiminas main plant in Ipatinga, Minas Gerais. Ternium wants to take Brazil’s largest flat-steel maker private.

What the reports say

The story broke on Monday, 24 August 2026, in O Globo. Columnist Lauro Jardim wrote that the Italian-Argentine steelmaker Ternium wants to take Usiminas private.

In Portuguese the plan is called fechar o capital, which means delisting the company from the stock exchange. Valor Econômico and InfoMoney both confirmed the report the same morning.

All three outlets stress the same condition. Ternium still needs the approval of Usiminas minority shareholders to complete the operation.

Neither Ternium nor Usiminas had issued a formal statement by Monday afternoon. The plan, for now, is a reported intention rather than a filed offer.

How the market reacted

Investors liked the idea immediately. Usiminas preferred shares rose more than 7% in early Monday trading on the São Paulo exchange, known as B3.

The move was sharp enough to trigger a trading auction. That is the exchange’s automatic pause when a stock swings beyond its permitted limit.

Usiminas ranked among the biggest gainers on the Ibovespa, Brazil’s benchmark stock index. InfoMoney said traders were reacting directly to the delisting report.

A delisting typically includes an offer to buy out minority holders. That prospect of a cash exit is what usually lifts the share price first.

A decade of boardroom war

Usiminas was founded in 1956 in the state of Minas Gerais as a Brazil-Japan joint venture. It grew into Latin America’s premier flat-steel producer for the car industry.

From 2012 to 2023 the company was the stage of one of the region’s longest shareholder wars. Ternium, part of the Techint group, fought Japan’s Nippon Steel for control.

The fight ended in 2023. Ternium signed an agreement to buy control of Usiminas, and Nippon Steel stepped back after six decades as technical partner.

A Ternium-appointed chief executive, Marcelo Chara, took over and launched an operational overhaul. The control question was settled, but minority shareholders remained.

How Ternium tightened its grip

The 2023 deal was only the first step. Last year Ternium acquired the remaining stakes that Nippon Steel and Mitsubishi held in Usiminas.

That purchase left Ternium leading the control block with fewer partners to consult. Taking the company private is the logical end of that road.

Ternium itself signaled the direction days before the report. On its 21 August earnings call, management described corporate simplification, including more Usiminas ownership, as a long-term objective.

The company made the same point in its 2025 sustainability report, also published on 21 August. It now consolidates Usiminas into its targets, including a 15% cut in carbon intensity per ton of steel by 2030.

Business ties were already deepening

The two companies are commercially intertwined already. On 19 August, Reuters reported fresh related-party contracts between Usiminas and Exiros.

Exiros is the procurement arm controlled by Ternium and its sister company Tenaris. One contract covers international trading and took effect on 10 August 2026.

A second contract covers domestic procurement support, logistics and import services in Brazil. It starts on 1 October 2026 and runs for four years.

Both agreements are priced at cost plus fees and carry no minimum volumes. They show how deeply Ternium already runs inside Usiminas operations.

What Usiminas makes and why it matters

Usiminas is Brazil’s leading producer of flat steel. That is the steel that goes into cars, home appliances and machinery.

The company is headquartered in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais. Its main plant sits in Ipatinga, in the state’s steel valley.

Flat steel makes Usiminas strategic for Brazilian industry. Car makers and appliance factories depend on its output and its prices.

That weight in the supply chain is why the plan to take Usiminas private matters beyond the stock market. Brazil’s largest flat-steel maker would leave public scrutiny behind.

What has not been published

The reports name no price. There is no published offer per share, no valuation and no indication of how Ternium would pay.

The structure is equally open. Brazilian law offers several routes to delist, and none of the reports says which one Ternium would choose.

There is also no timetable. No shareholder meeting, no regulatory filing and no deadline has been announced.

For readers the distinction matters. A reported plan can still change shape, run into resistance from minority holders, or simply wait.

Why delistings are spreading in Brazil

If the operation advances, Usiminas would join a growing list of large companies leaving B3. InfoMoney describes a wave of consolidation behind the trend.

Multinationals are tightening control over their Brazilian subsidiaries. Fewer public shareholders means simpler governance and faster decisions.

The costs of staying listed are real. Disclosure duties, independent board seats and regulator oversight all weigh on controlling owners.

For minority investors the trade-off cuts both ways. A delisting offer can bring a cash exit, but it also ends their ride on Brazil’s steel cycle.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is Ternium buying Usiminas outright? Not yet. O Globo reported on 24 August 2026 that Ternium wants to take Usiminas private. No formal offer has been filed, and minority shareholders must approve any delisting. Why did Usiminas shares jump more than 7%? A delisting normally includes an offer to buy out minority shareholders. The prospect of that cash exit lifted the shares on Monday and triggered a trading auction on B3. Who owns Usiminas today? A control group led by Ternium runs the company. Ternium agreed to buy control in 2023 and acquired the remaining Nippon Steel and Mitsubishi stakes in 2025. What does it mean to take Usiminas private? The company would leave the São Paulo stock exchange and its shares would stop trading publicly. Minority holders would be bought out under a formal offer. What happens next? Watch for a formal statement from Ternium or Usiminas and any filing with Brazil’s securities regulator. Until then the plan is a reported intention without price, structure or timetable.

Jazz na Serra, the free festival in Santo Antônio do Pinhal. Returns for its fourth edition on Friday 28 and Saturday 29 August 2026.

The mountain town in the Serra da Mantiqueira, about two hours from São Paulo, turns its centre into an open-air stage.

What Is Jazz na Serra?

Jazz na Serra means Jazz in the Mountains, a name that fits its setting in the Serra da Mantiqueira range. In short, this range divides São Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio de Janeiro.

It is a cool-climate holiday area popular with people from São Paulo. Meanwhile, the festival takes place in Santo Antônio do Pinhal, a small mountain town.

It is in the Vale do Paraíba region, next to the better-known resort of Campos do Jordão. G1 Vale do Paraíba, the regional arm of the Globo news site, confirmed the dates on Saturday 22 August 2026.

The festival’s fourth edition is scheduled for late August 2026. However, the exact dates are Friday 28 and Saturday 29 August, as confirmed by G1.

When Does Jazz na Serra Run?

Jazz na Serra 2026 runs on Friday 28 and Saturday 29 August only. Although Brazilian coverage calls this the last weekend of August, the calendar confirms 28 August is a Friday.

29 August is a Saturday. There is no Sunday programme, even though 30 August is the last Sunday of the month.

So plan for a two-day festival, not a three-day one. The festival runs Friday and Saturday only, not Sunday.

As a result, visitors should plan for two days of music, not three.

Where the Music Happens

In fact, all concerts take place in two public spaces in the town centre. These are the Praça do Artesão, or Artisan’s Square, and the Boulevard Araucária, or Araucária Boulevard.

G1 reported that the programme includes free shows in both spaces. Therefore, the araucária is the Paraná pine, the flat-topped conifer.

It is the emblem of the Serra da Mantiqueira and gives the boulevard its name. A praça is a town square, so both venues are open-air and public.

Both venues are in the town centre, but no street address is published. Therefore, visitors should look for the main square and the boulevard.

Free Entry and No Booking

Entry to every performance is free, as Folha de S. Paulo noted on 7 August 2026.

Veja São Paulo described it as an instrumental music festival that occupies squares and avenues with free live performances. Because the shows are in public squares, there are no tickets, no wristbands, and no registration or booking channel.

Just show up and enjoy. Since entry is free, there is no ticket to buy or reserve.

However, arriving early is wise to find a good spot.

Friday Line-Up at the Praça do Artesão

The festival opens on Friday 28 August at 7.30pm with Giu Nogueira Quarteto at the Praça do Artesão. At 9pm, Michael Pipoquinha Quarteto takes the same stage.

G1 confirmed these two concerts, and Veja São Paulo listed the identical times and venue. A quarteto is a quartet, so expect four-piece ensembles.

The Friday line-up features two quartets, starting at 7.30pm. Meanwhile, the second act begins at 9pm, so plan accordingly.

Saturday’s Seven Concerts

Saturday 29 August brings seven concerts, starting at midday with Grande Banda do Sertão at the Praça do Artesão. The day runs until 9pm with Banda Black Rio, also at the Praça do Artesão.

In addition, the schedule alternates between the two venues. Eloá Gonçalves Trio is at 1.30pm and DejaVu Session – Especial Jazz Brasil at 4.30pm at the Boulevard Araucária.

Jota P Quinteto is at 3pm and Juliane Gamboa at 6pm at the Praça do Artesão. Banda Mantiqueira plays at 7.30pm at the Boulevard Araucária.

Saturday’s schedule is packed with seven performances across both venues. Therefore, visitors can move between the two stages throughout the day.

More Than 10 Hours of Music

G1 reported that Saturday alone offers more than 10 hours of music, with seven performances from midday to 9pm. That makes the second day the heart of the festival.

By contrast, Friday has just two concerts, so the weekend builds to a full day of sound. The seven-concert count and the 10-hour figure both belong to Saturday.

The Saturday programme alone exceeds 10 hours of music. In addition, this makes the second day the festival’s main event.

Who Curates Jazz na Serra

The artistic curation is by Joabe Reis, an award-winning trombonist who selects the Brazilian instrumental names. Cultura UOL reported on a new edition curated by Reis with concerts in public squares.

The festival’s creator is the producer Pedro Pimenta. Even so, In&Out Jazz, a Spanish jazz site, quoted Pimenta in December 2025.

Therefore, the idea is not to hold a festival that could take place anywhere. Just putting the Jazz na Serra brand on it.

In addition, it’s almost inevitable that it will happen again, and we’ve already started thinking about ways to do that. The curator Joabe Reis selects the Brazilian instrumental acts.

However, the creator Pedro Pimenta confirmed the 2026 edition will happen.

Getting There and Planning Your Visit

By car from São Paulo, the drive takes about two hours via the Rodovia Ayrton Senna and Rodovia Carvalho Pinto. Then take the Rodovia Floriano Rodrigues Pinheiro (SP-123) towards Campos do Jordão.

Follow the signposted turn-off to Santo Antônio do Pinhal. By bus, an intercity coach runs from São Paulo’s Terminal Rodoviário Tietê to Campos do Jordão.

After that, connect on to Santo Antônio do Pinhal. However, there is no official festival shuttle or dedicated bus, so visitors without a car depend on this ordinary coach route.

For the latest details, the town’s tourism page directs readers to the festival’s official Instagram account. As of Monday 24 August 2026, the festival has not yet started, so there is still time to plan your visit.

The drive from São Paulo takes about two hours by car. By coach, travel to Campos do Jordão from Terminal Tietê and change there.

Yes, every concert at Jazz na Serra is free, as confirmed by Folha de S. Paulo and Veja São Paulo.

Jazz na Serra 2026 runs on Friday 28 and Saturday 29 August 2026. Plan for two days rather than a full weekend.

All concerts take place in two public spaces in the town centre of Santo Antônio do Pinhal: the Praça do Artesão and the Boulevard Araucária. No street addresses are published, but both are in the town centre.

By car, it’s about a two-hour drive via the Rodovia Ayrton Senna, Rodovia Carvalho Pinto, and Rodovia Floriano Rodrigues Pinheiro (SP-123). By bus, an intercity coach runs from São Paulo’s Terminal Rodoviário Tietê to Campos do Jordão.

By Zoila Palma: As part of Climate Week 2026 activities in Punta Gorda Town, the Toledo Institute for Development and Environment (TIDE) hosted 25 visitors representing eight government entities on August 22 for an educational and conservation-focused visit to the Port Honduras Marine Reserve (PHMR).

The group toured the marine reserve, which is co-managed by TIDE, and had the opportunity to learn more about its conservation efforts and operations.

Visitors were also taken to the Boardwalk and the Steven Page Ranger Station at Punta Ycacos, gaining firsthand insight into the work being carried out to protect Belize’s marine resources.

TIDE Executive Director Leonardo Chavarria and other members of the organization’s staff delivered presentations highlighting the institute’s operations and its ongoing conservation initiatives within the Port Honduras Marine Reserve.

Following the presentations, the visitors experienced the natural environment of the reserve firsthand, spending the remainder of the day snorkeling and enjoying the scenic West Snake Caye Beach.

TIDE said it was grateful for the opportunity to showcase its conservation work while strengthening collaboration among government partners.

World.title: International News:  World’s Oceans reach record high temperatures as El Niño adds to climate warming
World.content:
International News: World’s Oceans reach record high temperatures as El Niño adds to climate warming

By Zoila Palma: The world’s oceans have reached their highest recorded average surface temperature, according to new data from the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service, raising further concerns about the impacts of climate change and a strengthening El Niño weather phenomenon.

Global average sea surface temperatures outside the polar regions reached 21.1°C (70°F) on Saturday, slightly surpassing the previous record of 21.09°C recorded on three days in March 2024.

Scientists say the timing is particularly concerning because ocean temperatures typically reach their annual peak around March or April, rather than in August, BBC reports.

The unusually warm conditions are being driven by a combination of long-term human-caused warming and El Niño, which brings warmer-than-usual waters to the surface across the eastern and central tropical Pacific.

“This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress,” said Dr. Samantha Burgess, deputy director of Copernicus, adding that El Niño is “adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming.”

Scientists warn that further warming could have serious consequences for people and marine ecosystems, including stronger extreme weather, rising sea levels, coastal flooding and damage to coral reefs and other marine habitats.
