World.title: Wildfire burning near Nevada city forces evacuation of 90,000 residents
World.content:
A wildfire that mushroomed over the weekend in the Sierra Nevada foothills has spread perilously close to neighbourhoods in Reno, in the US state of Nevada, forcing authorities to urge more than 90,000 residents to leave their homes.

The out-of-control fire has already burned some homes, but there is concern that shifting winds could push the flames into newly developed and densely packed neighbourhoods on the edge of Nevada's second-biggest city.

Schools across the area were closed Monday because of the evacuations and to keep roads clear for emergency crews.

Authorities said on Sunday evening, local time, that the Hawk Fire had stayed in its footprint and firefighters were extinguishing hotspots while working to keep the fire from jumping a main highway and reaching areas filled with homes and businesses.

Satellite imagery shows the huge Hawk Fire encroaching on built-up areas. (European Union/Copernicus Sentinel-2 via Reuters)

The fire began on Saturday and grew to more than 60 square kilometres on Sunday across foothills ringed by neighbourhoods near the California state line. There was zero containment.

At least six people — three first responders and three civilians — were injured. Officials said the fire was "human-caused" but did not say whether it was intentionally set or accidental.

Videos posted on social media showed the smouldering ruins of homes and cars, with only a scorched basketball hoop still standing.

Smoke and flames rise from the Hawk fire in Reno, Nevada, U.S., August 22, 2026, in this screengrab from a video obtained from social media. (Reuters/Social media: @SquintDev/via)

Many residents had little time to evacuate after the fire exploded in size.

"Honestly, I thought it was like in a movie," said Ruby Delatorre, who got back from a concert only to find her home in the evacuation zone. She returned Sunday to walk to her home and get a few more possessions.

"I literally want to cry and go back for all my stuff. I just got what I thought I needed," Ms Delatorre said.

50,000 wildfires recorded across US

Some who spotted the smoke on Saturday thought it was from another wildfire that has been burning the past two weeks.

Teresa Lenshyn, who is among the evacuees, said being forced to leave was chaotic and stressful. "You don't know if the winds are going to shift and it's going to get worse," she said.

The Hawk Fire is the third largest wildfire in the rugged terrain north of Reno in the past two weeks, all caused by human activity, according to fire officials.

Extremely dry conditions across the American West have sparked a rash of wildfires this summer.

Fires in eastern Washington state forced the evacuation of 60,000 people in the Spokane area in early August.

Nationwide, there have been more than 50,000 wildfires, the most over the past 10 years covering the same time period, according to the National Interagency Fire Center.

AP

World.title: Ukraine marks Independence Day as UK vows support despite Russia's threats
World.content:
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has used a defiant speech on Ukraine's Independence Day to declare that the country wants peace but will not just surrender to Russia at any price, as foreign leaders pledged their support.

Flanked by British Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa, Mr Zelenskyy praised the resilience of the Ukrainian people during more than four years of war with Russia.

"Ukraine absolutely wants peace, but it is not ready to simply surrender," the Ukrainian president said, warning that Russia would not halt its aggression even if Ukraine ceded to its demands for more territory in the country's east.

Wearing a traditional Ukrainian embroidered shirt, Mr Zelenskyy thanked several foreign leaders for travelling to Kyiv to show their continued backing, on the 35th anniversary of Ukraine's break from the Soviet Union.

Hundreds of thousands of soldiers have died in fighting since Russia's invasion began in February 2022. (Reuters: Gleb Garanich)

Mr Burnham, who took office last month, said his choice of Kyiv for his first foreign visit showed the importance he attached to assisting in Ukraine's defence.

"We are with you in this struggle all the way, heart and soul," Mr Burnham said.

The British prime minister vowed to continue that support "despite Russia's outrageous threats to my country."

The British government announced on Monday it would allow Kyiv access to classified technology to start production of European SCALP long-range cruise missiles in Ukraine, capable of carrying out strikes deep within Russia.

In response, the Kremlin said the use of classified British technology would "add fuel to the fire" of their worsening relations, after it warned London last week there would be "consequences" for supplying drones to Kyiv.

Allies to hold military talks

Mr Burnham was scheduled to co-chair a virtual meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" — a group of countries backing Ukraine — with French President Emmanuel Macron and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The leaders were expected to discuss Ukraine's request for more air defence systems to stop Russian ballistic missiles pounding Ukrainian cities.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham is among world leaders in Ukraine to mark the country's Independence Day. (Reuters: Henry Nicholls)

Mr Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Ukraine's war effort was being complicated by a $US27 billion ($37 billion) defence funding gap this year.

He also warned that Russian could escalate the conflict later this year by mobilising some 300,000 additional troops after parliamentary elections in September.

Paying tribute to Ukrainian people and soldiers defending Ukraine in the war, Mr Zelenskyy called on allies to give it "everything" needed to stop the war.

"We are not asking you to fight for us," he said.

Hundreds of thousands of people have been killed, and swathes of Ukrainian territory have been laid waste, since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022.

US-led peace talks to bring a lasting end to the war fell apart earlier this year as Ukraine refused Russian demands to cede more territory.

Technological display

Fighting continues along a 1,200 kilometre front line and Ukraine has succeeded in bringing Russian advances overall to a virtual halt this year.

Hovering in the sky above Kyiv, a squadron of aerial drones carried out a demonstration of the Ukrainian military technology, which has helped to keep Russian forces in check.

Ukraine's drones could crash Russian banks On the outskirts of Russian cities, warehouses belonging to the country's largest online retailer are being struck by Kyiv's drones, with some analysts saying it could lead to a financial crisis.

Naval drones swept along the Dnipro river, while unnamed ground vehicles — some equipped with heavy machine guns — trundled in formation along one of the city's main commercial avenues.

While praising the achievements of Ukraine's defence industry during the war, Mr Zelenskyy called for an increase in cruise missile production to take the fight to Russia this winter.

Exploiting Ukraine's critical shortage of anti-ballistic missiles, Russia has stepped up its campaign of air strikes at cities far from the front line this summer.

Ukraine has also increased its long-range attacks on Russian refineries and logistics infrastructure, aimed at undermining Moscow's war effort.

It hit four logistics hubs owned by Russia's second-largest online retailer Ozon in southern Russia in drone strikes on Monday, the company said.

In a sombre moment, the Ukrainian leader rewarded fallen soldiers with state awards, which he presented to their mothers and family members.

He also announced the return of 10 Ukrainian servicemen, who were previously listed as missing in action, as part of a special prisoner exchange with Russia.

"We remember each and every one who remains in captivity," Mr Zelenskyy said, promising to do everything possible to bring them home.

Reuters

World.title: Swan's assistant takes-over as Essendon coach
World.content:
Mark McVeigh, a former Essendon player and Sydney assistant coach, will take over as Essendon's senior coach after what the club said was an "extensive" and "deliberate" selection process.

McVeigh, 45, won the role ahead of Bombers great and ex-coach James Hird, as well as Jaymie Graham and Murray Davis.

Essendon confirmed the announcement on Monday afternoon, a day after the stricken club's narrow loss to Port Adelaide.

McVeigh would take over "effective immediately", the club said in a statement.

The official announcement came following a day of speculation and a message of congratulations from former teammate and Bomber's legend, James Hird.

"I put my heart and soul into the effort, but obviously fell short and that's the way it goes," Hird said on Nine yesterday night.

James Hird (L) and Dean Solomon (C) speak with Mark McVeigh (R). (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Brad Scott was sacked on May 25, with Dean Solomon taking over as interim coach for the rest of the season.

Solomon rounded out the Bomber's worst season in club history with a 10-point defeat to Port Adelaide on Sunday.

McVeigh commits to building Essendon's 'next great era'

The search for a new coach has involved a tumultuous selection process, with opinion sharply divided on whether Hird should win another tenure in the role.

Club president Andrew Welsh, who played at Essendon alongside McVeigh and Hird, said the appointment was a unanimous board decision.

"Mark was clearly the best candidate for what this role demands," Welsh said on the club website.

"We are building the next successful era for Essendon, with a view to playing finals, winning finals and competing for premierships.

"We weighed every candidate against what this role actually demands, and Mark was the clear stand-out."

Hird congratulates McVeigh A 'very disappointed' James Hird congratulates former teammate Mark McVeigh, as the Bombers prepare to unveil their new coach.

McVeigh played 232 games for Essendon and returns to the club on a three-year contract after nearly 14 years away, which also included working as an assistant coach at the Greater Western Sydney Giants.

He also acted as caretaker coach at the Giants in 2022.

"We're not looking backwards, we're building the next great era of this football club," McVeigh said.

"That's not built on promises. It's built on our standards, our actions and the work we put in every single day."

AAP/ABC

World.title: New Zealand prime minister proposes Australia-style social media ban
World.content:
New Zealand's Prime Minister Christopher Luxon has unveiled a proposed law banning children younger than 16 from using social media platforms, citing what he said on Monday was "harm being done to a generation" of young people.

Social media ban spreads More and more countries are following Australia's lead and introducing social media bans for children, but US policies are piecemeal and vary from state to state.

If re-elected in November, Mr Luxon is seeking to make his conservative government the latest worldwide to enact age restrictions for social media platforms after Australia enacted its world-first under-16s social media ban in December 2025.

"We simply cannot accept the harm being done to a generation of New Zealand children," Mr Luxon said in a statement.

He said 2025 research showed a third of New Zealand teenagers spent at least five hours a day on social media.

" Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with and it's affecting their family life, mental health, sleep, and education. "

Platforms would be fined 10 per cent of their revenue

New Zealand's proposal includes platforms including Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook. (Reuters: Asanka Brendon)

Under the law, platforms including Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook could be fined up to 10 per cent of their global revenue for failing to meet their obligations — taking "reasonable steps" to check users were older than 16.

Age-check providers want social giants tested In a damning submission, an age-check firm warns big fines may be seen as a "small price to pay" if copping them allows Australia's ban to be "wrongly" be portrayed as a failure.

This could include "existing account information, facial age estimation, digital ID services and formal ID," according to material supplied by Mr Luxon's party.

Like Australia, New Zealand would not penalise parents or children under the proposed bill. However, its penalty system differs from Australia's approach of imposing a maximum fine of $99 million.

Excluded from both Australia's ban and New Zealand's proposed law are messaging platforms such as WhatsApp, online gaming platforms like Roblox and AI apps with productivity uses — including ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot.

Proposal comes amid criticism of Australia's ban

Loading...

Mr Luxon's government has considered such a law since Australia's world-first social media ban for under 16-year-olds took effect in December 2025.

Since Australia's law came into force, countries including Canada, Brazil and Indonesia have enacted bans too, while many other countries are studying or developing laws.

Albanese's social media ban has a shark problem Years into Australia's quest to get teens off social media, the Albanese government is suddenly in a hurry.

Child safety advocates and some parents have welcomed age restrictions, while privacy groups say the rules can be cheated and that forcing users to supply identification raises privacy concerns.

Professor Nicholas Carah, director of the Centre for Digital Cultures and Societies at the University of Queensland, says there are "two big problems that other countries ought to learn from the Australian experience".

"The first is that the ban doesn't actually work in practice. Young people are still easily able to access social media," he said, echoing reports that more than eight in 10 Australian teenagers are still using social media three months after the ban was enacted.

"The other problem is that the ban is regressive, it fails to recognise that social media platforms are important places for young people to learn, to socialise and to express themselves.

" If social media platforms harm young people then the real task is to make them safe. "

Hannah Storey, Head of Children and Young People's Digital Rights at Amnesty International, echoes this sentiment and adds that an under-16s social media ban does not address the harm platforms can inflict on adults too.

"Bans rely on age verification measures, which raise significant privacy concerns, while doing nothing to address the underlying design choices that make many platforms addictive and amplify harmful content," she told the ABC.

"Children who get around bans, and adults who remain on the platforms, will continue to face the same risks.

"We should use the momentum behind this issue to focus on making platforms safe by design for all users, rather than restricting who can access them."

NZ government divided on proposed ban

Some New Zealand political parties plan to vote against the law. (Reuters: Marty Melville)

New Zealand's proposed law has been vehemently opposed by the other two parties that make up the government along with Mr Luxon's centre-right group National — libertarian ACT and populist NZ First.

Both minor parties repeated on Monday their plans to vote against the law.

Politicians from the largest opposition party, centre-left Labour, have not decided if they would vote for it, leader Chris Hipkins said.

However, there would not be enough time for politicians to hold a vote on the proposal before New Zealand's parliament dissolves on October 1 ahead of November's general election, Mr Luxon said.

Bills in New Zealand are required to pass three rounds of voting, usually over a period of months, before they become law.

ABC/Wires

World.title: Suspended sentence, $100 fine for man's naked attack on country ambulance
World.content:
A man who smashed his head through the windscreen of an ambulance while naked on a public street in Western Australia's Goldfields has been handed a suspended sentence and $100 fine.

Brian Charles Parfitt attacked the ambulance, and the paramedics inside, on December 7 last year after he had been spotted behaving erratically on the streets of Boulder, 600km east of Perth.

Parfitt, 26, attempted to climb the first ambulance on scene before mounting the second and repeatedly smashing his head into the windscreen.

The paramedics inside drove back and forth in an attempt to dislodge him, before he smashed his head through the windscreen and began crawling inside.

The St John Ambulance staff fled the vehicle and ran to the second ambulance, with Parfitt apprehended a short time later and placed into an induced coma.

Parfitt's lawyers had previously indicated he was having a "mental health episode" at the time of the incident, but further details have not been mentioned during court proceedings.

Video of the incident, which the ABC has chosen not to republish, was circulated widely on social media and sparked a campaign from St John's around the near-constant violence faced by the ambulance service's staff.

Prosecutors said Parfitt threatened bystanders with a pair of scissors taken from the ambulance. (ABC Goldfields: Macey Turner)

Prosecutors urged prison term

As Parfitt faced the Kalgoorlie Magistrates Court on Monday for sentencing, prosecutors urged an immediate jail term.

Police prosecutor Carl Logan said the 26-year-old, who appeared via video link from Casuarina Prison, was naked in the vicinity of women and children, and had threatened to kill a bystander with scissors taken from the ambulance.

Sergeant Logan said Parfitt had a lengthy criminal record, with the attack coming four months after his release from prison on other charges and causing $4,000 damage to the ambulance.

The court heard he had failed to engage with rehabilitation programs and represented a high risk of future offending.

Defence points to family support

Defence lawyer Leneva Polmear submitted a letter from Parfitt's Perth-based father, describing his pride in his son's efforts to turn his life around.

Ms Polmear said the family had made arrangements with a metropolitan crisis support service to ensure Parfitt had access to appropriate help.

Parfitt's attack caused $4,000 damage to the ambulance. (ABC Goldfields: Macey Turner)

Sentencing Parfitt, Magistrate Donna Webb said she had only been willing to consider a non-custodial sentence if the 26-year-old's father was willing to take him in.

She told the court she was also required to factor in Parfitt's significant mental health issues and the 261 days he had already spent in custody.

Describing the 13-month suspended prison term as a likely "last chance", she said Parfitt would need to do everything right to avoid further time in custody.

Magistrate Webb urged the 26-year-old to remain in Perth after his release from prison.

"Kalgoorlie seems to be a trap for you," she said.

Attacks on paramedics rising

Parfitt's offending came amid a significant rise in attacks on paramedics across Western Australia, with incidents rising 11.9 per cent in 2025.

Rebecca Thompson says she was traumatised by the attack. (ABC News: Nic Perpitch)

Kalgoorlie patient transport officer Rebecca Thomspon was on duty and in the ambulance during Parfitt's attack.

"I have three young children at home and I feared for my life whilst I was on that job," she said at the launch of a campaign to tackle violence against paramedics.

"It shouldn't be like that."

She described the incident as the most traumatic moment of her life.

World.title: International company's plan for multi-billion-dollar data centre in regional Qld
World.content:
With the energy demands of artificial intelligence prompting broader policy debates across Australia, regional Queensland is now facing the reality of hyper-scale expansion with a $31.9 billion data centre being proposed for the Western Downs.

The Western Downs Digital Park, set to be the largest facility of its kind in Australia, has been earmarked for a 725.5-hectare plot near Dalby, roughly 250 kilometres north-west of Brisbane.

The company behind the project is Singapore-based developer Zerra DC, which operates hyper-scale data centres across the Asia Pacific.

A coal seam gas well near Wambo Feedlot, on the Western Downs. (ABC Southern Queensland: Nathan Morris)

The site, 37km north-west of Dalby, is currently home to a 24,000-head feedlot owned by Wambo Cattle Company.

Although this proposed data centre is strategically located near major regional power stations, there are ongoing concerns across the country about energy consumption and water security as the development and construction of data centres surges.

A map showing the proposed site of the Western Downs Digital Park and surrounding energy sources. (Supplied: Urbis)

The federal government is currently refining proposed new national rules for how data centres consume energy, including a requirement for them to purchase power from renewable energy sources.

In Southern Queensland, there has been a recent push from the Toowoomba Regional Council to ensure data centres do not encroach on drinking-water sources in the region.

Councillor Rebecca Vonhoff said the council took a national lead in passing a motion.

"We have this prime industrial land, we own our water infrastructure, we provide drinking water to our residents and, most importantly, we have a personal and very deeply felt connection to water, having lived through some devastating droughts," she said.

Water and energy consumption

While the Western Downs Digital Park plans to prioritise air-cooled technology and avoid reliance on town water infrastructure, the construction and operation will still be water intensive.

During construction, it would require about 522 kilolitres of water a day.

That would be followed by 26.9 megalitres per building for a one-time flush-and-fill process, equivalent to the average annual water use of 155 Australian households.

Under regular operation, the centre would use about 16.5kL of water each day.

It would source its water from coal seam gas water, rainwater harvesting, water delivery, recycled wastewater, and on-site surface water, according to the development application.

Western Downs mayor Andrew Smith says there are a lot of questions being raised about the data centre proposal. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Beyond water security, the centre could draw heavily on power networks, but Western Downs mayor Andrew Smith said, as the "energy capital of Queensland", the region was uniquely positioned to handle the load.

"We've built a lot of energy infrastructure in our region that has benefited our region," he said.

"So, if there needs to be more built, well, bring it on."

He said there would be a rollout of community consultation about the proposal.

"Questions around water, questions around power, around geography — they're the main questions that we're hearing out of our community," Cr Smith said.

"But certainly, those questions around water are very real and the applicant will need to deal with those."

Queensland Minister for Water Ann Leahy said the community should have a voice in this proposal, just like any other major project.

World.title: Matildas star receives rousing welcome in return after mother's death
World.content:
Matildas midfielder Kyra Cooney-Cross has played her first match in more than five months after taking time away from football to spend time with her mother before her death.

Cooney-Cross was sent on in the 63rd minute as Arsenal recorded a 1-0 pre-season win over Paris FC in Borehamwood.

The 67-time international recorded her first minutes since the 2026 AFC Women's Asian Cup final in March, when she started in the Matildas' 1-0 loss to Japan in Sydney.

Cooney-Cross announced on January 8 via Instagram that her mother Jessica Cooney was diagnosed with terminal Stage 4 bile duct cancer. She died on July 10.

Arsenal manager Renee Slegers confirmed on March 28 Cooney-Cross was granted indefinite compassionate leave and would remain in Australia after the Asian Cup to be with her mother.

"You're my biggest inspiration and the person I aspire to be," Cooney-Cross wrote on social media after her mother's death.

"Mum, my favourite part is knowing that I'm a little piece of you."

The 24-year-old returned to Arsenal's pre-season training on August 17, with the Gunners' Women's Super League campaign set to begin on Sunday evening against former Socceroo Dario Vidosic's Brighton & Hove Albion.

Cooney-Cross received a rousing ovation at Meadow Park as she was substituted on alongside compatriot Steph Catley.

Loading Instagram content

The former A-League Women's star with Melbourne Victory and Western Sydney Wanderers was involved in the build up to Canadian attacker Olivia Smith's 91st minute winner.

Arsenal's final pre-season match is against Charlton Athletic on August 26.

The Addicks signed Australian trio Emily van Egmond, who marked a national record 170 international appearances during the AFC Women's Asian Cup, alongside fellow Matildas midfielder Leah Davidson and youth international Grace Johnston, following the club's promotion from the Women's Super League 2 in May.

Meanwhile, goalkeeper Jada Whyman is returning to A-League club Sydney FC after a stint in Sweden.

Whyman is yet to play for the Matildas but has been selected in multiple national squads.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

AAP

World.title: Exclusive CCTV captures the violence facing Coles workers
World.content:
For teenagers looking for their first job, an opportunity in retail is one of the most sought after gigs.

But in Victoria, retail workers are facing growing safety concerns.

In exclusive video obtained by 7.30 and captured during the past four months, CCTV shows shocking incidents of aggressive behaviour towards Coles staff and, at times, other customers.

In one instance, a customer was armed with a hammer and threatens a staff member as they were leaving the store, and in a second attack, a security guard was physically thrown into a check-out machine by a customer.

Loading...

Ruth Sumner, 70, has worked at Coles for 30 years. She said it was time the abuse against workers stopped.

"I enjoy my job. I'd just like to be able to do it without getting abused basically or worrying about whether somebody's going to come flying around the plaza with weapons," she said.

Ruth Sumner says she experiences verbal or physical abuse on a regular basis. (ABC News: Andrew Altree-Williams)

Last year, in a union survey of about 3,000 workers across Australia, 88 per cent of people said they had been verbally abused.

One in four said they had been physically attacked.

Ms Sumner says she feels anxious about her safety when she clocks on for a shift.

"The physical violence, irrespective of what anybody thinks, once is too much. Because once could end somebody's life," Ms Sumner said.

" I've seen aggression progress, especially since COVID. I thought people would come out kinder and they've actually, I don't understand, but their mentality is worse. "

Incidents have almost doubled in two years

Coles's chief operations and supply chain officer Matt Swindells said there had been a dramatic increase in abuse towards staff in Victoria.

"We've had rising instances of what we would call threatening situations, particularly towards our team members and particularly in Victoria over the last two years," he said.

"To give you some idea, they've grown 85 per cent in Victoria over that period.

"Whilst we call them threatening situations, what we really mean are either verbal assaults or physical altercations, or in some instances using product as a weapon, like a bottle of wine or a tin of tomatoes."

Matt Swindells says staff look after each other and protect customers before worrying about stock. (ABC News)

In comparison, Coles said threatening situations across the nation have increased by 65 per cent over the same period. South Australia is the only jurisdiction where it has declined by 16 per cent.

"We would have an internal system that can provide a text alert when incidents occurred, and my phone would go off repeatedly every day, which in itself is pretty sad," Mr Swindells said.

In Coles stores across Victoria, there are more security measures needed than in any other state, like body-worn cameras on staff and motion detection cameras in aisles.

There are also security guards who patrol the stores to keep the peace but only intervene in violence if it is safe to do so.

Coles staff in Victoria wear body-worn cameras to deter violence and most stores have motion security cameras in aisles to track customers. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

"There are clear standards that we have, and we work with our security team on what we expect," Mr Swindells said.

"At every moment, the intent of the team, whether it's security or Coles, is to look after each other, protect their customers and protect themselves before we start worrying about protecting stock and putting anyone at risk."

The main challenge for retailers in Victoria is the repeat offenders.

"They will come back, and at some point there has to be an intervention that's more than us over-servicing a customer or the police making an arrest and to come back out on bail within hours," Mr Swindells said.

"We're not here to uphold the law or to be the judge, jury or government, but we clearly would ask for faster support with the workplace protection orders so we can support the police."

Victoria Police has increased the number of police officers patrolling Melbourne's CBD to combat retail crime and anti-social behaviour.

Since March, Victoria Police have flooded the city with double the number of officers patrolling high-risk areas to tackle retail crime and anti-social behaviour. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Assistant Commissioner Jo Stafford told 7.30 arrests were up since March, with 260 arrests made for a range of offences from theft to assaults and public disorder.

But repeat offenders remain a challenge for police and Assistant Commissioner Stafford said the force would support measures that would target them.

"That is an issue for government, but in terms of any initiatives that help protect our workers, Victoria Police would be supportive of," she said.

Workplace protection orders in Victoria

Workplace protection orders are court-ordered bans on violent repeat offenders that restrict them from entering a retail store for a period of time.

Last month Victorian Premier Ben Carroll promised workplace protection orders would be in place across the state by July 2027.

Ben Carroll says the Workplace Protection Order scheme will be introduced to protect workers. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Victorian state secretary of the Shop, Distributive and Allied Employees Association Michael Donovan said the laws need to come into effect much sooner.

"Ideally, we would like to see it before Christmas. It's a very busy period, and there does tend to be a spike in customer abuse and violence," he said.

" This is a crisis and the government needs to address it. "

Michael Donovan says there tends to be a spike in abuse and violence during the Christmas period. (ABC News: Rachel Clayton)

Workplace protection orders are already in effect in the ACT and South Australia.

Mr Swindells said Coles welcomed the Victorian premier's announcement.

"South Australia implemented the same policy from start to finish in six months. So again, we know it can be done. We know it works," he said.

"We welcome the change from the government in Victoria. We would just ask for it to be accelerated."

For Ms Sumner, she is nearing the end of her professional life, but she is speaking out to protect the next generation of retail workers.

"If I drop dead tomorrow, I want to know that I've done something to make life better or help make life better for the people to come after us."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: 1000 One Nation voters said why they were voting for Hanson – and what it would take to switch
World.content:
Exclusive PoliticsFederalOne Nation 1000 One Nation voters said why they were voting for Hanson – and what it would take to switch Paul Sakkal August 25, 2026 — 12:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Immigration rather than living costs is the top concern for Australians who have flocked to One Nation, according to research that suggests Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition Leader Angus Taylor must convince voters they’ve cut migration if they are to claw back support. A survey of 1000 supporters of One Nation, run by pollster John Utting and Labor strategist Bruce Hawker, shows a key difference between supporters of One Nation and those of other parties is that 91 per cent believe the country is heading in the wrong direction. Among all voters, it is 62 per cent. The poll also maps out the split between Pauline Hanson’s loyal voters – true believers who back her no matter what – and newer supporters who revealed what it would take for them to switch their vote back to the Coalition – and far less likely, Labor. Of the One Nation backers who say the country is on the wrong track, 39 per cent name immigration as a reason. Australia’s border controls and cultural diversity has turned into a flashpoint as Labor scrambles to hit its targets and the Coalition jibes One Nation over its internal policy confusion. In all major polls over the past few years, inflation has reigned supreme as the top issue.



The research painted a picture of One Nation voters, showing they are slightly less well off than the average voter ($101,000 versus the average $109,000 income), more likely to live outside major cities, and 12 percentage points more likely to hold a trade certificate. The majority are men. Utting, who helped conduct Labor’s polling for many elections up to 2019, said that “migration is the real thing motivating One Nation supporters”. “Cost-of-living rhetoric is everywhere these days and people are a bit deadened to it. Migration is the real hotspot. Everyone has a cost of living plan and it is hard to get cut-through,” he said of the research, conducted between August 7 and August 12. The importance that voters place on Australia’s migration system and population, which has grown quicker than it has in other democracies this century, was demonstrated in this month’s Resolve Political Monitor. It found that more than half of voters across the spectrum believed the government was running the portfolio in an “unplanned and unmanaged way”.



Related Article Immigration Pauline Hanson’s deleted post deepens One Nation’s migration muddle Labor abruptly delayed a migration overhaul this month as it agonised over the economic and social consequences of reducing net overseas migration from about 300,000 to 225,000. The Coalition has also been at odds over migration, but Taylor has proposed to cut net migration to 175,000. Utting and Hawker, a key adviser to prime minister Kevin Rudd, conducted weeks of focus groups followed by a survey to understand what was driving Australia’s populist surge. They will present their research at Parliament House in Brisbane on Tuesday. The work was commissioned by the Labor-aligned TJ Ryan think tank. The poll finds that about half of One Nation’s supporters are totally committed to voting for the party at an election due in 2028. The rest, however, can be persuaded in a process Utting described as “chipping away at an iceberg as it comes out of the Antarctic”.



Hawker said of Hanson’s movement: “It’s moving away from just being a party of protest to one which has some pretty entrenched attitudes about the way Australia should be.” The most recent Resolve survey showed core support for Labor, the Coalition and One Nation remained unchanged, with Labor at 28 per cent, the opposition steady on 23 per cent and Hanson’s party on 26 per cent. Opposition MPs were pleased by a poll on Monday, published in Capital Brief and conducted by research firm Demos, showing the Coalition up four points and ahead of One Nation for the first time in many months. The Utting-Hawker survey showed Hanson’s backers detest Labor and Albanese himself. Overwhelmingly, the respondents say that the only thing that could draw them back to the major parties is if Albanese or Taylor developed bold plans to reduce migration. About 27 per cent said a united, credible Liberal Party would win them over, suggesting replacing Taylor with Liberal MP Andrew Hastie may be unwise after months of internal chaos in the Coalition. But two-thirds have barely heard from Taylor, underscoring his challenge with communication.



“One Nation’s rise is as much a story of Liberal failure as of One Nation success. Immigration and

the cost of living created the conditions. Labor is overwhelmingly rejected by these voters, and

the Liberals have not offered them a convincing alternative,” the research states. A critical finding is that One Nation voters are split over migration issues. An anonymous One Nation backer said: “I’m not against immigration. Because the moment you say anything, people assume the worst. My issue is the arithmetic. You can’t bring in that many people and not build the houses.” Another argued: “It isn’t the number so much. It’s who, and whether they want to be part of what’s here.”



Polling shows more than half of those who say they will vote for One Nation will not change their mind. Alex Ellinghausen Asked what they feared, 57 per cent of One Nation supporters said Australia’s culture and identity were changing too quickly while 40 per cent said housing and infrastructure were strained. One Nation’s newer supporters were more likely to take issue with the volume of migration, a view Hawker said was shared by many migrants. However, her more traditional support base believes the background of migrants is of greater concern. Hanson spoke in plain and sometimes incendiary terms about Muslim Australians after the Bondi attack in December, after which One Nation’s vote rose. Hawker said the split emphasised a broader misalignment between Hanson’s core support and her new, expanded base. On issues such as Hanson’s hard line on abortion and sacking lazy workers, the survey showed many of Hanson’s supporters did not agree with her, providing opportunity for her opponents. About 20 per cent of Hanson’s newer supporters said they could change their vote after Hanson’s positions on those issues – plus others such as her relationship with billionaire Gina Rinehart – were put to them. Only 4 per cent of her rusted-on base said the same.



“Within One Nation, there is a schism between those I’d call the long march veterans who

World.title: ‘Sydney needs more housing’: The church adding an eight-storey unit block
World.content:
PropertyNewsNSW residential property ‘Sydney needs more housing’: The church adding an eight-storey unit block Sue Williams August 25, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In an unprecedented act of faith, the Anglican church has teamed up with a private developer to deliver housing for sale in exchange for the resurrection of a local church and the provision of new parishioner, and community, spaces – and dozens more parishes are interested in following suit. Construction work begins on Tuesday on 48 luxury apartments in Sydney’s Lane Cove, on land adjoining the 1924 St Andrew’s Anglican Church that will be renovated and extended with a new 400-seat auditorium, offices and car parking. An artist’s impression of Finrose Residences in Lane Cove, on land adjoining St Andrew’s Church. It’s the first partnership between Anglicans and a private developer and could lead to a slew of others that use church land and buildings located close to suburban centres. “This is a good project that will provide community space that wouldn’t otherwise exist,” said the Anglican Bishop of North Sydney, Chris Edwards. “In addition, Sydney needs more housing, and we want to help.



“The church in Lane Cove is growing, and parishioners need a bigger building and more facilities, and the community needs more cultural spaces. By selling the airspace, we’ve ensured this is a win for everyone.” The Anglican Bishop of North Sydney, Chris Edwards, at the development site in Lane Cove. Janie Barrett The Anglican Church in Sydney has, in the past, redeveloped an old, disused church and land in Beacon Hill to build specialist social housing for young people with disabilities. It has also secured approval to build new apartments integrated with churches in Bankstown and Regents Park for single women over the age of 55, to be operated by its sister organisation, Anglicare. “But in the case of Lane Cove, unfortunately the finances didn’t stack up for social or affordable housing,” said Sydney Anglican Property chief executive Ross Jones. “The key driver was that the parish is growing out of its space, and it’s no longer fit for a modern ministry. “So we went into this first partnership with a developer, Traders in Purple, and we’d love it to be the beginning of many more. There is a community housing crisis, and we want to help provide a solution.”



The Anglicans have 270 parishes in the Sydney diocese, with 1000 properties, and at least 30 of those have already expressed interest in pursuing projects with developers. Five sites – in Five Dock, Marsden Park, Riverstone, Box Hill and Catherine Fields – are now in the pipeline. Related Article Renting ‘Grossly unaffordable’: Sydney rents hit record highs The Lane Cove project, the eight-storey, $800 million Finrose Residences, at the corner of Finlayson Street and Rosenthal Avenue, is the first off the block, with the two- and three-bedroom apartments starting at $2 million. Pre-sales have, so far, been strong, with the penthouse selling for $5.5 million, a new record for Lane Cove, which has a median unit price of about $950,000 and a house median exceeding $3 million, on Domain data. Traders in Purple executive director Charles Daoud said his company has developed former churches in the past, notably South Cronulla Uniting Church into residences The Abbey, and another disused church in Goulburn into homes.



“But this is the first time we’ve partnered with a church that’s continuing its use on the site,” he said. “It’s a church that’s over 100 years old, but we’ve been building for its future to make it ready for the next 100 years. Bishop Edwards (centre), with Ross Jones, chief executive of Sydney Anglican Property (left) and developer Charles Daoud (right) at the site. Janie Barrett “Often, these churches are located in really good parts of suburbs because you often start with the church, and the suburb is built around it. This project is a great development in an excellent location, near the new Metro and The Canopy, and having the oversight of the church is an excellent endorsement.” The developer also acquired two neighbouring houses and was thus able to turn those properties and the 200-seat church into the 400-seat auditorium, another hall and offices and ministry facilities, as well as the 48 apartments. “It’s a little like the Bible story of taking five loaves and two fish, and providing a great deal more,” Daoud said. “We usually like to provide some element of affordable housing in our developments, but that’s easier with taller buildings and more density.



“Instead, we’re delivering tens of millions of dollars’ worth of community infrastructure. This partnership has become something of a model for renewing assets, God willing, with an innovative way of funding it.” An artist’s impression of the Finrose Residences apartments, which start at $2 million. Research conducted last year revealed that churches in four states – NSW, Queensland, South Australia and Western Australia – own 28.4 square kilometres of land, including 2430 sites within 800 metres of railway stations. Amanda Bailey, chief executive of the Faith Housing Australia alliance, which conducted the research with consultants Suburbtrends, says Sydney Anglicans have been a trailblazer in terms of developing land and old assets for all alliance members – Christian, Jewish and Muslim. “It’s a growing movement across Australia, and all faiths, to want to provide more housing,” Bailey said. “So many are providing social and affordable housing where there’s sufficient federal and state government subsidies available to make those projects stack up.



“But many of our not-for-profit faith organisations are cash-poor and have to take care of heritage assets which are very expensive to maintain, and the DA [development application] process can be very expensive and time-consuming.” An artist’s impression of the garden for residents of Finrose in Lane Cove. As well, many of the church, synagogue and mosque sites are zoned as “social infrastructure”, which doesn’t permit residential housing, Bailey says, but talks are ongoing between FHA and the Department of Planning to remedy the situation. Meanwhile, interest remains strong for Finrose apartments. Exercise physiologist Lynn Woodward, 57, and her husband, Gianni Totani, 60, who live in nearby Riverview, have bought a two-bedroom unit off the plan, planning to downsize later. “We want a low-maintenance lifestyle, and the location is just perfect, within walking distance to everywhere,” Woodward said. “I’m a Catholic, so I won’t be going to the church, but the auditorium is great and can be used by all groups.”

World.title: Data centre pipeline doubles as national power use to rise 40% over decade
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaData centres Data centre pipeline doubles as national power use to rise 40% over decade Kieran Rooney August 25, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The number of Australian data centres in development has doubled since 2025, but their strain on the nation’s power supply is expected to accelerate even further over the next decade. The rapid growth of the artificial intelligence industry has resulted in data centres accounting for 3 per cent of the nation’s energy consumption. However, their demand will grow to 13 per cent by 2035, according to the market operator’s latest report into the stability of the grid. On Tuesday, the Australian Energy Market Operator (AEMO) will release its Electricity Statement of Opportunities report providing a 10-year outlook on whether there will be enough energy to meet demand and how reliable the network will be. The completed first stage of a West Footscray data centre. Joe Armao A copy of the document released to The Age ahead of its official publication forecasts consumption across the National Electricity Market will grow by more than 40 per cent, jumping from 176 terawatt hours in 2025-26 to 250 terawatt hours in 2035-26. This figure excludes energy consumed by homes and businesses “behind the meter” from their own solar and battery systems.



The increase will be driven by the electrification of homes, businesses and industries, as well as the rise of data centres which have become a political flashpoint in Australia and abroad. Related Article Data centres Labor facing internal revolt over data centre spree AI companies rely on the centres for their business models, sparking a flurry of interest from governments and developers seeking to cash in on the massive investment. They have also sparked environmental issues and pushback from local communities. AEMO’s report estimates there are 225 data centres in development this year, up from 97 in 2025. Electricity consumption from data centres is forecast to be almost seven times higher by 2035, increasing from 5 terawatt hours now to 34 terawatt hours. This mean they would use 13 per cent of power supplied to the system, compared with 3 per cent now.



However, AEMO noted there was a stark difference between the number and scale of proposed data centres, and what ended up being delivered. AEMO found that 36 per cent of known projects listed in 2025 went on to be cancelled, including those that had agreements in place to connect to the grid. And the centres that were operational during the first three months of 2026 used only 26 per cent of the total energy capacity to which they had access. Loading Adding to the expected squeeze on the system, about 15 gigawatts of power generation from coal and gas will be lost over the decade as electricity usage rises at a rapid rate. This includes the anticipated closure of power stations at Yallourn in 2028, Gladstone and Eraring in 2029 and Loy Yang A in 2035. But AEMO’s outlook was positive about whether the grid could handle the increased consumption for the rest of this decade, and it did not forecast any reliability gaps, where demand outstrips supply, out to 2030.



This has been driven by 9 gigawatts of storage and generation that entered the system at full capability last financial year, a doubling of the year before. Another 40 gigawatts of projects are anticipated or committed to be delivered by the early 2030s, more than half the current 77-gigawatt capacity of the National Electricity Market. AEMO chief executive Daniel Westerman said the report showed continued investment was needed, but things were looking better for the grid. Related Article Energy Power struggle: Coalition pledge to scrap towers sparks bill warning “The reliability outlook has improved, supported by record levels of new generation and storage, and a strong pipeline of projects expected over the next decade,” he said.



“As electricity demand continues to grow and ageing generation retires, continued investment in generation, storage, transmission and consumer energy resources will be needed to maintain reliability.” Gaps are forecast after the early 2030s as demand grows and more coal-fired stations retire. Westerman said another wave of investment would be vital to ensuring reliable electricity supply was maintained over this period. Editor's pick Exclusive

Melbourne Demons Demons accused of wage theft and probity breaches by former CEO Energy Minister Chris Bowen said AEMO had made it clear they needed to keep building but the report supported the pipeline of projects under way.



“This is what getting on with the energy transition looks like, with record amounts of new generation and storage being built and connected, strengthening reliability as ageing coal-fired power stations approach their retirement dates,” he said. World.title: Tax attack: big business to serve it up to PM over dinner after Labor’s budget changes
World.content:
PoliticsFederalFederal budget Tax attack: big business to serve it up to PM over dinner after Labor’s budget changes Paul Sakkal August 24, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Big business is plotting a union-style campaign to convince “Betty from Blacktown” that Australia’s hard-to-grasp productivity problem hits family budgets, as corporate leaders put Prime Minister Anthony Albanese on notice at an annual get-together of political and business elite. After years of claims that it has been hoodwinked into close co-operation by Labor, the Business Council of Australia has joined 30 peak bodies, including pharmacists, farmers, builders and accountants, to make a louder argument for economic reforms that lead to better living standards. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese speaks with the BCA’s chief executive Bran Black (centre) and president Geoff Culbert in 2024. Wolter Peeters The new Alliance of Industry Associations is considering an online campaign that would begin next year and run up to the 2028 election, according to sources familiar with the plans. The moves are driven in part by anxiety about left-wing populist influencers generating support for higher taxes and heavier regulations on social media, which is feeding through to policymaking. With Prime Minister Anthony Albanese sitting in the crowd at Tuesday night’s annual BCA dinner, the organisation’s chief executive Bran Black will say: “Where we believe policies are taking our nation in the wrong direction, the BCA will say so”.



“Australia cannot tax, regulate or redistribute its way to higher living standards,” he said, according to speech notes. Related Article GST PM backs GST deal, leaves future taxpayers on the hook for billions Black argues that “Betty from Blacktown” cares little about productivity partly because “productivity and investment [are] words that belong to someone else’s conversation”. But the average voter does care about the cost of living, Black says, creating an imperative to explain how macro factors make it harder to get by. “Too often, we collectively fail to explain why it matters, and critically, why its absence or reduction affects people’s lives day to day.” This year’s BCA dinner will be held three months after Labor’s ambitious reform budget, which scrapped negative gearing and overhauled the way capital gains are taxed. A downturn in house prices – predicted to hit up to 15 per cent – and warnings that tax changes might sap investment in high-growth firms at a time of weak investment have sparked one of the most incendiary fights between Labor and the corporate sector since Albanese came to power in 2022.



Albanese will also address the dinner but Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, who hopes to recruit big business to his fight against Labor’s budget measures, will be absent as he cycles through Queensland in the Pollie Pedal charity event. The prime minister will not mention Labor’s heavily debated tax changes in the segment of his speech provided to this masthead on Monday. Instead, he will talk up an area of agreement with the corporate world: artificial intelligence. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese with Business Council of Australia chief executive Bran Black. Max Mason-Hubers Albanese, whose headline speech on AI was warmly welcomed by corporations last month, will seek support for his rules on data centres’ use of energy and water at a national cabinet meeting on Wednesday. National consensus on AI, which the Coalition has backed, will be key to driving growth and sovereignty, the prime minister will argue. “Our national economic success and strongly performing national institutions will help us see off the populist challenge now on the march across the globe,” he will say, alluding to One Nation.



“Australia’s economy and democracy are in an excellent place. By working intelligently together, we will keep them there.” Black will call for “balance” between safety and innovation in the government’s approach to AI. Related Article Exclusive

Data centres Labor and Coalition unite to ringfence AI from One Nation backlash Independent MP Allegra Spender, who co-founded the party Community Strong Australia in June, on Monday pleaded with Labor to rethink its CGT changes. Spender wants the government to come up with another way to make the CGT discount less generous. Instead of the old 50 per cent discount, Spender said Labor should pick a lower, flat discount, rather than an inflation-adjusted model that critics say will hamper growth. “The government deserves credit for taking on tax reform, but I am concerned with their approach to CGT, and I will continue to urge them to commit to return all taxes raised as marginal income tax cuts. Their preferred inflation-adjustment method for CGT is inappropriate for businesses and for rewarding risk-taking more broadly,” she said.



“If we want to effectively combat inflation and sustainably grow Australians’ real wages in the future, then we need to find ways to lift productivity. In a globally competitive market for talent and capital we need a regime that is broadly competitive and doesn’t discourage risk-taking more than other countries.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: How a personal pitch from the PNG prime minister helped seal Manu’s NRL return
World.content:
Updated SportNRLNRL 2026 How a personal pitch from the PNG prime minister helped seal Manu’s NRL return Dan Walsh Updated August 24, 2026 — 9:30pm ,first published August 24, 2026 — 7:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A personal sales pitch from Papua New Guinea Prime Minister James Marape helped seal Joey Manu’s return to rugby league, which is expected to begin with a short-term 2027 deal at an NRL rival before he takes up a two-year deal with the PNG Chiefs from 2028. The Kiwi international’s long-touted signing with the expansion franchise was confirmed on Monday morning. Loading Manu has already been offered to several NRL clubs as a potential short-term signing for the back half of 2027 once he completes the final year of his estimated €1 million ($1.6 million) contract with French rugby outfit Racing 92. He will be 31 by the time he links with PNG for their first pre-season late next year, and the Chiefs can see an advantage in Manu joining an NRL rival as a pre-June 30 signing, as was raised by the Warriors earlier this season.



Manu ultimately knocked back that approach to ensure he didn’t jeopardise his lucrative rugby deal. But his appeal and pedigree as a potential game-breaker in next year’s title race have been noted at several clubs spoken to by this masthead on Monday after his PNG move was announced. A $300,000 sign-on figure for a three-month return was reported earlier this year as a fair market value, according to the NRL salary cap auditor for the Kiwi star; it would equate to a $1.2 million salary. Former Rooster Joey Manu and his family – pictured at Port Moresby airport – toured the Chiefs facilities earlier this year. His signature comes as the Chiefs continue to reshape a volatile player market, with Hudson Young to begin formal talks with PNG next month despite Canberra tabling him a record $3.3 million, three-year extension offer – the richest deal in the club’s history. The Chiefs are also in talks with Titans star AJ Brimson after he was given permission to explore an early exit from the Gold Coast.



Speaking from France after committing to PNG as their seventh signing, Manu said Marape’s passion for bringing an NRL side to the wider Pacific region had helped sway him, while he had also been impressed by the Chiefs’ Port Moresby facilities. “Talking to the [PNG] prime minister, how passionate he was about making it not just a Papua New Guinea team but making it a Pacific team, and trying to get the Pacific nations behind this team, I think it’s going to be special,” Manu said. Joey Manu left the NRL as one of the best players in the game. NRL Imagery “I’m a really proud Cook Island and Māori man, and I know my family’s real proud back in Tokoroa in New Zealand – and also in the Cook Islands, too. “There’s so much talent in the Pacific Islands and rugby league is taking over the islands, so it’s really cool to have sort of a Pacific team.”



The Australian government’s much-discussed $600 million funding package around the club sets aside as much as $350 million in rugby league pathways development programs across PNG, Fiji, Samoa and Tonga, according to a Senate estimates committee hearing held last year. Related Article Analysis

NRL 2026 Good luck, NRL rivals. The Warriors can now stay in NZ until grand final week Manu looms as a potential fullback option given he regularly wore the No.1 for New Zealand at Test level. A rugby league return at centre – where he was widely regarded as the best in the game throughout a 181-game career with the Roosters – may be more suitable, though, given his age and the added running required of fullbacks under the NRL’s new set-restart rules. “It’s just been a few years now since I’ve been out of the game, and I still watch a few games when I can,” Manu said.



“You miss certain things when you’re watching, and I’m just grateful that I get to come back and play. Rugby league is a special game for myself and to come back and play in the NRL is very special.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: A piece o’ cord for bouncers
World.content:
“Adding to the ridiculous practice of establishments requiring a tie for entry (C8), in the late ’60s I was denied entry to the Chatswood Charles Hotel. They stated I needed a tie,” says Max Redmayne of Drummoyne. “My response was to take a shoelace and create a bow tie, and yes, that was acceptable, which points to the ludicrous practice.”

“During the 1997 Australian Professional Sumo Tour I was deputised by Wide World of Sports to take two sumo wrestlers to Eagle Farm racecourse for a day out and to present the trophy for the main race,” writes Katrina Watts of Murwillumbah. “They wore traditional cotton yukata (kimono) and zori (straw sandals). As they were greeted and ushered into the members enclosure I heard a dapper gent comment, ‘Just a minute, those two men can’t come in here. They are in dresses, have no ties and are wearing thongs!’”

Of course there are some establishments that secede from a typical dress code, as evidenced by Denis O’Calahan of Auckland, New Zealand: “In 1976, I was in Dallas, Texas, for training. They took us out to a restaurant called The Traildust where the sign on the door said ‘No Neckties’. If anyone tried to enter wearing a tie, a waiter would come out with a huge pair of scissors and cut it off. The walls were decorated with hundreds of the cut-off ties.”

James White of Beverage (Vic) reckons the media have blown the gig: “Whose cage do I rattle to get the news out that last weekend, Boyd Excell won his eighth consecutive title at the Four-in-Hand World Championship in Europe? He is a spectacular competitor in a sport that is spectacular But nothing in the news.”

“In the early 1970s, I was refused admission to Eastern Suburbs Leagues Club due to my hair being over my collar,” recalls Geoff Genford of Hurlstone Park.“I didn’t feel so bad when I read that hirsute star player and former rugby union international Russell Fairfax was taken into the club to sign his contract via the tradesman’s entrance.” Margaret Bellingham Holle of Woollahra remembers it, too.

World.title: ‘Could see myself sitting here’: One Nation MP Farley gatecrashes Liberal meeting
World.content:
One Nation MP David Farley has fuelled speculation about his future in Pauline Hanson’s party after accidentally walking into a private meeting of more than 20 Liberal MPs – then telling them he could see himself sitting with them. The extraordinary encounter happened in Parliament House last Wednesday when Farley wandered into a regular meeting of Liberal MPs from marginal seats. Several Liberals present said the Farrer MP took a while to realise he was in the wrong room before turning to leave. Farrer MP David Farley during his swearing-in on June 2. Alex Ellinghausen “I could see myself sitting here,” Farley told the MPs, before walking out. “We were all taken aback, to be honest,” one Liberal MP said. “It was a very loose thing to say.”



Farley confirmed the incident on Monday, but portrayed it as an off-the-cuff joke after accidentally entering the room. Editor's pick Immigration Every morning, a grandmother wakes 11 children. Their parents are thousands of kilometres away He said the Liberal MPs had a “who-hit-John” look on their faces, silent with their mouths open, before he “filled the empty space with my quip” and left. Liberal MP Andrew Hastie said Farley was currently a member of One Nation “but certainly let’s see what the future holds”. “He’s a decent fellow, I’ve met him a couple of times,” Hastie told ABC’s 7.30.



The remark comes at an awkward time for One Nation, with Farley again publicly at odds with Hanson over one of the party’s central political issues. The Farrer MP told ABC’s Insiders that while One Nation wanted to reduce net overseas migration to 130,000, it would allow another 100,000 migrant workers through skilled visas, backpacker programs and the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme. That would put the effective number at about 230,000 – broadly in line with Labor’s forecast of 225,000 by 2027–28. Hanson moved quickly to reject Farley’s interpretation, insisting One Nation’s policy was to cut net overseas migration to 130,000, with some short-term agricultural workers excluded from the official measure. One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Farley, pictured on May 13, don’t see eye to eye on the party’s net overseas migration figure. Alex Ellinghausen



One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce was then sent out to clean up the mess, telling Sunrise that Farley had simply got it wrong. “Show me a political career where people haven’t made a mistake, and I’ll show you a person who’s not told the truth.” Joyce said One Nation had seemingly raised the matter with Farley but refused to elaborate. “Oh, look, I’m not going to throw anybody under a bus,” he said. “When people are new in parliament, they can sometimes get things incorrect, and that’s what happens. God knows I’ve done it enough.” “I think [Farley] would have been offended by [One Nation’s head of operations] James Ashby going on News24 last night with a mop and essentially mocking what I thought were his thoughtful contributions on [ABC’s] Insiders yesterday,” Hastie said.



Hastie was referring to Ashby’s appearance on News24 on Sunday night where he brandished a mop and clarified One Nation’s migration policies, stating he’d spoken to Farley and that “people make mistakes”. “For a new member of parliament, it’s always difficult getting your head around those [net overseas migration] numbers,” Ashby said. Farley’s comments were also savaged by online news site One News Australia, which branded his appearance a “rookie blunder” and claimed his “clueless” performance had given Labor an “escape route” from its migration policy. The criticism is notable given One News Australia’s origins as the One Nation Supporters Network before it was rebranded as a news organisation. The site and the party say they have no affiliation, although its coverage is strongly pro-One Nation and Hanson. Farley was previously counselled by Hanson during the Farrer byelection campaign after he agreed a net migration figure of 306,000 last year was “probably not” too many.



The pair also exchanged harsh words after it was revealed that he’d previously tried to seek preselection with Labor for the seat and not informed anyone within One Nation before it was revealed by this masthead. Related Article Immigration Pauline Hanson’s deleted post deepens One Nation’s migration muddle Farley has already shown he is prepared to depart from Hanson’s position in the parliament. Last week he voted with the Coalition on an amendment to Labor’s wagering legislation, despite Hanson having previously committed to supporting the government’s ban on foreign matched lotteries. His growing independence is being watched closely by Coalition MPs, particularly given his conservative and agricultural background.



Sources in the Coalition said Opposition Leader Angus Taylor knew Farley from his time as an agribusiness leader and could potentially use the relationship to court him in future, although there are no immediate plans to do so. “He is a Nat or a country Liberal, not a populist,” one Liberal MP said. Farley told Insiders he came from the conservative LNP tradition, joined the Nationals after returning to Farrer and later explored joining Labor and running as an independent. He ultimately chose One Nation because he said it offered the “political courage” and “tenacity” he wanted. “I have the full support of the party to pursue what I’m doing, especially for Farrer,” he said.
